subsubtopic: MEETING IN ABUJA, NIGERIA-TABLING OF LETTERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 32, I would like to lay upon the table three documents emanating from the recent meeting of the Commonwealth Committee of Foreign Ministers dealing with southern Africa which met in Abuja, Nigeria, on May 16 and 17.
I would like to table the concluding statement of that meeting, a copy of the Abuja commitment that was signed at that meeting and the text of a letter sent to the foreign ministers of the European Community and the foreign ministers of the G-7 signed by the nine ministers who are members of the Commonwealth committee on events in southern Africa.
With the indulgence of the House, I might perhaps ask members to pay particular heed to the letter, a quite
extraordinary document, signed by nine ministers sent to members of the European Community and the G-7 setting forth our view on the appropriateness of maintaining sanctions now in place with respect to South Africa.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the honour to lay upon the table a petition signed by numerous electors of Sarnia and other places in Ontario. This petition is being submitted pursuant to Standing Order 36.
The signers of this petition object to the GST because they consider it unfair and regressive, and they call upon Parliament to reject it.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Let us do it now!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have here a petition signed by numerous residents of the electoral riding of Ottawa-Vanier; this petition was circulated in the riding by way of circulars, and it is meant to express strong disagreement with the government's proposed goods and services tax.
These Canadians fear that the proposed tax will have an inflationary impact and will decrease our ability as Canadians, to maintain our standard of living. They therefore humbly submit a proposal to the effect that this House, and this Parliament in particular, reject the proposal to impose on Canadians a 7 per cent goods and services tax beginning in January 1991.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is also my honour and privilege to submit a petition pursuant to Standing Order 36. This petition is signed by a number of residents of the riding of Kingston and the Islands, who, since the last election, have been so well represented in this House by my distinguished and erudite colleague.

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
I would like to voice my support for this petition which the electors of Kingston and the Islands have signed to ask the Conservative Government to withdraw its proposed goods and services tax forthwith.
I am convinced, Madam Speaker, that we could all make up our minds immediately and withdraw this tax which is so regressive. Let us do it now!

Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure today to present, pursuant to Standing Order 36, a further petition signed by people in my riding from such places as Osoyoos, Penticton, Summerland, as well as other places in the province of British Columbia such as Hope and Kelowna.
These are a further 163 names that I am adding to the thousands of names on petitions which I have already placed before the House from people within British Columbia asking this government to reject the current proposal for the goods and services tax. This petition asks the government to cease with its proposal that would shift the tax burden on to ordinary Canadians-through a regressive consumption tax instead of through real tax reform.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the commentary from the other side of the House on the competence of our members who should all be ministers.
I rise today to address you, Madam Speaker, on the issue of abortion, one of the most controversial and divisive issues in society today, an issue about which we all have very different views.
Government Orders
As colleagues and parliamentarians, our roles have been challenged as never before on the subject of abortion.
We have been challenged by the strongly held views of our constituents and by the debates which have occurred over every element of the physical, intellectual, moral and spiritual aspects of abortion.
The members who sat on the legislative committee on abortion heard arguments from individuals and groups representing all sides of the debate.
The arguments advanced by the proponents of free choice as well as by the representatives of the pro life movements were founded on principles and were convincing.
As individuals, our views on abortion are no less strong than those of the voters whom we represent or of the lobby groups defending a particular position.
In fact, certain ministers and members have publicly expressed their personal views on this matter, and rightly so.

As parliamentarians, we are all aware of our duty to act not in our own interests, but in the interests of those we represent.
Given the diversity of beliefs held, there are those who might question whether it is possible to find some common ground to meet the expectations of Canadians in our role as representatives of the Canadian people.
The Supreme Court of Canada stated in the Morgen-taler case that while the function of the Supreme Court is to review legislation in order to determine if a particular legislative balance of interests was consistent with constitutional guarantees, it is up to parliament, first, to strike that balance.
Two years have passed since the Supreme Court declared the former abortion law unconstitutional. All three majority judgments of the court concurred that Section 251 of the Criminal Code, which had been the law for 19 years, was a violation of the security of the person and the principles of fundamental justice as guaranteed under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
In so stating, the highest court in the land has recognized that there is a balance to be made in society between what they describe as the state's interest in the foetus and the rights of a woman.
It is our job to strike that balance.

Despite the problems this represents, it is possible for us, as parliamentarians, to find a common ground on which to meet the expectations of Canadians.
If we hope to find this common ground, it is very important for us to understand that the legislation will necessarily reflect more than one viewpoint.
When we speak of common ground, we are not necessarily speaking of a compromise, but rather of coming to some sort of arrangement. An accommodation on such a thorny issue as abortion is extremely difficult for those who were involved in the drafting of the proposed legislation.
Nevertheless, Bill C-43 is the end result of a marvelous exercise in parliementary responsibility, in that it reflects the different viewpoints and interests of society, while upholding constitutional guarantees.

I have enormous respect for the process by which this bill was created and for what it represents in terms of common ground.
Very often, as I said in my speech at second reading, we have shared common ground, but for very different reasons.
Bill C-43, in my view, is a remarkable creation and a tribute to those who put it together.
We have been elected to provide leadership in dealing with the situation we now face.
As the Prime Minister said in his speech before you in November of 1989, "we must achieve a solution that is philosophically sound, constitutionally correct, politically acceptable and administratively practicable; that is, a solution which can be understood and implemented".
Bill C-43 exemplifies such a solution.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare, who has been a committed supporter of the pro-life position over the years, supports Bill C-43.
In the debate on second reading I explained why I, committed to pro-choice, was able to support the bill before the House.
I remain confident that Bill C-43 reflects a balance of the views of the Canadian people and protects their vital interests in a way that will be acceptable to the majority of Canadians.
I would now like to present a brief overview of Bill C-43.
The government has proceeded by using the criminal law power because this bill is primarily related to the protection of fundamental values, reflecting our commitment to the protection of life, health, human dignity, equality, and social order.
Criminal law embodies deeply held social values and attempts to balance them with the rights of individuals. It is therefore appropriate that we deal with the abortion issue within a legal framework which is based on these considerations.
All of the judges of the majority, in the Morgentaler case, recognized the usual purpose of the Criminal Code provisions relating to abortion, that is, the protection of the life and health of the woman, and the protection of the foetus.

The justices also acknowledged the validity of the legislative objective aimed at offering this protection. Mr. Justice Beetz stated that it was a valid objective in Canadian criminal law.
The Supreme Court of Canada showed that it was mindful of the role of the legislative branch. We realize that the legislative balance we are seeking will be examined by the courts to ensure that it is consistent with the Charter. However, we must first begin by assuming our responsibilities in the democratic process and seeking out this balance.
However imperfect it may be, the legislative process is still the best way to achieve a consensus. We cannot refuse to do our duty, which is to resolve this matter. Nor can we force the courts to do our job for us.

I wish to emphasize that provinces cannot stiffen the criminal law, nor can they weaken it. The criminal legislation should enable us to establish a uniform

standard for all of Canada, something that does not exist at the present time in the area of abortion.
Abortion has been put into the Criminal Code in order to balance and protect throughout the pregnancy the rights of the woman who seeks an abortion and the societal interest in the protection of the foetus.
It is thoughtless and misleading to say that Bill C-43 is making criminals out of women and doctors. This bill prohibits a number of specific activities: abortions performed by non-medical practitioners who may carry out abortions under unsanitary and unsafe conditions, abortions performed without forming an opinion as to the health grounds, the unlawful sale of unauthorized abor-tifacients, toxic devices or equipment used to induce abortions, and self-induced abortions.
To understand the effects of Bill C-43 on access to abortion, it is necessary to appreciate its implications for clarifying and helping to establish a national standard of entitlement to abortion.
The provision of abortion services as a health care issue falls under the jurisdiction of the provinces. Thus, it is the responsibility of each province and territory to deal with access to abortion services.
The federal government does not have the jurisdiction to regulate health practices in Canada.
Nevertheless, this bill does assist in providing access.
Not only does it lack a number of legal impediments that existed under the old law, such as therapeutic abortion committees, restrictions on which doctors could perform abortions, and hospital requirements, but it also improves upon the current situation.
Bill C-43 will give the provinces the guidance they have asked for on the legal framework and national approach to entitlement to abortion.

From a constitutional perspective, I would like to point out that the provision of health care services is not regulated under the Canada Health Act. Rather, this act is a financial statute adopted pursuant to the federal government's spending power.
Government Orders
To suggest that it would be possible to incorporate in the Canada Health Act a provision ensuring access to abortion services is wrong. This reflects a poor understanding of Canada's constitutional reality.
The federal government does not have the power to regulate the provision of health care services. The definition of "health", which includes physical, mental and psychological health, is consistent with the Supreme Court ruling in the Morgentaler case according to which the provisions of Section 7 of the Charter respecting the security of the person include physical and psychological security.
It is important to look at health as it relates to the human being as a whole. The circumstances which compel a woman to seek an abortion will most certainly be taken into account by the medical practitioner when he or she arrives at a decision and determines whether not performing an abortion is likely to threaten the physical, mental or psychological health of the woman.
This decision by the medical practitioner is not an abstract one. Rather, it takes into consideration the personal situation of the woman.
This approach allows the medical practitioner to examine all the repercussions, should he or she decide not to perform the abortion, and not only to consider the effects that continuing the pregnancy would have.
The foetus is protected throughout the pregnancy because of the non-gestational approach of the bill. Those who oppose abortion do not wish to see gestational limits in the legislation because such limits suggest a varying value of human life at different times of pregnancy. Those who favour a woman's choice view gestational limits as unnecessary and based on the myth that women seek abortions late in pregnancy when, in actual fact, 89 per cent of abortions are performed in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.
The bill achieves protection for the foetus in the Criminal Code which generally protects fundamental social values. The bill does not allow for abortion on demand since specific health grounds must be met. Only therapeutic abortions are permitted based on health grounds and a doctor's opinion.

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
The generally accepted standards of the medical profession apply to any opinion formed by a doctor. The decision a doctor makes is an opinion formed in good faith as required by the canon of medical ethics of the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada.
The Canadian Medical Association has expressed a concern that the doctors of Canada will be under a fear of prosecution if this bill becomes law. Doctors should not be afraid. I would suggest that what this bill describes as legal behaviour is nothing more than good medical practice. It must be remembered that the responsibilities of doctors under the terms of Bill C-43 are similar to their responsibilities under the former legislation.
The veiy real difference from the old law is that no extraneous administrative procedures or outside opinions are required. Under the new bill the doctor will apply accepted medical standards in order to decide whether or not to induce an abortion, how and where to do so, and whether or not to seek outside opinions.

Given all the benefits of the bill that I have outlined for you, I believe that Bill C-43 is the best legislative formula and that it can stand up to any legal challenge based on the Charter.
It achieves a balance reflecting the concerns raised by the Supreme Court.
The bill provides that the decision to have an abortion or not is based on health reasons.
A person desiring an abortion must consult a physician, as for any other medical procedure.
The definition of "health" is broad and allows taking into consideration all factors essential to the protection of the woman's right to security of her person.

But the Supreme Court did not speak only of a woman's rights under the Charter. There were a number of references to the importance of the protection of the foetus by all.
Madam Justice Bertha Wilson who wrote one of the reasons for judgment said in the Morgentaler case: "The situation respecting a woman's right to control her own
person becomes more complex when she becomes pregnant and some statutory control may be appropriate."
In introducing Bill C-43 we have made a very careful effort to comply with constitutional requirements and we believe that the proposed bill would be a workable law within constitutional parameters.
The federal government cannot prevent people from attempting civil actions since civil actions are governed by provincial law. However, in the Daigle decision the Supreme Court of Canada gave a strong indication against the availability of civil actions to prevent women from exercising their rights.

Private prosecutions are extremely rare in this field.
Anyone can lay charges under a provision of the Criminal Code.
However, the attorney general in each province has the power to suspend proceedings in a case where the private prosecution is undertaken for frivolous or malicious motives or is not in the public interest.
In light of past experience and the requirements for evidence for charges laid under this provision, an unfounded lawsuit is very unlikely.

As the Minister of National Health and Welfare has made clear, there is no intention that this bill be used to harass Canadian women or doctors. Aside from the factors I have just mentioned which make such harassment highly improbable, attempts to abuse the criminal process themselves incur severe legal penalties.

Many Canadians did not hesitate to express their various interests, which occasionally reflected contrary opinions.
We respect their opinions.
Nevertheless, we must assert our responsibilities and fill the void created by such divergent views.
If we are unable to achieve this balance, we are not meeting our responsibilities as representatives of the people.
May 24, 1990



Earlier I spoke of leadership in our roles as parliamentarians. Leadership means having the courage to bring forward an abortion bill which seeks to answer the concerns of Canadians. Parliament is not perfect but each of us comes here as a representative of Canadian people with particular outlooks. If we take our responsibilities seriously, we will not simply be advocates of one particular position but we will recognize that the most important issues in our society are not always black and white.

Our work as elected members requires us to try to "square the circle" and seek common ground.
This bill is remarkable evidence of the finest parliamentary tradition and we have the required expertise to find the common ground on which Parliament can pass a law on this most controversial issue.

We may not be imbued with all wisdom and knowledge in this endeavour, but there can be no doubt that we have given every ounce of our energy to arriving at a suitable solution and we have fulfilled our duty in addressing the issue of abortion in the best interests of Canadians.
My colleagues and I are convinced that this bill comes closer than any practical alternative in a moderate, practicable and balanced solution. It is philosophically sound, constitutionally valid and workable. I would ask that you support Bill C-43 and vote in favour of its successful passing into law.

Madam Speaker, I listened very carefully to the Minister of Justice and her rationale for the government proceeding with this bill.
She said that the bill is in the interests of those whom we, as members of this House of Commons, represent. I would like to comment that by reducing access for women who are seeking abortion by throwing this issue back into the courts of this country, which is sure to happen as women have already said, and by agonizing doctors and women in this country, I do not believe is in the interests of those we represent.
Government Orders
She talked about a balance of views. Whose views, Madam Speaker? Sixty-two per cent of Canadians in an Environics poll in November said they did not want criminal legislation on abortion. The majority of Canadians are opposed to it. She said we cannot refuse to perform our duties as legislators. I would say to the Minister of Justice that we do have a duty. Those of us, particularly those of us who are women and have articulated a position in favour of the integrity of Canadian women, have also a duty to those women. The minister has articulated that position in the past and she is now reversing that position.
Our role should be to do something effective about this issue, to do something that is truly effective and compassionate about unwanted pregnancies. Of course, that would be to support families and research into family planning, to support research into safe and effective methods of contraception, to support women and children and not to throw this bill into the Criminal Code.
She said it was misleading to say that Bill C-43 criminalizes women and doctors but it is not. That is what this bill does. She talked about national entitlement. The constitutional experts and the lawyers in the universities across this country have written to her and said that this is legal nonsense. They have said that she is relying on jurisprudence that is 20 years out of date as far as federal paramountcy goes.
My final comment is that the minister said she was committed to the pro-choice position in this country. I would like to ask her, in view of supporting this legislation and in view of standing in this House last night and voting in opposition to the only pro-choice amendment that was before this House, how can she stand here and tell Canadian women and the people of this country that she is committed to pro-choice?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am quite pleased to say that I am committed to the pro-choice position and have been. The point that I have made is that I think this bill is consistent with the pro-choice position. The hon. member has made a number of comments which I would like to address but I realize that there is limited time.
One thing that I would like to point out though is that she makes reference to lawyers' opinions which have challenged my view on the relationship of this bill to other legislation. First of all, those opinions which were commissioned have never been provided to me. People

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
have felt free to call into question ray competence and integrity without providing to me the opinions on which those were based. I have succeeded in getting some of them, not all of them, and I understand that the group which commissioned the opinion is not circulating the opinion which happens to agree with me.
I would refer the hon. member to the footnote of Mr. Bruce Ryder's opinion which in fact makes the point. All I have said with respect to the relationship between this bill and provincial legislation is that I believe that this bill will make it more difficult for provinces to use their jurisdiction in ways that will reduce access to abortion. I believe the effect of actually having a federal law on the books is a positive one and will be taken into account by the courts.
One of the opinions that was solicited, and I refer the hon. member to it, in fact makes that point. I suggest most of the opinions are worthless because they address things that I have never said. By parodying my views, of course you can solicit whatever opinion you want.
Mr. Ryder makes the point in footnote 14 or 16 of his views, quoting Professor Peter Hogg, who is one of the great authorities on Canadian constitutional law, in a line of authority that culminated in the Westendorp case, which is still good law in Canada. It is a Supreme Court of Canada decision of 1983. He says perhaps in theory the courts should not take into account the existence or absence of a federal law in determining the validity of provincial law, but in practice the case law shows that the presence of a federal law does, in fact, influence the courts in determining the validity of provincial law.
That is the point that I have made. It is a point well founded in the law of Canada, in the 1983 decision of the Supreme Court of Canada, which has not been departed from by the Supreme Court of Canada. I am quite content to allow the courts to vindicate me in that view because it is a well-founded view. I assign no value whatever to legal opinions which attempt to challenge views that are a parody of what I have said, as opposed to a realistic representation of what I have said.
The hon. member says that 62 per cent of Canadians have said they do not want criminal law in this area. Most Canadians do not understand the division of powers in this country and the limited authority that the federal government has because, in fact, a majority of Canadians have said they would prefer to see some legal framework.
The only constitutional power that we can use to do that is the criminal law power and the criminal law power is a very important power of this Parliament. It enables this Parliament to do some very important things and there are many every-day activities in Canadian society that for some purposes come under the purview of the criminal law power. To caricature that power and to use the term "criminalization" in emotive terms that have nothing to do with the way the law functions, I think is not very helpful in helping Canadians to understand the role of parliamentarians and the effect of legislation.
Of course, we should be doing things that are effective for women and children, but those are not answers to the problem that is before us.
This law attempts to recognize the fact that abortion is characterized in two fundamentally different ways in Canadian society. For people on my side of the issue, a view the hon. member shares, it is fundamentally an equality rights issue, but for other Canadians it is basically a moral issue. It is very difficult to reconcile these two points of view.
This bill attempts to reconcile these two points of view. It is a conciliatory gesture. It says to those great many Canadians, for whom abortion will never be just another issue, that it is an issue we take seriously as a society. At the same time it is a bill that is deeply respectful of the relationship between a woman and her doctor. It is deeply respectful of the professional ethics of the medical profession in Canada. It does not seek to intrude into that relationship or look behind opinions formed by doctors, opinions which they must form to practise ethical medicine under the canons of their own college. It does not seek to look behind those opinions but to recognize them and to provide in those opinions and in a standard of good medical practice, a protection for doctors from any kind of legal sanction.

Madam Speaker, the Minister of Justice indicated some question of morality here and that this
May 24, 1990

was a moral position of her government. For two years in this country, we have had no criminal law on abortion. Has she seen any indication that Canadian women have not behaved with integrity or have not taken this issue very seriously themselves? Does she truly believe that the state knows better than Canadian women, on then-own, when they agonize to make this decision themselves? Does she not respect the morality of Canadian women?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think that is a foolish question and typical of the way the hon. member tries to characterize questions which bear no relation to what I have actually said.
Many Canadians regard this as a moral issue. It is an issue that is troubling to them. In making a moral balance between the question of ending a pregnancy and the right of a woman to make that choice, I come down very strongly on the right of a woman to make that choice. I recognize that there is a moral balance and a moral dilemma. It is an appropriate function for Parliament to recognize that this is an issue unlike any other in Canadian society.
Women make this decision best. The determination of the health and well being of a women, in the context of medical practice, is one in which the woman's own aspirations play a very significant role. Doctors do not ask their patients to be quiet while figuring out what their situation is. The patient is a fundamental participant in the determination of what is in the best interest of the patient. It is precisely that relationship which is respected in this bill. It is precisely the formation of that opinion which a doctor must form to practise ethical medicine which is not intruded into or looked behind in this bill.
I think it is very sad that the hon. member cannot recognize that this is a troubling issue for many Canadians. It is appropriate in the House to come up with some kind of legislative structure that will pay homage to the concerns of a great many Canadians who send people to the House of Commons and who also have a right to be represented. I believe this bill does so, but not at the expense of the security of the person of Canadian women. That is a value which we have to respect. The Supreme Court of Canada has told us that. We have done that in this bill.
Government Orders
I believe this bill is an honourable accommodation between two fundamentally different ways of characterizing one of the most divisive issues in Canadian society. I am sorry that the hon. member does not see, within her role as a parliamentarian, the obligation to find that common ground. If her party has aspirations ever to be government, she will find that the positions it takes on many issues do not translate well into public policy which will command the support of all Canadians. All Canadians are represented in the House, and require some acknowledgement of their position.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I do not mean to interrupt, but I just want to announce that there is agreement among the parties that the debate will continue on through the lunch hour.

Madam Speaker, the motions to amend the bill, which we all know failed last night, were largely an attempt to improve the bill in the interest of protecting the most defenceless, smallest, and weakest members of our society, the prebom.
Abortion kills a human being. This bill, if passed, is a licence to kill human beings. It does not matter that the human being is in its early stages of development. What matters is that this bill, if passed, will permit open season on defenceless human beings.
The dispute lies in whether it is right or wrong to kill defenceless human beings. In attempting to explain then-position on the abortion issue, civil leaders frequently speak of not wanting to impose their morality on others. Let me remind them that all civil law involves the imposition of someone's moral principles on someone else, including those who do not agree with them and on those who believe they should be exempt from those rules.
The Criminal Code prohibits rape, theft, arson, and many other things. Obviously the rapist, the thief, and the arsonist do not subscribe to the Criminal Code's principles. However, no sensible person would suggest that these offences should be removed from the Criminal Code because they impose someone else's morality.
The civilization of a society can be judged best by how it treats its most defenceless members. Compassion dictates that we protect children in the womb and, just as importantly, provide real and substantial help to their mothers. That is what a civilized society would do. Distressed pregnant women need and deserve and have

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
a right to the assistance required to help them give life and support to their children, as much before as after birth. This is an obligation which society must address.
Compromise on abortion means legalizing the deaths of some unborn children. We would not legalize the rape of some women or the abuse of some children. Neither is the murder of some victims acceptable.
The true test of an advanced civilization, which we purport to be, is how society treats those in the dawn of life, the margins of life, and the twilight of life. There is no place in our society for select living and select dying.
In general, should Bill C-43 become law, access to abortion will be even easier and quicker than under the 1969 law which permitted the killing of over a million and a half prebom children in the country. This bill will remove the few restrictions that the 1969 law had imposed and, regardless of how one looks at it, Bill C-43 is nothing more than abortion on demand. Anyone who thinks otherwise either has not read the bill or refuses to believe what history has taught us.
Instead of approval from a therapeutic abortion committee, the opinion of only one doctor will suffice and an abortion may be performed by anyone under his or her supervision. Instead of being restricted to hospitals, abortions may be carried out anywhere: doctors' offices, clinics, homes.
Even the pretence of needing a reason or an indication, as was previously required in requesting an abortion, has now been removed by permitting abortion for physical, mental, and psychological reasons, which may even include economic and social factors.
Bill C-43 is the worst gestational law possible in that it places absolutely no time limit on when an abortion can be performed.
Let me quote the last sentence from the 1974 book, Morality and Law in Canadian Politics:
For a society to have many illegal abortions is no doubt a very serious
situation. It will be very difficult to stop them. But to legalize abortions
is to corrupt the law and, thereby, ultimately to corrupt society. It will
prove far more difficult to stop that corruption than it will be to stop
illegal abortions.
A child on the verge of being bom is developmentally indistinguishable from a newborn infant. The mere fact that the unborn child is inside someone else's body does not imply that it is not a person. If it is not a person at this stage, presumably the reason is that it is still physically dependent on the mother. But if personhood is diminished in this way, the matter of dependence being the determinant, then the personhood of seriously ill people on life-support systems would come into serious question, as would the personhood of other seriously dependent or handicapped persons.
Surely, a woman's right to have control over her own body should not be extended to the level at which it gives the mother the right to terminate the life of someone else.
We get upset and very disturbed when we read about or watch on TV the terrible atrocities that go on almost daily in our society. The mass killings of a group of students recently in Montreal is an example, as are the needless slayings of innocent people, young and old in our society. These things prompt us to ask what is wrong in our society. Why is there this lack of respect for life in our society? Are we growing immune and becoming more accepting to these indignities that we cause one another? The answer is yes. If Bill C-43, which will allow abortion on demand, becomes law, it will be a major setback for our society which is attempting to present itself as a highly civilized nation.
In closing, what I am asking for is a new approach to something that is very old. If we take away life as a basic right, then all other rights that we would extend to the foetus are meaningless. Why not reject this proposed law in favour of a family policy that is positive? That policy would see the family elevated above every other social unit or organization as being the ultimate unit, the one of prime importance if we are going to advance as a society on the world scene.
Canada has an opportunity to show leadership. Forget about Party differences. What I am proposing is developing an attitude that will respect the family and will transcend all petty things such as party lines and differ-

ences. I think if we permit ourselves we could elevate our purposes and, for once, do something because it is right, although it may not be popular in all quarters.
Our obligation as human beings is to protect the lives of others who are in no position to protect themselves. The inconvenience that one life may cause to another is not a justifiable reason for the dominant one to discontinue the life of the innocent one.
I ask hon. members from all sides, if they are not sure what position to take, if they have not thought it through, or if for one reason or another they cannot make up their minds, to vote for life. Come down on the side of human dignity. Be a promoter of life. Defeat this bill and ask the government to come up with a new bill with its soul purpose being to protect life. To vote in favour of this bill as it is now is so final. All we are saying is give life a chance.

Madam Speaker, I wonder if I could ask the hon. member how he thinks criminalizing abortion, making women and/or doctors criminals, will possibly deal with abortions taking place?
He will remember, prior to any criminal provisions with regard to abortion, that abortions were generally unsafe, back-street operations, essentially for poor women, and that rich women could always find appropriate doctors to perform abortions, here or elsewhere.
Perhaps the hon. member could deal with that one point. If the point is that we should try to reduce the number of abortions, how does he feel that criminalizing the matter would achieve that, bearing in mind that past practice and history would not substantiate any suggestion that that would happen?
Would there not be a greater likelihood of success in reducing the number of abortions if we addressed concerns such as child care, effective education and effective contraception, and essentially give women an opportunity to see their way clear to raising children in other than poverty? He knows as well as we do that one in four Canadian children is raised in poverty.
The main point is, how does he feel criminalizing women and criminalizing doctors could possibly deal with the question of abortion?
Government Orders

Well, it is not a question of criminalizing women and doctors. Members of his party seem to be presenting themselves as the social conscience of the world and not seeing that the basic need is to create conditions in this country-we are a rich country-in which those conditions would not exist that require abortions.
If it is through poverty, let us correct that. If it is through poor housing, let us correct that. If it is through lack of education, let us correct that. But if we are going to start with the assumption that this is going to go on and we have no intention of trying to jar society into elevating its sights at all, how are we ever going to address the problem?
I know abortions have gone on and probably will continue to go on. But I do not think that should be the base from which to start to improve conditions under which abortions go on. Let us correct the social conditions that create the need for women to have abortions in this country.

Madam Speaker, I am sure no one in the House would disagree with the sentiment presented by the hon. member for Leeds- Grenville that society should be doing more for families and for children.
I remind him that in the last 20 or 30 years we have had deindexing of family allowances, a reduction in the proportion of family income that is free from income tax for raising children, and an inadequacy of social services for the increasing number of single-parent families, most of them headed by women. Society has failed miserably. Governments all across the country, federal and provincial, and the two main parties that have been in power federally have not addressed that. In fact, they have exacerbated the problem.
Can he perhaps explain why there has not been emphasis on correcting those problems, rather than attempting to portray the difficulty, so-called, as one of being a moral issue when there are social and economic factors to it? Among those economic and social factors, the experiment that has existed for the last year and a half or two years where women and doctors were free to make these decisions does seem to indicate that they were conducting themselves appropriately.
I wonder if he could tie those two factors together and explain why?

May 24, 1990
Government Orders

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: A very short comment from the hon. member. The time has expired.

If you are asking me to defend the record of previous governments, regardless of politics, I would not be prepared to do that. There have been some horrible examples, perhaps with good intentions, of trying to create the social climate that I am proposing should be created, so that women are not put in a position where their only alternative, seemingly, is to have an abortion. I think that indicates a preposterous kind of economy. We have a great economy in this country, if we wanted to direct it in the right fashion. There seems to be a tendency to have all kinds of money for certain programs but the one that is most basic, the protection of human life, seems to be the one that gives way whenever there is any kind of a crunch.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member. The time for questions and comments has now expired. Resuming debate with the hon. member for York West.

Madam Speaker, as everyone knows, the question of abortion is a very emotional and complex one, one that is so fundamental that it continues to occupy this House and this country.
It is complex and fundamental because it incorporates a number of different overtones, whether they be moral, religious, social, or philosophical. It also incorporates a debate between individual rights, in this case of women, versus collective rights of a family, of a society. Finally, important among those elements are the rights of the unborn.
This is the third occasion I have participated in a debate on the matter of abortion. I spoke in the second reading debate of Bill C-43 a few months ago. In the last Parliament, I also participated in the debate on the number of various options offered to the House of Commons. At that time, I certainly was in favour of the pro-life option.
I wish to say again today that there are three exceptions that I feel very strongly about that were not incorporated in the official pro-life option; where an abortion was performed if the life of the mother was seriously endangered, where the pregnancy was the result of a rape, and where the pregnancy was the result of incest.
I realize that in some of those cases the numbers are few, but nonetheless we have to legislate for all possible and potential possibilities. Therefore, in my judgment, those exceptions are certainly real and must be addressed. I feel very passionately about them.
I also voted against second reading of Bill C-43, mainly because the legislation as drafted is essentially abortion on demand. The law would make it very easy and very open-ended for most women in this country to obtain an abortion; open-ended for any health reason, which is loosely defined; open-ended for any medical practitioner to approve the abortion; open-ended for ending a pregnancy at any stage. The fundamental question that I asked myself during second reading and I continue to ask myself now at third reading is, what is the difference between this piece of legislation, and abortion on demand, or no legislation at all?
There was no attempt to define the rights of the unborn, the rights of the foetus, which is a very central dilemma that we as a Parliament in 1990 are supposed to resolve. Previous Supreme Court decisions challenged Parliament to come to grips with the question of the rights of the unborn, and at what point in the pregnancy do we have the right as a society and as legislators to protect that life.
It seems to me that this piece of legislation skated away completely from that challenge, from toiling with that dilemma so that we can somehow as legislators and as a country come to grips with that very moral question.
What alternative or encouragement through legislation or programs did this Parliament and government provide or offer those women in Canada who may have wanted to stop their pregnancy through abortion?
Are we to accept that an unwanted pregnancy must equal an unwanted child? I am not prepared to accept that. Must we accept that somehow an unwanted pregnancy must hurt a woman or stop her career or penalize her because there are no structural elements or programs to allow for that option? I do not buy that.
Are we to say that we should not be encouraging the gift of adoption for those who unfortunately cannot have children and who would love to know the feeling of parenthood but who have to go through red tape abroad in order to bring in an adopted child because there are

May 24, 1990

not enough children in this country to adopt. I am not prepared to accept that.
Those were some of the challenges for me that were inherent in the abortion debate. People are looking to this Chamber and this government to resolve these dilemmas. We chose to exclude the most difficult variables and deal with those which are perhaps easier to deal with at this particular junction.
I voted against the bill at second reading because in my opinion and in the opinion of many constituents of York West, whom I have the honour to represent, the legislation was bad legislation. I thought that it was so seriously flawed that it had to be sent to committee so that it could be amended to make it a better bill.
I voted against this bill because the government signalled very early in the debate that it would not permit any amendments, that not one comma would be changed. Therefore, I was not prepared to put my feelings aside in the hope that a committee would come up with amendments that would somehow correct the flaws and right the wrongs.
There were many individuals who wanted the pro-life option who were prepared to vote in favour at second reading in the hope that some amendments would see the light of day. We found out that the committee experience was a different story. We also found out last night about that story when all amendments were defeated, that the so-called free vote of my friends and colleagues on the opposite side was a three-line whip to ensure that all members on the government side supported the piece of legislation unchanged.
In my judgment, the defeat of those amendments was the defeat of any possibility that we would have legislation in this country that would try, on the one hand, to protect the unborn and, on the other hand, encourage alternatives to the abortion option and facilitate this option by supporting women in Canada with mechanisms that would enable them to continue with the pregnancy without any cost to their personal being.
Therefore, I return to the principle of my debate at second reading. What is the difference between this piece of legislation and abortion on demand? What is the message that we are transmitting through this bill to a
Government Orders
society at large, above and beyond the elements surrounding the question of abortion?
I believe that this bill has failed the country badly. I believe that this piece of legislation is morally bankrupt and does not speak to or embrace any set of values that a civilized society with concern for the multifaceted elements of this debate should have had and obtained. That is the first message it sends out.
Second, I believe that this debate has failed in addressing the inherent variables that were at play in the question of abortion. We chose to exclude many variables that are pressing and that we think have gone away or have been resolved, because we chose to ignore them.
Third, this debate and this legislation have failed to come to grips with the rights of the unborn. For me, this bill was not worth supporting at second reading. It is not worth supporting at third reading. Instead of participating in a debate over a piece of legislation that has very little substance and is more of charade than anything else, I believe that parliament should have come to grips with a piece of legislation that should have had the courage and the integrity to address all the elements in the abortion debate; not some, but all of them.

Madam Speaker, yesterday I spoke against the very restrictive and punitive criminal measures that were presented in this House by men who in my view wanted to punish severely women and doctors who have performed abortions.
As I listened to the debate I became more and more upset. It was very difficult to try and be sensitive to why members were feeling this way and to respect then-different views, which are very different from my own. I became very upset and very angry, because it seemed to me that the principles and the policies that were advocated in these extreme amendments were akin to the dreadful situation that has existed for some time in Romania, which we learned about recently, where women have been treated as handmaidens of the state and forced to become baby factories. That is not a nice term, but that is in fact what was happening. Unwanted children, as a result, were neglected and abused. We remember those frightening and sickening pictures on TV of children in institutions where they were left to die or vegetate.

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
I am sure that many women who would not go through with pregnancies, as the state required, died or were permanently damaged from illegal or self-induced abortions. It was really sickening.
I was extremely disappointed in many of the Liberal MPs, particularly, for supporting these amendments. I expected more to come from the other party. The majority of people who stood up time after time to support those amendments were from the Liberal caucus. I was sickened that they and Canadians who support this position would support such punitive measures in the name of life. I will not pursue this point, because I am sure we have different views on it, but that is the way it seemed to me and it was very sickening and depressing. Fortunately all these amendments were voted down by members from all parties.
I was particularly moved by the remarks of the member from the eastern Arctic. He was telling us about the culture and the caring of the Inuit communities where children belong to the whole community, where pregnant women are treated with great care and the children can be adopted in a very positive way by other people and still share relationships with their natural parents. This was a very moving statement and an example of the kind of caring community I wish we could somehow recreate in our southern urban communities. We have much to learn.
Today I want to try to be more positive in speaking on this final third reading of Bill C-43. Last November 22,1 outlined my objections to the bill in considerable detail and tried to present positive alternatives we in this party see which would allow personal reproductive choice, would help to prevent unwanted pregnancies, and would provide support for parents and children in a caring society.
I want to summarize once again at third reading why we in the New Democratic Party oppose Bill C-43 and why I personally will be voting against it.
First, there is no need for a bill that will recriminalize abortion. It just is not needed, and the last two years have shown this. We know that this bill attempts to be a compromise. Some would like it to have tougher sanctions, but the sanctions under the Criminal Code affect both women and doctors, and this really is not necessary.
If we look at what has happened since the Supreme Court decision in the Morgentaler case over two years ago which struck down the previous abortion law, women and doctors have been left to make their own private decisions concerning abortion. I think this has worked well. There is no evidence that this has been abused or irresponsible.
The main concern that continues is that access is limited across the country, particularly in the Atlantic region and in rural and remote areas. This bill will not extend that access. In fact it will further restrict access, and I will come back to this point later.
The rate of abortions has not risen over the last two years. The kind of openness and the privacy of this access to abortion mean that a whole range of services has been offered in clinics such as Every Woman's Clinic in Vancouver, which has offered a first-rate service despite the protests that continue outside its doors. Hospitals also have been able to proceed without those cumbersome and delaying committees that formerly were a legal necessity.
Second, as we have said over and over again women can be trusted. As we have said over and over again- and the women of Canada have said it- this is insulting to women. It says that the state will tell a woman what she should do about plans for her own reproductive choice and if and when she should have a family despite what her conditions and her situation are.
Abortion is not used as a method of birth control. I have not personally met anyone who is in favour of abortion. I must say that I really wish, when referring to those who support the so-called choice position, people would not interpret this as a pro-abortion position. It certainly is not.
If a woman has to make a very difficult decision on the question of abortion she should be able to speak with counsellors, as she does now under the present situation, and consult with her doctor, but only she can and should have the right to make the final decision. After all, she is the one who has to care for the child, often without the support of a partner, and only she knows the real situation in her case.
May 24, 1990

No law can make this decision for her. This is what this bill is doing. It is saying that the state will interfere, that the state will impose the kind of situation, and that the state will also have criminal sanctions against women and doctors.
As the minister herself said this morning, women and doctors are responsible. Eighty-nine per cent of abortions are in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy. Both women and doctors know, if the difficult decision of having an abortion is what they conclude is right for them, that this must be done long before a foetus is viable.
I should not have to say this, but I want to stress that women do have rights in this country. We are not in Romania. We no longer are chattels of men or chattels of the state. Surely everyone in the House appreciates this fact.
Women do not have to be told what to do. They can make their own decisions, particularly on this all-important decision of child birth and pregnancy.
Our rights have been spelled out in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. This was recognized by the Supreme Court when it declared that the former abortion law was unconstitutional. As the minister said this morning, it was judged to be "a violation of the security of the person and of fundamental justice". The courts in the Daigle case also recognized a woman's right to make her own independent decision about abortion and denied the injunction of a boyfriend who tried to prevent this for very questionable reasons.
An abortion should be treated as a private medical procedure, as it is now, performed by qualified persons under medical regulations in safe conditions. Access will be restricted by this bill. We know that anxious, desperate women who may fear that they will not qualify for an abortion under the restrictions imposed, or who sense that their doctors are reluctant to get into any legal complications under Bill C-43, will find another way of having an abortion. It is not going to stop abortions.
History shows repeatedly that legal prohibitions and criminal sanctions do not stop unwanted pregnancies or abortions that result. The experience in Italy showed that when it had the toughest possible law, there was the highest incidence of abortions and deaths. Since there has been a more liberal policy, this rate has gone down.
Government Orders
Undoubtedly this bill will result in an increase in self-induced abortions and illegal back street abortions which are so dangerous, as well as being illegal.
Doctors also can be trusted. Physicians do not need to have punitive criminal laws to overrule their medical judgments. They operate under professional ethics and under provincial regulations. Good doctors will take cognizance of the total person: her needs and desires as well as health factors, her family, and her economic situation. He or she will respect the right of a woman patient to make her own decision as to whether or not to terminate a pregnancy.
This bill imposes a whole new situation. I am sure it will intimidate doctors. We already had an indication of this point. The Canadian Medical Association is veiy much opposed to recriminalizing abortion. It has stated the following:
Our figures indicate that approximately 800 of the 45,000 physicians in the CMA perform abortions. Approximately 325 perform the majority of abortions. We understand that a significant majority of physicians providing abortion services would seriously re-evaluate their position.
That is, if this law is imposed. It is quite easy to understand why. As I said, the bill will intimidate doctors. It limits legal abortions to only situations where the continuation of a pregnancy would threaten a woman's physical, psychological or mental health.
There were some medical doctors who said in the House yesterday that they want to have "health" interpreted very, very narrowly rather than having the UN definition of it. I am sure that if they are faced with a possible legal challenge they are not going to be willing to take a risk. It is going to be very difficult for clinics to hire physicians if they are going to be threatened with two years in prison and costly legal charges.
This means that access for women will be seriously limited. The CMA has pointed this out. It is also grossly unfair and insulting to doctors who can make their own judgment on this matter. Doctors prefer to work under medical rather than criminal legislation and regulations.
I would now like to talk about alternatives to Bill C-43. As I have said many times, we must lessen the need for abortions. I know of no one who favours abortion. It is far preferable to prevent unwanted pregnancies. Why has the federal government then not addressed this question as its priority? Why have we had to spend so much time on this negative, punitive bill and

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
all the public furore it has created when the need for abortions could be done away with if the government would only put an emphasis on finding that solution?
It is extremely important, first, that men take a much greater responsibility for birth control and family planning. We have to change our culture in this respect. We must promote male contraceptives. Men have to see and accept that it is their responsibility. They contribute to the need for abortions and they must prevent unwanted pregnancies. They cannot just leave it to women, which seems to have been the old way of thinking in so much of our culture.
Young people, from childhood, must learn healthy sexuality. As adolescents they must have open discussions of sexual relations, pregnancies and contraception, and it should be done in schools openly. We need youth clinics and peer group discussions. We do not want contraception to be associated only with the prevention of AIDS, although this is very important. It should also be taught as part of a positive family planning and family life education program.
This is why the government must provide increased funding for school programs, for public education, and particularly for public media such as TV. It must especially reinstate and increase funding for planned parenthood associations. They have expertise in all of these areas. They are not just going to go out and promote abortions as one alternative.
Abortion is a symptom of our societal inadequacies. It is really a sign of our failure. This bill is the extreme negative way of dealing with this failure. We need prevention, but we also need many more supports for both fathers and mothers and for their children. Children and parents need programs to ensure their economic and emotional security. They must have this kind of security to plan for, bear and raise children. This is not always easy in the very competitive, costly society in which we live.
We must end child poverty and offer many more supports and opportunities for single mothers or fathers. This should be a government priority for funding and a first priority in our social policy.
It is deplorable and unconscionable that this government continues to ignore the urgent need for quality, affordable child care despite two task forces, constant presentations from witnesses across this country and repeated promises to introduce a national child care program. This is unconscionable.
We also need to extend parental leave and encourage family benefits for working parents. Employers should contribute to this and the government could start as a federal employer, another thing it is neglecting.
Immigrant parents must have language instruction and support programs to encourage their easy settlement into a new country, particularly women who often do not get the same opportunities because they are rearing children. They need opportunities for their children, including child care, as well as employment for themselves.
There are many things that we need to do to achieve a caring society, a society where people are valued and respected, where there is opportunity for people-women, men, young people and children-to develop their full potential, where they are allowed to determine their own future and make their own choices, not on only this question of reproductive choice but on all matters that affect them. We particularly want a society where children are wanted and loved, where they are nourished by parents or by alternate parents, by extended families and by a caring community.
I am pessimistic but I hope that there will be support to defeat this bill and I hope that the government and all of us in this House and across the country will work for these goals.

Madam Speaker, the member and I share the wish that the bill be defeated, although for very opposite and polarized views. I respect the member's full right to explain her views.
In a previous Supreme Court ruling one of the female judges on the bench wrote, in her own personal decision, that Parliament should be debating and challenging itself to come to grips with the rights of the unborn. She said in her decision that she felt that at some point in the pregnancy the right of the foetus becomes paramount.
May 24, 1990

I know that the hon. member has spoken at great length about the paramountcy of trying to cope with the woman in this debate of pregnancy and abortion, as we should. However, could she perhaps cast her mind on that decision written by a woman on our Supreme Court bench and explain to Parliament her opinion of the right of the foetus, at some stage in the pregnancy, becoming paramount over some other factors.

Madam Speaker, I think that is a very important question. Of course, the member is referring to the comments of Justice Bertha Wilson. If he read the full judgment he would know that it was this judge who spoke so strongly on the question of the rights of women and the need for them to not be controlled by the state.
I do not recall that Bertha Wilson used the term "should". If I recall correctly, she raised the question in a very thoughtful and important way on the rights of women, and she certainly gave that paramountcy in the early stages of pregnancy, and also raised the question of rights of the foetus. She talked about the possibility of time limits.
Let us not forget that that was two years ago. I would be very interested in what her position might be today having consideration for what has happened over the last two years. She did not direct Parliament at all, she offered that as one question for Parliament to struggle with.
I would point out to the member that the minister said this morning, and our figures would certainly substantiate this, that 89 per cent of abortions are done in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy. That is certainly the period when Bertha Wilson herself said that the woman's rights should be predominant. And although you cannot put an exact timing on it, it could perhaps go up to 20 weeks.
I would think that those cases where the abortion is done a little later would predominantly be cases of teenagers, adolescents. I have known young children, actually, in their early teens, who were not aware that they were pregnant until later. That is another very deep concern that we have.
I cannot speak for Bertha Wilson, but I do not think she suggested that Bill C-43 was the answer to the balance of rights.
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, I listened to and have read the comments the member for Vancouver East made yesterday on the report stage of the bill. I have to say that I am a little disturbed at what I believe to be the unnecessary, overt partisanship that she exhibited in her remarks today. Members on this side of the House have been freed to vote as they see fit on this legislation. I have carefully followed the debate in the House through all stages and have found that there has been a marked absence of partisanship on this issue. It is a fundamental issue and many members feel very differently on it. I think the NDP caucus is voting as a party on this and that is fine, as long as those members want to do that.
Members on our side have varying views on this very fundamental issue. Yet the member started her remarks today by taking a wide partisan swipe at some people who voted for amendments, saying that she was absolutely sickened by that. I am on a particular side of this debate, but I would hope the hon. member would read my comments on second reading of the bill, because I tried my very best, as I think most people did, to be conscious and respectful of points of view other than the ones that we individually hold. I have listened to her position, which she has articulated very carefully and very well.
I am concerned with some of the comments that she made today and, in particular, comments that she made yesterday about those members of the House who were supporting or putting forward some of the amendments which were debated yesterday. She said:
It is sickening to know that there are people in Canada, and members in this House, who support these resolutions, who want to impose the kind of inhumane policies that we saw in Romania where women were forced to have babies and these babies were neglected and abused.
That is a very strong comment which perhaps is unwarranted, knowing the spirit and the complexity of the debate that is at hand. I would certainly hope that no one who holds a point of view contrary to hers would be so loose in condemnation of her point of view.
I would like the hon. member to comment on that. I would hope that she did not mean to put that particular light on all members who have a different point of view than her on the resolutions that we voted on last night.

May 24, 1990
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, the member raises two points. First, he says that I am partisan. I think that is probably true for a reason, although I hope I am expressing this as a person who cares very deeply for the women of Canada and the whole question of abortion.
The reason I mentioned that I was surprised that so many Liberals took what I consider to be an anti-choice stance-I do not like to use those terms but I guess everybody is using them-is that the member's party is aspiring to be the next government. So are we, of course. I think it is very important that the women and men of Canada know what the Liberal Party position is on abortion, and I take it that there is no position. There is a chance, God forbid, that the Liberals will be in government in the not-too-distant future. If this happens, what is going to be the policy then? What kind of criminal sanctions are we going to have at that time? Can women expect that the new government will be more progressive than the present government and will rescind this recriminalization of abortion that is represented in this bill? I do not think so. I think it is very important that people in Canada know what they are in for.
I do apologize to my colleagues if I personally insulted them yesterday. I was feeling very, very upset, to tell the truth. I do not like to criticize people personally because they have the right to their views, even though I get very upset at what those views are.
I would like to pay tribute to a number of the Conservative members, women in particular. In the debate on this issue a year or two ago, some of them spoke so movingly. Several of them said they were Catholics and they would never have an abortion, as many of us would not. But they felt so strongly for women who were in very desperate situations and had no alternatives. They respected their decision and their right to make that decision. I wanted to mention that because I know there are some very caring people on all sides of the House, but I was very disappointed that there were not more of them in the Liberal caucus.
I do respect peoples' right to have a different opinion, even though I do not respect those opinions that are, in my view, anti-women. I would urge members to listen again to what the member from the eastern Arctic said yesterday. To paraphrase it, he said: "If men were able to bear children, I do not think we would have this bill".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have been participating in debate on this issue for about 15 years.
I want to begin by thanking the Prime Minister for exercising leadership on this issue last summer when the country was tom by what we saw on television. He determined then that the government would introduce legislation and that Parliament would make a decision. I want to thank him personally for taking that leadership and exercising that initiative.
In these past 15 years there has been an emotional tug of war in our land between what is right and what is wrong. As that emotional tug of war developed, the confusion increased as to what is right and what is wrong. It brings to mind the famous lines by that great Irish poet, W.B. Yates, who said, about 55 years ago:
Turning and turning in the widening gyre The falcon cannot hear the falconer;
Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold;
Mere anarchy is loosed upon the world,
The blood-dimmed tide is loosed, and everywhere The ceremony of innocence is drowned;
The best lack all conviction, while the worst Are full of passionate intensity.
Yates was being very prophetic about the days in which we are living, particularly on this issue.
We are living in a period of a redefinition of norms. All through civilization there has been an aspiration for freedom which has been the norm. But that freedom was always integrated with our relationship with our fellow human beings. It was never seen as individual islands of freedom, but rather communities of freedom. Today we are facing a redefinition of that term and it is becoming increasingly individualistic, narcissistic, and egocentric, as though the rights of the other person do not matter as long as my own freedom is preserved.
There has always been a norm about the sanctity of life. Strangely enough now, with the increasing knowledge that science has given us, there are other views regarding the sanctity of life. Is it not strange that the planet and all of life on the planet now is sacred and we are doing everything we can to preserve the planet, but
May 24, 1990

we want to take the opposite view when it conies to the life of the unborn? It is strangely ironic.
In Vancouver last winter there was a bizarre theatre. A young man was going to drop a stone or brick on a rat and there was public outrage about that demonstration in the name of art, as there should have been. But at the same time, bystanders were asked if they were pro-life and they said no. You would almost believe, as one writer put it, that society was pro-rat but not pro-life. We are destroying that norm.
We are seeing also the disintegration of the moral leadership of institutional influence. In the midst of the redefinition and a growing moral confusion about what is right, we need a reference point. Since the institutions are not fulfilling their functions in instructing us on what is right and wrong, as they did at one time, we do need moral reference points and that has seemingly been left to the law.
We need the law. Without that, society cannot function in a coherent way. For this coherence we must have dependable responses to one another. We must be able to depend on our responses to each other.
I would say that the first universal principle accepted around the world is the preservation of life. That is a universal principle accepted in all societies. There is a dependable group response to that principle everywhere. Societies have as their first goal the preservation of life, but this is now clashing with personal agendas.
We heard in committee that 95 per cent of abortions are performed for socioeconomic reasons. Regardless of how that is defined, it comes down to personal agendas clashing with the right of the unborn and the defenceless to life. To preserve self-will we want to dispose of a defenceless life. But to do that and still preserve our conscience, we have to rewrite the definitions.
Rather than talk of the unborn child, we want to talk about a foetus. That becomes a little less personal and easier to deal with. We can destroy the norm that way. We do not want to talk about an abortion. We want to talk about terminating a pregnancy, or evacuating the womb. That becomes less personal, less offensive, easier to handle.
Government Orders
The whole focus and goal is to disintegrate the norms that have governed our society throughout the centuries. It is the self-will and the personal agendas that we have established that are doing this. Yet, we still want to cling to the notion that there is respect for life at any stage.
The second erosion is the institutional influence on moral issues. There is a confusion of positions in spite of empirical evidence regarding all this. Science is telling us so much about life.
We had before the committee a world renowned geneticist who said the following:
Using Jeffrey's method, we can determine the bar code for each human being. It has been shown that there is a unique code for each human being. One person cannot be mistaken for another. From the moment of fertilization, every human being has his or her unique bar code. Using another method, the in-vitro polymerization of DNA, we can study the bar code in a single cell.
We thus have an experiment that proves that each human being is unique and therefore irreplaceable, from the moment of fertilization on. The only difference between the genetic bar code which defines each of us and the bar codes we find in the supermarket is that when we run the item over the optical character reader in the supermarket, the bar code tells the computer how much the item costs. The genetic bar code does not show the price of a human being. Science tells us that each human being is priceless.
That is what science tells us.
But then we heard from a woman from one of the leading churches in our society in Canada, with one of the largest denominations, who said:
I did not miscarry a person, I miscarried something that looked rather like a mass of liver. That sounds crude, but it was not a person physically, and all women know in their hearts that this is so.
On the one hand, science gives us the empirical evidence that every person is unique and priceless. On the other hand, a woman from the church says it looks rather like a mass of liver.
The geneticist went on to say:
I know that the embtyo, before becoming a foetus, was already that same being, and I know that you and I too were once 2.5-cm beings in our mothers' wombs.
In other words, what we have learned from genetics and embryology, is that the Tom Thumb story, the story of the man who is notallerthanathumb, is not an old wives'tale. It is the truth. It is a very factual story-it is biologically absurd to imagine that you can measure human dignity by the size of the body. I have never measured the dignity of a human being in kilograms or centimetres. Only one parameter can be used for measurement: is it a member of our

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
species-and then it deserves respect whatever its colour, size or state
of health-or is it a member of another species? Ido not hold the same
respect for a mouse foetus as for a human foetus.
That is what science tells us.
But the Canadian Medical Association, which ought to be protecting our values, stated that "the CMA is in fact in the process of preparing a position paper on the status of the human foetus".
The institutions that ought to be protecting and educating our values are no longer the guidance mechanisms we need to make moral decisions. When we cannot trust the institutions, then there has to be a law that gives us some guidance as to the ultimate-the furthest we can go in our behaviour. We do not have to go that far, but there has to be a guidance mechanism.
Bill C-43 is an attempt to provide that. Basically, Bill C-43 says that life is important, it is sacred from the beginning, and it deserves protection. The Supreme Court has said that there are justifiable limits of choice and that society has a legitimate interest in the welfare of the defenceless or the foetus.
But there are exceptions, and here is where the avenue of freedom lies in the bill. I want to say this with some caution. This is important. The ability to choose is important in our society if we want to be unique beings. It is our ability to choose that defines our uniqueness. The freedom of choice determines moral growth or moral deterioration. If we remove the freedom, we begin to deteriorate. Choice must be an integral part of our society.
The exceptions and the definitions of "health" introduce an incredible risk in this legislation because they introduce the freedom to choose, to do right or to do wrong. The fact is people do make wrong choices. I am appalled at the wrong choices we are able to make. When we do make wrong choices, we must know that we are making wrong choices. Unless there is a law, we have no way of measuring whether we are right or wrong. This is the moral morass in which society will be if we have no law. The ten commandments were given to prevent people from doing wrong, to let them know when they were in danger of doing wrong.
The failure of the so-called pro-choice concept is not in the freedom to choose-and we respect the freedom to choose-but it is their desire to choose in the absence
of any reference points of what is right or wrong. There is nothing to guide them, they want no law, so people will never know if they are doing right or wrong.
We are not talking about the arrangement of potted plants, or how to arrange the books on a shelf, or whether to get rid of a used car or not, we are talking about human life.
