We have to know beyond a shadow of a doubt, are we right or are we wrong? In the absence of moral guidance systems, which have deteriorated over the years, we need a law. It is not good enough to say, "If this law is not perfect then there should be no law". We need a law. That law has to define the value of human life.
There will be some patients who will exaggerate then-health problems in order to get an abortion. There will be some doctors who will exaggerate the diagnosis in order to provide an abortion. I think that that is a fact of life. We cannot have the freedom to do right without the opportunity to do wrong. That is the risk in our society. The alternative is a state sponsored morality. You cannot have the option to do right without the opportunity of doing wrong.
Bill C-43 sets the standard around which people must make conscious decisions and deliberate choices about what is right and wrong. What the bill does is establish the value of human life from the very beginning. Abortion, it says, is wrong. It is a criminal offence to provide an abortion because human life is important from the beginning. That is what Bill C-43 does.
At the same time, we cannot stop there because the law is not enough to give us a moral guidance system. We have to rebuild the laws of institutions that once gave us that guidance. I think churches have to re-examine their instructional system to teach people how to come to grips with right and wrong. The Canadian Medical Association and all other institutions, such as universities, must have a code of ethics consistent with the universal norms that say life is sacred in all forms and at all times. We have to get these institutions to rebuild a moral framework which will help people to make individual choices that will enhance their own personal morality.
The law sets the limits of morality that should control our behaviour. It should control that behaviour long before we reach those limits. Therefore, we must rebuild a moral support system superior to the law that will help

May 24, 1990

us all to be more complete human beings capable of making moral decisions.
Bill C-43 is a balance, which establishes the right of the human being to exist from the moment of conception, and tries to introduce and reintroduce the notion that we all have a right to be. People must make a choice about their own integrity and morality based upon a code of ethics that has a universal norm built into it. Then we can go on to be the kind of people we ought to be.
We have lived in the kind of a world that W. B. Years prophesized would come, that there would be anarchy and,
The blood-dimmed tide is loosed, and everywhere The ceremony of innocence is drowned;
The best lack all conviction, while the worst Are full of passionate intensity.
It is not acceptable that Canadians should tolerate 80,000 abortions a year. It is not acceptable that we should have such disdain for human life. It is not acceptable that we should reduce human sexuality to a mere biological coupling without any coherent relationship between the two parties. It is not acceptable to live that way.
This bill is the threshold of what we can do as a society in order to build the kind of moral framework that will help our people to decide the moral issues that influence their lives in a way that is acceptable to all and preserves the right of freedom.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker. I want to take this opportunity to congratulate you on your appointment as Assistant Deputy Chairman of Committees of the Whole, and I hope you will be able to perform these duties for several years or at least several months.
The bill on abortion before the House today is not an easy subject to discuss, and it is with some trepidation that I rise in the House to take part in this debate.

Mr. Speaker, the options in this debate have been made clear over many months. The bill we are discussing in this debate has been before the House for some time and many of us, as members of Parliament, have had the
Government Orders
opportunity to express our views on this issue over an extended period.
In June, 1988, shortly after my nomination as a candidate in the election for this House, I was asked for my views on this very important subject. I gave those views forthrightly, openly and honestly whenever I was asked, notwithstanding my knowledge that the views would be unpopular in some quarters throughout my riding and indeed throughout the country where they were promulgated. Nevertheless, I felt it was my duty as a candidate to inform the electorate of Kingston and the Islands in particular, as to what I thought on this issue and I did so.
Bill C-43, now before the House, comes close to what I said would be my preferred legislation. It is not the same, it is not identical, and in a way it is a disappointment, but nevertheless the bill is close to what I thought was a reasonable attempt to deal with an issue that is extremely difficult.
I indicated to the press in my riding shortly after the bill was introduced last November that I would support this legislation through all stages, assuming that no amendments could be made. I indicated I would seek amendments to the bill. These amendments have been considered and rejected by the House and, somewhat as expected, this bill has come through this debate at third reading without any amendments. The choice that we face today as members of Parliament is to accept or reject this particular bill that is now before us and no other.
I have indicated in discussing my views on this subject-I have indicated this freely in my riding when asked-that my opinions are shaped by my experience as a lawyer. They are shaped by my training in legal matters and in jurisprudence. I want to say at the outset that while that training has shaped my views on the subject, it is not the sole criterion by which I weigh the issue of abortion and on which I made my decision to support this particular legislation.
The bill is a balancing of rights. That is really what this debate on abortion is all about. We are balancing on the one hand the rights of a woman and on the other hand the rights of an unborn child or a foetus.

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
I want to state at the outset that I firmly believe in the rights of the woman. I think that the question of her right to make a decision or a conscious choice is paramount and must remain paramount.
I know there is disagreement on this view with some of my colleagues and the public, but the woman who is living and breathing deserves all the protection the law can afford. I believe this bill does exactly that. I believe the Supreme Court cases, Morgentaler and others, have reflected this, but the foetus also has rights. Those rights are undefined in our law. The bill does not define those rights but does give some protection.
The rights of the foetus must increase as the birth date gets closer. I believe the bill recognizes that, perhaps not to the extent that many would prefer, and perhaps not to the extent that I would prefer, but it does recognize it in that it requires a doctor's consent for an abortion. The limited value of that consent in the early stages of pregnancy is well recognized.
Members of this House who have spoken eloquently on the pro-life side said that this bill gives away everything. In the early stages, it may. The pro-choice groups on the other hand argue that it does not. Perhaps it does not. We will have to wait to see how judicial interpretation treats it. My thinking on this is influenced by the fact that under the old law, which contained similar words to this bill, there was not a single successful prosecution of a medical doctor for performing abortions under the law.
Given that, and given the extended definition contained in Bill C-43, it is very unlikely that a physician would be convicted of an offence under this act without having carried on in a way that is grossly outrageous and in apparent violation of the idea of sanctity of human life, both of the mother and of the unborn child or foetus.
The bill has been before the House since November last year. It was considered at second reading and debated extensively. It was considered in committee with many amendments put forward and defeated. I am soriy that our rules prevented some of those amendments from being voted on last night when we voted on the other amendments debated at that time.
Last evening there were eleven separate votes on different amendments before this House. Every single
one of the amendments was defeated. Those amendments presented a range. They were strong pro-life amendments, for the most part, and one was a very strong pro-choice amendment from the other side. Every one of them was defeated by a substantial margin.
As a result of those votes last evening and the activities of the committee, no other bill could pass this House of Commons except Bill C-43.1 do not believe it is possible for a majority of members of this place to pass any other bill. If that is so, what is our responsibility as members of the House of Commons? In my view, we are elected as members to represent the views of our constituents, yes; to represent our country, yes; and to make decisions on issues such as this one. Parliament must speak on this issue. We cannot leave this matter of abortion, and the great debate that rages in our country on this issue, to the courts. As members of a legislature, we have an obligation to speak on this issue.
Parliament does not speak just through speeches. Each of us can be here and make our own speech and say we are representing or making our views known in Parliament, whatever they may be. Parliament speaks through legislation, through pieces of legislation or resolutions that are adopted in this House.
We have before us a bill which in my view represents the collective will of the majority of the members of this place. This is the way we deal with the public and this is the way we speak for the public: by enacting legislation and by dealing with resolutions. This bill, as it does in representing that majority view, is the way in which we as a Parliament ought to address the Canadian pubic on this issue.
In my view Bill C-43 does that. It says to the Canadian public that we regard abortion as something very important. We feel that there should be some protection afforded to both women who may be pregnant and to unborn children. Therefore we will put a law in place that will require that a woman who wishes to have an abortion will obtain the consent of a physician before obtaining that abortion. That is all that is required in this law. It allows the physician to grant the abortion whenever he feels the physical, mental, or emotional health of the woman is threatened. That is included and any other health matter will also be included. It says: "when the health or life of the mother is threatened".
May 24, 1990

In other words, it is a veiy wide discretion given to physicians in Canada to make those decisions in consultation with the woman who comes to them for an abortion. I believe that is a reasonable and fair compromise, given the very significantly different views held on this issue by members of the House.
This may not be the first choice for any member of the House. It may be a second choice for most of us, but I say that as members of Parliament we have an obligation. Sure, we have difficulty. Sure, our constituents have very widely held views and very sincerely held views on this issue. I expect that very few members have been written to, demonstrated against or heard from so many constituents by telephone or otherwise as I have on this issue.
I recognize there is a divergence of view, but surely as legislators, as members of Parliament, we have to act together and make a decision. Having voted down all other options and having come up with a bill which in its evident simplicity is and which is very short, I think we have an obligation now to say: "All right, we cannot do anything else. The only thing we can do is adopt this bill".
I say to hon. members that although it may not be their first choice-and it is not mine-we have to look at it and ask: "Is there anything else we can do? Is this not a reasonable thing to do, to balance the rights that we all wish to protect in Canada and to give some recognition to the competing interests reflected in this great debate that has gone on for so many years in Canada?" It is time to bring the debate to an end, to pass this legislation, and to see how the courts interpret it.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry I did not arrive sooner to hear the speech by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands who, I feel, has shown considerable leadership today by recognizing the fact that the abortion issue is controversial, complex and divisive, and that pro-choice and pro-life supporters are miles apart on this issue, so much so, that-and the hon. member is absolutely right-it is incumbent upon Parliament to take a serious look at this question, because Canadians expect us to produce a bill that seeks to reconcile these two views.
Government Orders
I want to ask the hon. member, who was elected for the first time in 1988, whether he thinks this issue is so important it could mean losing one's seat in the next election. Will his constituents hold it against him- There are members who say: I have no choice, because otherwise I would lose my seat on this issue. Does he believe that the abortion issue can have this kind of impact on the electoral process?

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
I will be quite frank with the hon. member who asked the question, and I want to thank her, if I may, for her compliment.
I don't know the answer to this question because I don't know how many people in my riding consider this policy, this bill to be very important. I don't know how many.
I believe that if this bill is passed by Parliament, by this legislation, the court decisions on this bill will be very important. I think they will show Canadians, especially those who are pro choice, that the bill is not a disaster at all. It is a good bill for everyone.
I imagine people who are pro life will not be very pleased with this bill. However, if the Supreme Court or other courts decide that the rights granted women under this legislation are more restrictive than they are without the bill, then we will have a problem.
I am almost certain that this bill gives women the rights they desire, and despite speeches by hon. members in the New Democratic Party and others, I think we will have fewer problems with this bill than the gentlemen of the NDP have suggested.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The time for questions and comments has expired. The hon. member for Dartmouth on debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am participating in this debate for the second time. The last time I participated was at second reading. I said then, and I repeat, that this is perhaps one of the most difficult debates members from all sides of the House would probably face in their period of time in the House of Commons.
I say this for a couple of reasons. With all due respect to my colleagues in the NDP, one reason is that this issue does not lends itself easily to strict party discipline or ideology. It is an issue with which each and every

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
member of Parliament has had to grapple and to find a rationale to determine how we as legislators at this particular time and how Parliament, given the importance of this debate, fit in.
During debate there has been frequent mention of the rights of women and the rights of the foetus. It seems that the debate has centred on those very rights. Indeed, if we go back to the Supreme Court ruling, it seemed the ruling that struck down the current legislation was primarily concerned with the rights of women. I quote from the ruling of the Supreme Court of last January 28 when Chief Justice Dickson wrote:
The precise point in the development of the foetus at which the state's interest in its protection become "compelling" should be left to the informed judgment of the legislature.
Like Beetz and Wilson, I agree that the protection of foetal interests by Parliament is also a valid governmental objective. It follows that balancing these interests with the lives and health of women as a major factor is clearly an important governmental objective.
He has clearly outlined the complexity and the nub of the current debate in trying to balance rights.
In the initial debate in the House I said that the labels have done nothing to assist in finding common ground. The level of debate in this place has been refreshingly calm, well reasoned, and well put. Only a few times has it got down to the partisanship to which we are all used and in which we participate in most nearly every debate that takes place in this House.
I said during second reading that I would support the bill at that time to get it into committee. I wanted to see if it could be improved upon in committee.
As much as I dislike labels, I have been labelled as someone who leans more toward the protection of the rights of the foetus and are therefore pro-life. I do not like labels because I have been criticized by people on both sides of the debate. That is the nature of politics and human nature.
During the debate and committee hearings I hoped there would be a better definition of some of the key elements of this legislation. I hoped some amendments would come forward which would better define health and at risk. I hoped that through those amendments there would be recognition of the balance between foetal rights and the rights of women.
I want to quote from page 11666 of Hansard for May 22 when at report stage the Minister of Justice said:
This bill has been carefully drafted to achieve a delicate balance between the conflicting views on the abortion issue.
It complies with the ruling of the Supreme Court of Canada in the Morgentaler case with respect to a woman's constitutional right to security of the person guaranteed in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and to reflect the societal interest in the protection of the foetus.
I submit at this point at third reading that this bill has failed, even though the minister opposite holds the point of view that it has not. Nothing has been changed since introduction of the bill in Parliament. There has been necessary debate in Parliament, by parliamentarians in committee, and by Canadians on this issue. I regret to say that I still cannot see that the bill has been altered in any way, shape or form to strike, in my view, the balance between the rights of women and the rights of the foetus.
The bill still leaves the decision as to whether an abortion is warranted to medical practitioners who, with all their medical training and professional experience, will subjectively make the decision as to whether or not an abortion is warranted, as to whether or not the physical, mental, or psychological health of the woman is at risk as broadly defined in the bill. We saw amendments defeated last night after thorough and proper debate, as was the will of members present in the House of Commons. I can no longer look with any hope at this bill being refined to the point where I-and I have been labelled by others to be on the pro-life side of the debate-can support it.
I want to tell the House that I did not come here so wildly zealous that I did not want to see or could not understand other points of view in the debate. I have listened carefully to people on the other side of the issue, people whose judgments I truly trust. They seem to me from past experience to be logical and fair in their comments in opposition to particular points of view. I have heard the debate of other people who are perhaps closer to pro-life, and the quandary in which I found myself when this issue was first raised in the House has not been lessened.
When the vote is taken at third reading I will have no choice but to vote against this bill. I know some will criticize me for my position, as members on the other side have been criticized for their position. I am not here
May 24, 1990

to talk about taking rights away from women. That is not my intent.
People who characterize the debate as my way or the doorway or harshly criticize anyone in this debate do a great disservice to the issue. I have listened to some members in the Commons during this debate who got perhaps a little too entrenched in their own position and maybe did not listen to what some of the other people were going through.
This is not one of those bills where you come in and say: "Okay, what is the party line? How do we deal with this? What are the zingers? What are the things that we do to try to make the government or whoever proposed the legislation look bad?" It is not one of those debates.
This is a unique debate that is taking place in the House. Some people still claim this is a compromise piece of legislation. I cannot accept it as such. I might be able to change my position if I thought this bill could somehow would progress so that glaring omissions, such as the social net that should be in place so that women never again have to look at abortion as an option because of economics, could be added.
If I had seen a willingness or undertaking by the government to address that particular economic problem, if I had seen a consensus developing and a program and timetable put into place whereby education was the basis for progress, perhaps I would have been a little more able to move my position. This has been such a divisive debate and I have heard members on all sides of the House say they will be thankful when it is gone. They say, "It will be out of the House and we will not have to deal with it again, to answer those letters that we don't like to answer from people who just cannot stand our point of view, whatever it is".
I do not believe that when this bill is passed, imperfect as it is, it will voluntarily ever be revisited in this place. So when people say that it is a start, I say it is a start and a stop because, if passed, this law will grant almost unrestricted abortion on demand. I do not think that that bodes well for the Supreme Court ruling, nor do I think that it protects those who have no voice, the foetuses. I will be voting against this at third reading.
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, I would like my hon. friend to comment on what he feels is the male responsibility in the whole question of preventing unwanted pregnancy.
He talked about wanting to see social programs, or something to that effect, in the bill. This seems to be after the fact and directed again to women having the sole responsibility.
What is the primary responsibility of men in reproductive planning, family planning, and prevention of unwanted pregnancies? What does he think can be done so that there would be greater responsibility on the part of men so we would not have this need for abortions?

Mr. Speaker, I am going to start off by saying to my hon. colleague that I read her remarks of yesterday and I have already commented on them earlier. I find it distressing that she has intimated, at least in her remarks yesterday, that perhaps men do not have a right to participate in this debate, or to vote.
Now that is what I read in yesterday's Hansard. It shows the entrenchment of some positions. Some people who believe as the member does will still quote men who support their particular point of view.
The whole area of prevention is not solely a woman's nor a man's responsibility. It is a joint responsibility because it does not take only one gender to procreate and create new live. It takes both.
There has to be a determined, well-directed approach to prevention of unwanted pregnancies. It is true that perhaps at this time many in our society believe that the woman is solely responsible for not getting pregnant. Maybe that is the way it was when I grew up as well. But I think it is incumbent upon society and its legislators, such as ourselves, to ensure that we embark on a national program of education so that we do not have unwanted pregnancies. If that means making contraceptive technology more easily and readily available in the schools and across the counter, so that nobody ever has an economic reason for pregnancy because they cannot afford contraception, then so be it.
The whole area of preventing unwanted pregnancies is something that, as a society, we often decided to ignore. Many times parents will not sit down at an early enough age and discuss these real problems with their children. Inevitably, we end up dealing with the consequences of our own insecurity in dealing with the sexuality of our own children. The consequences of not being able to

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
deal with the sexuality of our own children through education, through prevention and through dialogue is unwanted pregnancies; it is the new scourge of the eighties and nineties and perhaps the next century in communicable diseases such as AIDS.
What I am saying, in response, is that it is equally the male and the female responsibility. It is the responsibility of families, legislators and educators. It is a societal responsibility to ensure that we deal with these very major issues so that we are not forced to deal with the consequences. Many women, and men because they also play a part in this debate, have to deal with the consequences of being ill-informed about sexuality and such things as unwanted pregnancies, abortion legislation and the crippling and deadly illness called AIDS.
In conclusion, I think that governments have to play a role and I would like to see governments play a much more pro-active role in that direction.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this being the first time I have the floor while you are in the chair, I should like to extend to you my sincere congratulations and best wishes in the performance of your duties. I am sure you will prove to be an outstanding Assistant Deputy Chairman of Committees of the Whole.
Mr. Speaker, of all the debates in which I spoke the one on abortion has to be the debate to which I devoted most time and consideration, first as a woman, second as a politician. I am sure that being a woman member of government faced with the decision involved in a vote on a measure such as Bill C-43 does not have the same implications as for our male colleagues-like yourself, Mr. Speaker-if only because nature did not intend them to carry a foetus.
In 1978 I had a miscarriage after three and a half months of pregnancy. Quite sincerely, I had yet to feel the presence of a child in my womb. It was not unwanted and the only bad memory I have is the fact that a small army of medical students kept parading through my room over the weekend. Mr. Speaker, when that topic is
being debated I feel as if my intimacy as a woman has been invaded.
I am deeply shocked when I hear pro-lifers say that women are immoral and child killers. Given the various comments I heard in this debate, I was outraged when a physician told the legislative committee members that the best thing that could happen to a 12-year-old girl impregnanted by her father was to bear his child. This is undue imposition of one's personal views on the entire life of a poor child victim of incest. Conversely it would be just as outrageous to hear a woman say she is seeking an abortion for purely esthetic reasons.
That being said, here we are again debating Bill C-43. Never have I witnessed such antagonism as I did when people appeared before the legislative committee to give evidence on Bill C-43.
With a few exceptions-two, I think-all those who took part opposed the bill, but for opposite reasons: for some, C-43 was pro-choice; for others, it was pro-life.
Every day, from coast to coast, we had almost equal numbers of witnesses with diametrically opposite opinions appear before us. It was very hard, Mr. Speaker, because as legislators, we must weigh the pros and cons to be in touch with all the people, who expect their government to make decisions. This led me to think further on the real significance of Bill C-43-access to abortion.
I do not at all share the viewpoint of the Canadian Medical Association that physicians, for fear of prosecution, will no longer perform abortions. Come on! Physicians are constantly liable to prosecution for any medical act they perform. Why should abortion, which is a medical procedure, be subject to different standards?
Neither, Mr. Speaker, do I share the opinion of those who say that the doctor, rather than the woman, will make the decision to have an abortion. Come on, Mr. Speaker, with or without a law, a woman must talk to her doctor in any case! She does not sit in front of him speechless. She must explain her situation; the doctor must examine her, whether there is a law or not. The doctor will tell her that the pregnancy has reached a certain stage and that according to his standards, he may or may not-We know that even Mr. Morgentaler, who

May 24, 1990

is the most open on this issue, does not perform abortions after 18 weeks, or at least he thinks it over seriously.
Actually, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-43 is a formal acknowledgment of what is now current practice. I listened to hon. members talking about their draft amendments, and once again I noticed that in many cases-I am not saying all, but in many cases-there is a tendency to ignore the fact that women are quite able to make such important decisions, which are never made lightly. People seem to think that women like having abortions. When a woman has to decide, who are we, who are you to judge or decide on her behalf?
In other words, Mr. Speaker, it is none of our business. To say that women who are faced with unwanted pregnancies should carry those pregnancies to term and then put these children up for adoption is narrow-minded and shows contempt for women.
I would remind those who feel insulted by what I just said of the case of a young single woman in Vancouver. In 1948, after being denied an abortion by Dr. William McCallum, who is still living with this on his conscience, she committed suicide. You may say that she committed suicide for other reasons, but in any case, she gave that particular reason, and that was one too many.
There are also thousands of women who are victims of family violence in their relationships with spouses or boyfriends. What about young women in blended families who experience situations that are extremely complex? For instance, one of my constituents came to see me, Mr. Speaker, and told me her mother's boyfriend had made her pregnant and that her mother was pregnant as well. Lovely family!
Where are all those members who are against abortion, when these women need your compassion and your understanding so that they can live like human beings? Why do you lavish all your attention on the foetus, instead of giving these women the moral support they have a right to expect? What kind of logic is this, that a foetus has as many rights as a living human being who needs help?
Over the past three years, Mr. Speaker, I have often put this question to pro-life men with whom I had lengthy discussions: You who are so adamantly pro-life, as I too am pro-life- People who believe that prochoice advocates are against life are completely off the
Government Orders
track. We are all pro-life. I would ask such a man if his beliefs were strong enough that he would readily tell his legitimate wife that his mistress is pregnant and that henceforth the family would have to make sacrifices in order to support that woman and her child. This may sound funny, but such is reality. That sort of thing is a common occurrence, Mr. Speaker. You are aware of that, take a look in your own backyard. I was given a very simple answer: Of course not, its up to society to look after that. Some people profess to be pro-life because it seems to be the thing to do, but it is a different ball game when concrete gestures are called for.
I know I will be called everything under the sun, but I have had enough being branded as irresponsible for accepting baby killings. The day before yesterday the hon. member for Hillsborough told the House, and I quote:
I am horrified that anyone could say that a procedure which kills one human being for the convenience of another is a medical procedure.
A few statistics might enlighten the House. In 1985 only 3 per cent of abortions were performed at 17 weeks, and 89 per cent at 13 weeks. As you can appreciate, Mr. Speaker, this is a far cry from what pro-life advocates would have us believe, a far ciy indeed. Women do not kill babies.
Pro-life radicals tell me that no matter how conception took place-abuse, violence, incest, you name it- the foetus has the right to live. We are not thinking about the woman who will have to bear this child conceived in extraordinarily violent conditions. It is like being forced to bear children. I wonder what these people would do to enforce an anti-abortion law. We can talk and make long speeches all we want but, in the end, we must think about the consequences. What are they going to do? Build more prisons for women? Issue an injunction against my belly? Nobody in Canadian society has a right to do that to me.
We should perhaps listen to reason and realize that women have rights, as the Supreme Court recognized in the Morgentaler case as well as in the famous Dodd and Chantal Daigle cases. It is easy to spout out great moral principles. Of course, Mr. Speaker, we all wish no woman had to go through an abortion. If that were the case, it would mean that women's economic and emotional situation is perfect. There would not be a problem.

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
But that is not the reality. As you know, most single mothers live below the poverty line. They are destitute. In the name of morality, some people want to- The women having abortions will only be judged after they die and come face to face with God like everyone else. It is not up to us human beings to decide for them.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know how much time I have left but I hope the bill is passed by the House. At last, after all these years of wrenching debates, I am sure it will be challenged before the courts, as the Committee was told. Has there ever been an act of Parliament that has not been challenged before the courts? They all are. In the final instance, the Supreme Court will decide.
Mr. Speaker, the Supreme Court will decide that Parliament has made its decision, and I think that after royal assent, people will say: This bill isn't so bad after all. Of course, personally, I would have preferred no legislation at all. However, I was elected and I have a seat in the House, on the government side. Decisions must be made. If I were on the other side, it would be easy. I would say no, no legislation, and I would object to any legislation at all. That is how things work in this country. That is how democracy works in our political parties. I am on this side of the House, however, and I am faced with Bill C-43. What I want is for the House to finish this debate, because I want to go on to something else. I want to make the public aware and demand public attention for the worst crisis in society today, and I am referring to the sexual abuse of children. It is a tragedy, and a national disgrace, and we must come out and say so. We have to rescue these children and give them love and affection. We have to get them out of the horrible environment in which they live. We cannot let this go on.
Mr. Speaker, we have seen what is happening in the case of Judge Andree Ruffo in Quebec City, a woman who has my unqualified admiration and who is fighting the bureaucracy because she believes in children. We all believe in children. I was so pleased when the former leader of the New Democratic Party decided, in his last debate in the House, to talk about child poverty. That is another disgrace we must talk about. Instead of having these futile discussions, instead of trying to make women
do certain things and prevent them from doing others, we should sit down and talk about what we can do to deal, once and for all, with child poverty. What can we do to deal with the tragic financial circumstances of Canadian women? In my riding there are women who have trouble making both ends meet, who are poor, sick, and the rest. They have to cope with just about everything, and their husband, the father of their children, has left. Sometimes they don't even know where he is. He is in love with some other woman. Great! That is reality. Those are the sordid facts. Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I hope that all members will realize we are going to pass Bill C-43. It isn't perfect. Nothing is ever perfect. However, I was closely involved in preparing this legislation, and it was a long, complex and difficult process.
I would like to take this opportunity to thank all my colleagues on the government side who worked with me, in the Conservative caucus and on the legislative committee, so that finally we were able to produce a bill that in the circumstances, I believe, provides the best possible compromise Canadian society can expect from a government that has shown leadership.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member feels very strongly about what she has just said. Her emotions came across the House very strongly, but she mentioned one thing that bothered me a bit.
This is a free vote in the House of Commons on the abortion issue. The hon. member said that, because she is sitting on the government side of the House, she must make a decision, and that it is harder for her because she is on the government side of the House than if she were sitting on the other side. I want to state very clearly that, in a free vote in the House of Commons, it is up to every individual, no matter where he or she sits in the House, to make that personal decision on his or her own.
Is the hon. member telling us that she has been pressured by the government into voting for this bill or is she, indeed, voting in accordance with her conscience? I am sure I am speaking for people in every comer of the House when I tell her that, on this issues, all members have to stand and be counted. Whether they belong to one party or another does not matter. They are still
May 24, 1990

accountable to their constituents and a free vote in the House must be precisely that, no matter where we sit.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not received any pressure, none whatsoever, from anybody on this side of the House regarding this bill. I just say, because the debate has been going on for 10 years or more, since the first legislation came into force under the Trudeau government, that I hope we can deal with this bill now and then go on to more important questions.
I am sure that Hansard tomorrow will show that I said that, as the government, we have the obligation to present legislation. The Prime Minister has said that because of the various views on this question there is going to be a free vote. No one on this side of the House, certainly not myself, has been pushed to vote for this bill. I think the hon. member is as sick and tired of the debate as we are. I would hope that he would vote for the bill so that we can carry on to other important matters. That is what I was trying to say to him, and that is what I hope he is going to do next Tuesday.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, would like to congratulate the hon. member on a very passionate, forceful speech, although I disagree with most of what she said.
Through the process of committee hearings in which she claims to have participated, did the hon. member have any remorse at all at the fact that the bill has a wide-open gestational period? There is no limit as to when a woman could ask for and receive an abortion. The child could be hours, days, or weeks from delivery and there would be no problem at all if the doctor agrees an abortion should be performed, for whatever reasons. Did that cause any qualms in the hon. member's mind at all?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the facts speak for themselves. In the 1985 Statistics Canada report, it is very clear that no abortion was performed after 20 weeks unless for a very, very important reason. Only 0.3 per cent of abortions are performed after 20 weeks, and I suppose then only for very dramatic and important reasons. The facts speak for themselves. Doctors in the country do not perform abortions after a certain period.
The Chantal Daigle affair was a different matter because it is one case among thousands and thousands of cases. Are we going to legislate regarding this one case?
5. ft 31
No, because the facts are there and I will urge the member to read the 1985 report.
Of course, I totally disagree with a woman having an abortion after 20 weeks, unless it is for very dramatic and important health reasons.

Mr. Speaker, more than 5,000 aging Canadian veterans residing in long-term care hospitals were dealt a blow in the government's harsh cutting measures contained in the Wilson budget.
They will have to pay more than $3,000 each for their lodging in an effort by the government to save $18 million. In addition, as a result of the government attack on the Veterans Independence Program, 16,000 veterans who are living at home will lose some of the help provided for their heavy house cleaning because of an $18 million cut from this key program to aging veterans to which the government refers to as streamlining.
This saving of $35 million against of a deficit of $30 billion, on the backs of the veterans, is a poor way to show our appreciation of their valiant deeds on behalf of all Canadians during the war. It is especially so as these veterans' sources are severely limited.
This shameful and disgraceful way to go about finding means to reduce the deficit will not be taken lying down. That message is coming in more clearly every day. We hope that the Prime Minister and his government will listen to the plea to rescind these cuts and allow our veterans to retain their well-earned dignity.

Mr. Speaker, Dominion Textile recently won an award of excellence in the Quebec business community's most prestigious competition for the growth of its business outside the country. Dominion Textile won the Mercure prize for international development. This competition was started by the Quebec Chamber of Commerce 10 years ago to

May 24, 1990
5. ft 31
celebrate the outstanding achievements of business people.
As a result of their acquisitions and expansion of their operations, Dominion Textile has become the world's largest denim producer and a leader in many other products as well. The corporation went ahead with major investments in technology for several plants, including a $35-million modernization program now under way in Drummondville and Saint-Timothee-all this without subsidies.
Dominion Textile, which began business in 1905, is the largest supplier of textiles and related products in Canada. Its international network of offices, factories, subsidiaries and associated companies now extends to nearly 50 countries.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to offer the management and workers of Dominion Textile my warmest congratulations.

Mr. Speaker, my NDP colleagues and I were saddened today to learn of the death of Val Orlikow, wife of our former colleague David Orlikow and the former member for Winnipeg North, who served this House and his constituents with distinction for over 26 years. I am sure all members would want to join with me in expressing sincere condolences to David at this very difficult time.
Val Orlikow has a place in Canadian history independent of David. She has a place as one of the victims of CIA psychiatric experiments conducted in Canada at the Allan Institute in Montreal. One of her goals in life was to see justice done with respect to these experiments, and others like them, not just those done by the CIA. The case of Linda McDonald of British Columbia comes to mind.
Val Orlikow has died without the Canadian government ever admitting its own complicity in the CIA experiments that so damaged her life.
Out of court settlements in the United States are one thing, but having your own country own up to its part and promising never to do again what was done to her, was something worth waiting for, and wait she did.
For Mrs. Orlikow the wait is over. For the government, the shame continues.

Mr. Speaker, the Presidents of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania met in Tallin, Estonia on May 12 to reinstate the 1934 treaty that established close political and economic ties between the Baltic republics when they were previously independent.
At this meeting they issued of the Joint Baltic Council statement requesting that the conference on security and co-operation of the European member countries arrange a hearing in Copenhagen in order to present a mutual declaration and statement requesting that Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania be admitted as members.
The 35-country membership currently includes such countries as Cyprus, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, both Germanys, Poland, Yugoslavia and Romania.
I believe it is only fitting that legitimate member states of the east European community be allowed access to address a plenary session at a human rights conference in Copenhagen.
I urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs to draw this issue to the attention of the Canadian delegation to Copenhagen, to develop a favourable stance and to report subsequently back to the House his suggested stance.

Mr. Speaker, since deregulation came into effect two years ago, the trucking industry has suffered at the hands of the federal government. This government did not plan ahead for deregulation. It has refused to listen to the concerns of the industry.
This past week and until this morning we were faced with a crisis. The various blockades represent the anger
May 24, 1990

and the frustration that truckers feel because the concerns of their industry have been continually ignored.
This situation demands attention. In my riding of Malpeque, one trucking organization had 150 trucks delayed on the highway between Prince Edward Island and Ottawa.
I urge this government to resolve immediately the concerns of the trucking industry. It is time to begin listening to the industry, and to ensure that concerns are attended to so that critical emergencies like the one we have experienced do not happen again.

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow, Friday, May 25, is Sneaker Day, when all Canadians, including members of Parliament, are invited to wear their sneakers in order to promote a healthy active lifestyle. Sneaker Day marks the beginning of Canada's Fitweek, a week of activities which runs from May 25 to June 3.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add that Canada's Fitweek is the most important celebration of its kind in the world. All Canadians should be proud of this achievement. Last year, eight million people from coast to coast took part in over 14,000 events.
The Government of Canada, through Fitness Canada, is a major supporter of Canada's Fitweek, which is presented in co-operation with the provinces and territories, 17 national organizations and 12 sponsors. Canada's Fitweek is really a popular event.
Over the next 10 days, I call on all hon. members to join Canadians across the land by promoting and participating in the many activities planned for their ridings.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George -Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government's Green Plan is collapsing with the resignation of the minister and the
appointment of a part-time Minister of the Environment.
One way the government can show its commitment to the environment and our forests would be for the Minister of Forestry to announce today, as forestry ministers in the west, especially British Columbia, are expecting him to do, that a new tree planting agreement will be signed today to help renew our forests.
The Minister of Forestry has not lived up to five previous commitments to sign a B.C. agreement. He should help himself, this government and our forests by moving immediately to have these agreements signed and implemented.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to announce the kick-off of Canada's 1990 Fitweek which starts tomorrow, May 25.
All Canadians are invited to join me and my House of Commons colleagues in donning their sneakers, no matter how flashy or conservative they happen to be- mine are pink-to partake in a physical activity such as running, rope jumping or a stroll in the park.
Canada's Fitweek, May 25 to June 3, is the largest annual celebration of physical activity in the world. Again this year over eight million participants will take part in every type of physical activity available.
It is truly an event where collaborative efforts between the public and private sectors promote a united message about the importance of an active lifestyle.
Sneaker Day is just one of 12 national projects. In addition, municipalities have organized activities in the spirit of friendly competition with other municipalities.
On this Sunday in my riding of York-Simcoe there is the Persechini Easter Seals Fitness Centre Walk-a-Thon to raise funds for crippled children.
In Ottawa, we have the run for retinitis-pigmentosa research.
Sneaker Day could be the mark of a new day in each of our lives, a day where physical activity, a healthier lifestyle becomes the national, the Canadian way of life.
We are all aware of the increased benefits of maintaining an active life. I invite all members to join Canadians

May 24, 1990
in promoting and participating in the many events planned in their own constituencies as part of Canada's Fitweek.

Mr. Speaker, western diversification was supposedly the answer to western Canada's economic woes. It was going to produce less dependence upon the agricultural sector.
Interestingly enough, eight months before the election there were expenditures that exceeded $400 million. In the fiscal year after the election, expenditures were only $136.8 million. What a coincidence!
This year's Estimates have no reference whatsoever to the Centre for Sustainable Development, no reference whatsoever to the renewal of infrastructure program that was promised for rural Manitoba, and mentioned by the Prime Minister in Portage la Prairie when he visited.
We note with much chagrin that Manitoba and Saskatchewan do not have their fair share. Sixty-three per cent of these projects are in urban areas, and only 37 per cent in rural communities.
Tory ministers and big business-and I do not say that, it is the Canadian Federation of Independent Business-are getting too much of these funds.
There is a large bureaucracy-over 300 people-which is consuming 20 per cent of the expenditures.
We can only diversify if we look at diversification in the total context of high interest rates, the reduction in expenditures for health, education, agriculture, and the shutting down of VIA Rail. We must take all of those into consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity today to say a few words about the Meech Lake Accord because I think that what is happening to the Accord is unacceptable.
The Meech Lake Accord as signed on June 3, 1987 by all First Ministers has been criticized, debased and worse by people who are negative, suspicious, impatient and lacking in any kind of generosity towards each other.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is intolerable that negative feelings that have sush a destructive impact on the goal of national unity set by our government and its leader, Mr. Mulroney, should be allowed to prevail. We should all realize that the little guy from Baie-Comeau, as he has often said, this great Quebecer and this genuine Canadian, will never again let Quebec be insulted as it was under the Trudeau and Chretien regime.
For him and for us, the elected Conservative representatives from Quebec, it is more than a question of honour, it is a matter of the heart.
I have confidence in our Prime Minister and his sensible attitude, and I hope I will never have to doubt the intelligence of some of our provincial First Ministers.

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow, Argentina commemorates its National Day. It will be the 180th anniversary of what has become in Argentinian history the most important event, an event that marks Argentina's true independence and its existence as a free country.
The Argentine revolution of May 1810 was the initial step of a long process in the region which culminated in the independence of various countries of Latin America.
In 1983 Argentina was one of the first countries to initiate a remarkable process of democratization that rebounded through every country in the whole region.
Just a few days ago we hosted a very important commercial mission from Argentina. That mission was headed by two governors, Dr. Eduardo Angeloz and Dr. Rodriguez Saa, both of whom happen to be representatives of two major political parties in Argentina, indicating that every co-operation is possible if there is enough will.
May 24, 1990

As former principal of Argentina School here in Canada and in my present role I would like to extend to Argentina my very best wishes and every success in all future endeavours as they commemorate Argentina National Day.

Mr. Speaker, within the text of the Special Meech Lake Committee Report-which I had the honour with other colleagues in this House to help prepare-are some passing observations about our hearings which may in fact be more powerful for current considerations than any of the other important messages it contains.
Witness after witness, even those most critical of the Meech Lake Accord, expressed support for Canadian unity and the need to make Canada's second most populous province, Quebec, a participating member in the Canadian constitutional family. There was also general agreement that Quebec's five proposals were reasonable for that purpose.
Surely by now most will realize that therein lies the very essence of the Meech Lake Accord, and it is attainable if only we have the resolve to take it within our grasp.
Let us all support and encourage our First Ministers throughout Canada to bear this over-powering single purpose above all other considerations as they reflect upon the future of our country in these critical days ahead.

Mr. Speaker, Canada Post continues to cut back on service to rural Canadians. It is contracting out its rural delivery in such a way as to make effective service impossible.
According to officials in Percy township in my riding, Canada Post's tender form for delivery in that area states all mail is to be delivered by three o'clock in the afternoon, seven hours after the local post office opens.
The route is 168 kilometres long with 480 delivery points. Sorting takes at least three hours. To drive from
one end of the route to the other at the speed limit and without stopping takes over two hours. Even if driving up to each mailbox and inserting the mail were to take only a minute for each delivery point, this activity alone would take a total of eight hours. Simple calculations indicate that deliveries would only be finished at nine o'clock at night.
Canada Post not only needs outside help to deliver the mail, it seems to me it needs outside help to do its math.
I urge Canada Post to ensure it reduces the size of its new rural routes to ensure timely delivery. As the Liberal report on the post office specifies, the minister responsible should ensure Canada Post consults in a meaningful way with its best source of information, local citizens, before making major changes.

Mr. Speaker, the corporate welfare bum of the week salutes the wheeler-dealers of Canadian finance. The first nominee is Bums Fry Ltd. which gave $56,000 to the Conservative party in 1988 and $21,000 to the Liberals.
The second nominee is Merrill Lynch which gave $106,000 to the Conservative party in 1988 and only $43,000 to the Liberals.
The third nominee is RBC Dominion Securities which gave $50,000 to both the Conservative and the Liberal parties in 1988.
Now for the winner. The envelope, please.
The winner is Merrill Lynch. It bet on the Conservative party in a big way in 1988. For mastering the art of the deal, Merrill Lynch is the corporate welfare bum of the week.

Mr. Speaker, I speak of an event which knows no political boundaries, no racial boundaries, no prejudice of any kind. It is an event which springs from compassion and the kind of caring of which humans at their best are capable.

May 24, 1990
Oral Questions
The annual Muscular Dystrophy Telethon taking place May 26 to May 27 gives residents of Brampton-Malton and surrounding communities an opportunity to come together as one community and support this very special cause.
I would like to pay particular attention to the involvement of our Brampton fire-fighters in the telethon. Not only do these men and women protect our communities every day, without their support the fight against muscular dystrophy would surely be a much harder battle.
I urge everyone in the riding of Brampton-Malton to play their part, as usual, in the race against this debilitating disease and to prove once again that in Brampton- Malton muscular dystrophy faces a tough opponent.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have questions for the Prime Minister about the constitutional situation, a matter of growing concern for Canadians.
Yesterday in the Elouse the Prime Minister told us that he and Senator Murray were developing new proposals, that he would be speaking to the premiers about them and, further, that he would be reporting to the House on the results of these contacts.
Will the Prime Minister inform the House and therefore Canadians of the exact content of these proposals, of the reactions of the premiers to them, and the extent to which the recommendations of the special committee, the Charest committee, are being taken into account in these efforts to bring about a fair solution to the constitutional impasse?
Mr. Speaker, I plan to begin a series of direct meetings with the premiers beginning tonight at six o'clock at 24 Sussex with Premier Don Getty of Alberta.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this will be encouraging news for Canadians.
However, yesterday, the Premier of Ontario, Mr. Peterson, and Mr. Getty met in Toronto. Both of them called for an early meeting of all first ministers-the Prime Minister of Canada together with all the premiers of all the provinces.
Speaking of the present constitutional accord the Ontario Premier said:
We don't have a lot of time. I think at best we have another week.
Premier Getty said:
So how do we make progress without meeting?
I think he was talking about a meeting of the Prime Minister with all the premiers.
Even though the meeting the Prime Minister has spoken about I hope will be helpful, I ask the Prime Minister: in view of the views of Mr. Peterson and Mr. Getty, does he not now agree that the time has come to call an early meeting of all the first ministers on this constitutional situation?

Mr. Speaker, I think we are going about it in the proper way.
I have been in touch with the premiers. This is an effort to meet individually with all of them to attempt to narrow the differences and at the conclusion, hopefully, if it is at all possible, it will give rise to the reasonable possibility of calling a First Ministers' Conference that might be successful.
By way of illustration, I point out to my hon. friend who raised the question of Premier Peterson, that he neglected to mention that Premier Peterson yesterday made a very thoughtful and compelling call to the three premiers, who have either repudiated or failed to sign the Meech Lake Accord, to do so, and to consider doing so urgently, because of the importance of the constitutional family being made whole.
I think Premier Peterson was speaking on behalf of a growing number of Canadians when he called upon those three provincial governments to do everything they could to honour the signatures provided at Meech Lake by predecessor governments.
May 24, 1990

I can inform my friend that after I meet with Premier Getty this evening I will be meeting with Premier Peterson tomorrow at one o'clock at 24 Sussex.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my second question I made specific reference to the views of Premier Peterson because of the constructive approach he has been taking to the matter of nation building and his openness and understanding of the concerns not only of Quebec but of all the regions and provinces of our country.
[Translation}
Mr. Speaker, when people ask him to call a First Ministers' Conference to get us out of the constitutional impasse, the Prime Minister keeps answering that the chances of failure are too high. Doesn't the Prime Minister realize that the risk is far greater if we do not call a conference, if we do nothing, than if there is a conference?

Surely, I ask the Prime Minister, is it not better to meet and risk failure than to fail by not meeting at all? Why not have a Conference of all the First Ministers before June 23?

Mr. Speaker, I know that my hon. friend had questions prepared in advance, but I have been trying to convey to him that there is serious movement going on and there are very serious meetings that have been lined up. I begin this evening with the Premier of Alberta, who was the host of the premiers' conference in Edmonton in 1986 that gave rise to the unanimous call for the equivalent of a Quebec round to seek to bring Quebec into the Constitution following the failure of 1981-82 to do so.
Premier Getty has been a staunch and unfailing ally of Meech Lake ever since.
Premier Peterson, speaking on behalf of the province and the people of Ontario, provided very significant leadership at Meech Lake. He, too, has been unfailing in his support of the Meech Lake Accord as a great instrument of national unity.
It was in that spirit I think that Premier Peterson, well qualified to speak to this issue, called upon the three recalcitrant provinces, if I may put it that way, to sign the
Oral Questions
Meech Lake Accord as quickly as possible so that we could in a very constructive and thoughtful way get on with the process of building a greater Canada.
The meetings that we have called are designed to do precisely that. I think my hon. friend would agree that at this particular point some prudence in meeting with the premiers and trying to prepare an effective First Ministers' Conference is worth the time rather than calling a First Ministers' Conference simply for the sake of having called one that might result in failure. I want success for Canada. I want a Constitution that binds all Canadians together.

Mr. Speaker, the country is being plunged into an economic crisis by the government's monetary policy. Today there was an increase in the Bank of Canada rate by 25 basis points.
How far is the Minister of Finance prepared to let the Governor of the Bank of Canada go in his obsession with zero inflation? Is he prepared to ruin the manufacturing sector in this country? Or, will he come to his senses and direct the Bank of Canada Governor to reflect the reality of the Canadian economic condition?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is correct when he says that there has been a 25 basis point increase in the bank rate today.
I would say that this is in good part due to some of the uncertainties surrounding the ongoing constitutional discussions. The sooner we can get these discussions behind us in a successful way, the sooner we can get behind this uncertainty.
My hon. friend refers to policies of the government. I think that the policies of the government are on track. We are consistently following a series of policies.
I might say to my hon. friend that the financial requirements that were evident for the year ending in March of this year indicate that the budget deficit is about $1 billion less than what we had previously projected.

Hear, hear.

May 24, 1990
Oral Questions

I think this indicates quite clearly the consistent and conscientious approach that we have been taking to economic policy.
This is the fourth consecutive year in which the budget deficit has come in less than the projections that we have made. The policies that we are following are paying off. They are producing effective results for this country.

Mr. Speaker, on February 20, the Minister of Finance projected an annual average of 11.1 per cent for interest rates in this country.
He talks about his revised deficit figures. Are the minister and his government going to continue with this high interest policy in the face of evidence from every sector of our economy that it is destroying the economy of this country?
The interest rate today of 14.05 per cent is the highest it has been in eight years. How high does it go before the government realizes it is on a track to destruction?

Mr. Speaker, I do not think my hon. friend wants to lead with his chin and talk about the heights of interest rates, since I only need remind him that what we are trying to do is stop inflation from getting out of control so that we can avoid the very high interest rates that we had between 1980 and 1982 when inflation did get out of control.
My hon. friend refers to inflationary pressures. We started in 1989 with an increase in unit labour costs to 4.5 per cent. This is the best example of the broadest measure of how our industry and businesses are competing with the rest of the world.
They started the year at 4.5 per cent and ended at 6.9 per cent. That is the best measure that we can show of how our companies are gaining business.
That increase in inflationary pressures means lost business. Lost business means lost jobs.
We are trying to turn that 6.9 per cent number down so that we can get the pressures and the cost structures of Canadian business under control in order to save and build jobs as well as to have a much brighter future.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Right Hon. Prime Minister.
I want to say at the outset that I am pleased that the Prime Minister is going to begin meeting directly with the premiers of this country to discuss the serious situation that we are in.
I would also like to say to the Prime Minister that the objective is a united Canada. The winner in the end has to be Canada itself. I am glad there is now some movement in terms of meeting with the premiers.
In light of these discussions with the premiers and the Prime Minister's talk in the House yesterday about some new proposals now being discussed with them, is he now ready to elaborate a bit on what these new proposals might be?
I realize the sensitivity and delicacy of some of these issues. In light of that, is the Prime Minister in any position today to elaborate to some degree on the direction of these new proposals he is taking to the premiers of this country?

Mr. Speaker, first, in a personal way, but probably on behalf of all members of the House on this very important issue, I would like to convey congratulations to the member of the NDP for his role on the questions of national unity that has been unfailingly positive and constructive at all times.
Hear, hear.
You just dropped 20 points in the polls, Lome. There goes your re-election.
The kiss of death.

Mr. Speaker, I did not mean to hurt the hon. member with that comment, but I think he knows exactly what I mean. This is a delicate subject which, as Premier Peterson pointed out yesterday, requires a great deal of statesmanship and a very constructive approach because the stakes are very high. What we are talking about is the future of Canada.
May 24, 1990

Yesterday, Premier Getty said "I was at Meech Lake, as were the other premiers. I put the signature of Don Getty and the signature of the Government of Alberta on a piece of paper which was designed in Alberta's interests, in the interests of western Canada, and most of all in the interests of a united Canada". He said "I propose to honour that because it is indispensable that we all do so in the interests of Canadian unity".
Hear, hear!

I will discuss some ideas we have with the premiers. I will ask for some of their thoughts. There have been a number of conversations ongoing among them and, hopefully, out of these intensive consultations will come a consensus reasonable enough to give rise to the view that we might hold a constructive first ministers' conference which will result in what every member of this House wants, a firm irrevocable statement of a united Canada.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question to the Prime Minister is in the same vein, about a national problem that we have. I wonder if the Prime Minister can account for the latest tremendous jump in interest rates in this country? We now have an increase of 25 basis points. It is the highest bank rate in the country since August, 1982. The inflation rate has dropped to 5 per cent. I wonder if the Prime Minister agrees with the Minister of Finance that the latest increase in the bank rate of this country is due to the constitutional impasse and, if so, does that not create more of a sense of urgency to try to resolve this question as quickly as possible?

Mr. Speaker, I agree with both my honourable friend and the Minister of Finance that it is due in part to the political instability that has been engendered because of serious questions raised here and in money markets around the world about our ongoing discussions. It is precisely for this reason why it is so absolutely indispensable for every Canadian, particularly those first ministers whose predecessors had signed a constitutional document, to understand the importance of constructive and thoughtful compromise.
Oral Questions
I thought Premier Getty, and I am paraphrasing, put it best of all when he said that to some extent constitutional discussion among Canadians is an act of faith. He said Alberta did this in the interests of national unity, believing that in subsequent discussions Alberta, which has been a chief proponent of Senate reform for many years, would be able to achieve that in ongoing and subsequent discussions.
Premier Getty is right. I believe that the faith he showed at Meech Lake will never be abused by any first minister or by any Canadian. Any first minister who would do that, I think would be doing a profound disservice to Canada and to Canadian unity. Premier Getty, Premier Peterson, and others, are entirely right. Some degree of good faith, of course, is required from Canadians among one another so that the document, having been signed, can give rise to Quebec coming back home into the constitutional family and will allow us to move on finally to second and third, and no doubt fourth rounds, into the future, as one strong, united Canada.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my final supplementary is directed to the Minister of Finance. I suggest that the interest rate policy itself is creating instability in this country. I wonder whether the Minister of Finance is ready to send a clear signal across the country and around the world that this country is indeed strong by insisting that the Bank of Canada, and the Governor of the Bank of Canada, drop interest rates immediately in this country?
Is he willing now to stand up and say to John Crow that enough is enough? High interest rates in this country are hurting ordinary Canadians from coast to coast, our bank rate is now 5 per cent higher than the American bank rate, our inflation rate is dropping in the country, and because of these factors, because of the situation in the country, let us send out a strong signal to say that we are a strong country. Let us drop those interest rates so we can appropriately become more productive as an economy in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in saying that this is a strong country and that we do have a strong economy. That is precisely why the budget deficit has come in $1 billion less than we had projected.

May 24, 1990
Oral Questions
Hear, hear!

The policies we have been following, whether they be monetary policy, interest rate policy or budgetary policy, or policy to improve the efficiency of the economy, all of these are broadly supported by the major international economic organizations, such as the International Monetary Fund or the Organization for Economic Co-Operation and Development in Paris. These organizations state that our policies are the right policies we should be following. The facts are there themselves.
Canada has been second only behind Japan over the last five years in economic growth. We are number one of the major industrialized countries in the creation of new jobs. Ten years ago we were number ten of the trading countries in our trade performance. In the latest figures, we are number seven in ranking. We are improving our ranking in many, many ways. That says a good deal about the strength of our economy. It also says a good deal about the wisdom of the policies we have been following.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wish to draw to the attention of hon. members the presence in the gallery of a delegation from British Columbia to the Government of Canada headed by the Honourable Stan Hagen, Minister of Regional and Economic Development and the Honourable Bruce Strachen, Minister of Advanced Education, Training and Technology of British Columbia, and two distinguished scientists, Nobel prize recipient, Dr. Carlo Rubbia, Director of Cem in Geneva and Dr. Val Fitch, Dean of Phsyics of Princeton University and 1980 Nobel prize recipient.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. The trucking crisis in Canada is a direct result of this government's policy of deregulation.
Since last Monday, General Motors in Quebec sent home 3,000 workers; 15,000 workers were sent home in Oshawa; Chrysler's van plant in Windsor was shut down
and Ford shut down three plants in St. Thomas and Oakville. Fresh produce needed by Canadians was left rotting at border crossing points.
Will the minister inform the House of the commitments he made to Canadian truckers today, and, in particular, the remedies that will go into effect to protect truckers against cabotage and the unfair pricing practices that American truckers have been imposing on Canadian truckers?

Interestingly enough, Mr. Speaker, the truckers did not mention deregulation as their problem at all.
I went to Windsor last night in order to meet with representatives of the independent truckers. We had very helpful discussions during which we agreed to examine further methods of eliminating cabotage in co-operation with the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
Second, there was some concern with respect to unfair competition. I agreed that we would look into that matter. We went into some discussions as to whether the appropriate amount of fuel tax is being paid at all times by all carriers. We are prepared to look into methods to sort that out. I also would say that I had the assistance of the Minister of Transport for Ontario in this matter.
When the discussions were concluded, the representatives of the independent truckers were satisfied and undertook to see that the barricades would be lifted.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the same minister. The big question remains: why must there always be a crisis before we get involved in settling the problem? Look at the air traffic control problem, the airport security and shipping problems and the unfair competition that was levied against the Canadian truckers. We warned the government about what deregulation would do to the Canadian trucking industry.
When will the minister deliver a new transportation policy for Canada and Canadian workers that will not only protect the Canadian trucker but will protect all Canadian workers in the transportation industry? This government has an obligation to do that.
May 24, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I think perhaps a discussion with my friend's colleague from Winnipeg might be a little helpful in informing him as to exactly when deregulation started. It was before the hon. member's time but deregulation started certainly in my hon. friend's time.
All of those problems occur from time to time. We have taken the necessary steps. We went down to Windsor to look at the problem and to come up with some answers. We have come up with some answers. The truckers said they would lift the barricade. I take them at their word.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the right hon. Prime Minister. Today the crucial consultation sessions on the government's Green Plan for the environment began the long-awaited legislation on the environmental assessment process is expected in the House of Commons shortly. Despite the importance and the fullness of the environmental agenda in Canada, the Prime Minister has appointed a minister who admits he can only be a part-time environment minister.
Does the Prime Minister believe protection of the environment is a part-time job?

Mr. Speaker, no. Indeed the protection of the environment is a full-time job. It is one of the highest importance which is why, I believe for the first time in Canadian history, under this government the environment minister was brought into the Priorities and Planning committee of the Cabinet of Canada, indicating the highest priority that this government attributes to the environment. I may be mistaken on that but I think it is right.
With regard to the question, my hon. friend knows that there was-how might I delicately put this-an unplanned vacancy in the department, as a result of which I have asked to act on an interim basis one of the most senior ministers of the government, the President of the Treasury Board. He is also a member of P and P, he has been a member of the ministerial committee preparing The Green Plan from its inception and was specifically
Oral Questions
charged by me, as Prime Minister, from the beginning with ensuring that full financing was there for The Green Plan. I can think of no one more qualified than him to do it.

Mr. Speaker, the fact remains that the minister in question did say in answers to some questions from the news media that he could only be a part-time environment minister.
A part-time environment minister is not acceptable to Canadians. Will the Prime Minister agree today, because of the very busy schedule of the President of the Treasury Board, to assign these important responsibilities to a full-time senior minister with the authority and mandate to provide the leadership necessary to meet today's environmental challenges?
