Mr. Speaker, while I indicated in the release yesterday that this assignment of responsibilities is on an interim basis, all who know the President of the Treasury Board and know his work habits will know that he will work full and complete days at the environment ministry to make sure that that job is done exactly the way my hon. friend would want it to be done.
Speaking of which, because of his interest in the environment, I know my hon. friend would want to celebrate today the fact that, after some six years of hard slugging by this government and by many members of the House, yesterday the House of Representatives in the United States passed the Clean Air Act. We are now well on our way to an acid rain treaty with the United States.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the government wants me to congratulate the government. I will wait until the acid rain legislation is through the United States process before I give any accolades to anyone.
My question is also directed to the right hon. Prime Minister and is about the environment. Canadians are deeply concerned about pollution, about drinking water quality, about global warming and about the inaction of the government.
By nature of the portfolio, the recent resignation of the former Minister of the Environment has meant the loss of two years time, hope, and energy put in by

May 24, 1990
Oral Questions
Canadians across the country in pursuit of policies on the environment. My question to the Prime Minister is also in relation to his appointment of a part-time minister. The Minister of the Environment is here but the hearings are being launched today in Winnipeg and the Minister of Energy is there. Would the Prime Minister at least assure Canadians who are participating in the consultations in Winnipeg that the part-time minister he has appointed will be the minister who carries through the consultations and carries through implementation of the Green Plan when it comes before the House?

Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend is needlessly churlish in regard to a situation that I have explained at great length. He implies that the resignation itself of the minister means that two years of effort and energy have been lost. If that were true, then the recent resignation of Ed Broadbent would mean that two years of energy and effort were lost by the NDP and that is clearly not true. You are as energetic and as brilliant as you have has always been and I congratulate you.

Mr. Speaker, let me respond with great celerity, as the Prime Minister would always want to say, and ask a question of the new part-time Minister of the Environment, who himself described to me yesterday the job as being part-time. The most important cabinet portfolio in Canada today is a parttime one.
Another minister drafted the Green Plan over the past year. A minister who has continuously sent out mixed signals on the environment and is generally seen by Canadians as being anti-environment, the Minister of Energy, is at the launch of the Green Plan hearings today. Does the new Minister of the Environment plan to participate in the consultations fully and completely, and does he intend to stay for the implementation of what he learns from the consultations, or will some other minister take on that job?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would just like to tell my hon. colleague across the way that there are at least three things that have not changed at all.
The first one is the timetable that we are following on our environmental agenda. That timetable will be respected and I expect that we will be able to meet our targets as announced before.
The second thing is that our commitment has not changed. The environment is at the top of our agenda as a government and will remain there.
The third point which has not changed is that there is a full-time Minister of the Environment. I expect to be in Halifax on Monday morning, I expect to be at all the hearings and I expect to see the process through.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Agriculture and concerns the Canadian Egg Producers Council which complains that importers of table eggs from the United States repack eggs imported in bulk in containers labeled "Product of Canada".
Can the minister reassure this House and the producers and tell them what he intends to do to stop this fradulent labeling practice?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we were informed of this matter in recent months.
Canada's position is very clear: table eggs must show the country of origin. The Canadian Egg Processors Council, unfortunately, does not support us in this position.
On several occasions, we have brought those concerned together and it is obviously in our interest, that this policy be respected by people here in Canada. I can assure my colleague that this matter has already been discussed and we will continue to work on it so that consumers who buy products on the market know the country of origin of these products.
I can assure you that we will take it into account.
May 24, 1990

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the House echo the remarks made by the minister last Tuesday when he expressed Canada's dismay concerning the unprecedented violent acts following the murder of seven Palestinians at Richon-Letion near Tel-Aviv.
We also believe that the current deadlock in the peace process contributes to create instability and violence.
This is why I want to ask the minister whether Canada is prepared to support the Americans who would send United Nations observers to the occupied territories, and what will our ambassador have to say at the Security Council sessions scheduled for tomorrow or Saturday?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In fact, Mr. Speaker, neither the United States nor any other Security Council member have actively advocated dispatching such an observer team. However the American Secretary of State did say that the U.S. administration would certainly entertain this kind of proposition.
For our part we in Canada are also prepared to consider this proposition because our country has always been a strong supporter of peacekeeping activities and observer teams. Hon. members would know that Canada did lend strong support to the rather limited but no less important UNRWA mission concerning the Palestinians.
Canada's ambassador will indeed play a significant part in the Security Council discussions.

Mr. Speaker, will the minister and the Prime Minister raise the issue with UN Secretary General Perez de Cuellar and also with President Gorbachev during their respective visits next week in Ottawa? If so, what will he tell them regarding Canada's position?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we certainly do intend to discuss the question of the Middle East and, particularly, the
Oral Questions
matters now before the Security Council with the Secretary General of the United Nations and with the leaders of the Soviet government when they are here next week.
We will indicate to them that Canada is prepared to support any constructive activity that might be taken by the United Nations, and we will certainly take the opportunity to reiterate the point that was made by the hon. member in the introduction to his question and that is that the situation now is creating circumstances of increasing instability. One cannot assume that the status quo is neutral in terms of the lives of people in the territory. It is becoming increasingly dangerous. Among other things, the capacity of moderate leadership on both sides to retain their efforts to exercise restraint is put under strain every day.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Fitness and Amateur Sport.
The Sports Federation of Canada, in its brief to the finance committee, stated that "the application of the GST would have a devastating effect on the activities of amateur sport".
My question to the minister is this: In recognition of the importance of amateur sport here in Canada, will the minister increase the funding to these organizations to offset the negative impact of the GST?
I hope so.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Danis (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have met with the Federation of Canadian Amateur Sport. I understand that prior to my becoming minister in that portfolio, it had met with the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Revenue. As a matter of fact, it was very happy with the solutions they proposed and what the Minister of Finance had done for sport in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would have liked to hear what benefits are being given to amateur sport.

May 24, 1990
Point of Order
I have here a copy of a 20-page report filed by the Nepean Minor Hockey Association which has concluded that the total adjusted impact of the GST will result in thousands of dollars in over-all price increases to the annual operating budget of the MHA.
Will the minister take steps to persuade the Minister of Finance to exempt amateur sport from the GST or, better yet, to scrap the tax?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Danis (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance, in the GST bill proposed to the House, has put in a number of special provisions to assist non-profit amateur sport organizations. I think he has done a tremendous job for amateur sport and should be congratulated.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Transport. I am glad to see that he has returned alive from Windsor. It is something for which he deserves congratulations.
The Minister knows that the negotiations which he undertook with truckers in Windsor led to some kind of an agreement which he was finally required to promise to put in writing. Has he, in fact, sent those promises in writing to the truckers in Windsor? If he has done so, will he stand in the House and make a commitment to make them public, here and now, so that truckers all across Canada can see what the minister has decided to do?

Mr. Speaker, I wish to advise my hon. friend that those commitments were made public by myself and the Ontario Minister of Transport immediately after our discussions. They are already public.
I had offered to put commitments I made, with my word, in writing. We are in the process of formulating such a letter. The minute we have it formulated, then it will be in writing as well as on camera being made public by myself at about 10 o'clock this morning.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. I think it is important that those commitments be publicly put to
truckers. If it does not happen, I can tell the minister, frankly, he will not see that demonstration end.

I have a supplementary question for the Minister. Quebec truckers have also decided to hold demonstrations on this issue. After this morning's discussions, will the Minister promise them that, in areas of federal jurisdiction, legal or police action will not be taken against the protesters?

As to the
first part of my hon. friend's question, vis-a-vis Windsor, I am sorry, but I cannot think of anything more public and more on the record than a media conference with all of the reporters and the television cameras there. If there is something more public than that, I would like to know what it is and that will be done.

In the case of Montreal, I can assist the provincial Minister of Transport but any police intervention would fall under Quebec's jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Right Hon. Prime Minister on a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. During Question Period I referred to the fact that I believed that the Minister of the Environment, who had just resigned, was the first to serve on the Priorities and Planning Committee of Cabinet. This in fact is a serious error, because Your Honour himself was the Minister of the Environment and a member of P and P in the government of the distinguished member for Yellowknife.
Hear, hear!

Indeed, his tenure is widely remembered with great admiration by all environmentalists across Canada.
May 24, 1990

But I make the correction for two reasons. First of all, that it had to be made and, second, if I had not, my chances of speaking again in this Chamber will be greatly reduced.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Under all the circumstances, I shall refrain from speaking.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it being Thursday, I would like to ask the Government House Leader to give us the legislative menu for the coming days.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tomorrow will be an allotted day, and I understand that the Liberal party will be leading off the debate. I would appreciate knowing what the subject is so that we might prepare.
On Monday, we will commence report stage consideration of Bill C-69, if there are report stage amendments. If not, we will proceed with third reading.
On Thesday and Wednesday it is my intention now to call Bill C-58, the Young Offenders bill, followed by Bill C-63, establishing the Canadian Race Relations Foundation, and Bill C-65, technical amendments to Customs Thriffs.
Thursday, May 31, will also be designated an allotted day.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since the minister has now designated the day, I guess we can name the subject matter. It will be on municipal infrastructure and how the federal government needs to get involved in that again.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I thank the hon. member. I hope that included in the debate will not only be how we should get involved, but how we should finance it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
No comment, Mr. Speaker. We will debate that tomorrow.
Government Orders
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Ms. Campbell (Vancouver Centre) that Bill C-43, an act respecting abortion, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, it is quite obvious from having heard many speeches in this House that the bill before us has brought from individuals many very deep-lying emotions. It has been a very strong debate. It has been a debate in depth, as far as the issue is concerned.
In order to understand the positions of some people, it is important to have an idea of what in their lives promotes the feelings in them that they are expressing on the floor of the House and then we will understand this debate very clearly. Obviously, those who have spoken very strongly fully understand that there is something in their background, in their thinking, and in their life's experiences with other people that has led them to feel the way that they do.
In a debate of this nature, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that you would agree it is very important that common sense and coolness rule the day.
I have some very important points that I want to make. I realize that this is a very crucial debate and the feelings that I will put on the record this afternoon are very sincere and they are certainly the way I feel about this issue personally. No matter how one looks at the abortion issue, I feel in all conscience that I have no right, and I do not think that any of us has any right to unnecessarily destroy life before or after birth.
God brings us into this world and he takes us out. Sometimes it is extremely difficult to accept the death of a loved one, but there is a purpose and there must be a faith. Therefore, we must talk about this debate today in good faith, because as we discuss it we must bear in mind that we are talking about the future of young people in this country, whether or not they are going to be bom.
On the other hand, you can imagine the horrible thought, Mr. Speaker, that those loved ones that we have lost would have never been here if their father and

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
mother had believed in abortion and you would have never known them. So this begs the question, how many potential friends, how many potentially great citizens, how many community leaders, how many leaders in general, how many internationally influential people, how many professional people, how many farmers and other people in various walks of life have never had the opportunity to play their roles in life because they were not allowed to be born? That is a serious question.
In this debate, it has been mentioned that the Liberal party has no policy on the abortion issue. I for one make absolutely no apology for that, because there are two types of debates in this House that by tradition and by practice have become free votes on the floor of this House. When a political party decides that it is going to have a strict policy that everybody must obey and then calls it a free vote, it is hypocrisy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It's not true though, Len. They have not forced everybody.

The hon. member for Niagara Falls felt touchy when I said that, but I am not saying it in the sense that he is thinking about it and I want him to know that. I am saying it in the sense that no political party should be accused of not having a policy.
It is true that the government must bring forward a bill, but to say that it is the total policy and sincere belief of every member of a Cabinet is probably being inaccurate too. We know that the Minister of Justice who brought in this bill has some very strong views on it. That is her right and it is possible that the bill mirrors her feelings. Let us not argue that point. She is part of the government and has the right to bring in the bill. Every member of every party in this House has the right to vote on that bill as they see fit. We have the right to bring in amendments to it. If our amendment is accepted, that is fine. If it is not, we have to live with the parliamentary system. It is a fact of life.
So let us not get hung up on the idea that parties as a whole must have a very definite policy on these great emotional issues, that are personal and conscience issues to many members on both sides of this House. I feel very strongly about that.
The public at large also has its personal feelings and agendas. That is why we get representations from all sides of an issue such as this. That is why we have to rely, as I said at the beginning, on cool heads and common sense in an emotional debate such as this.
The old argument as to whether or not the foetus is a human life will go on ad infinitum. The foetus follows through to a human life. There is a right to be bom, in my view, and there is a right to live. We have no right to destroy life before birth any more than we have a right to destroy life after birth. I emphasize that the health of the mother is indeed a crucial decision, and a must.
One can take a look at a happy teenager today and realize that that person would never be here if the parents had decided that they would have the abortion. I remember a great moment of silence one day when speaking to a group of students here on Parliament Hill. There was one student who asked a question on the abortion issue and argued very strongly, quoting the parents, until one of the other students said: "Do you realize that with what you are proposing today, you may not have had the opportunity of being here with us in this group if your parents had exercised the philosophy that you are espousing?". These questions put forward the seriousness of this issue.
Economics has been mentioned as a factor in this debate. I feel very strongly that family planning must become a far greater priority than the economic factor. Are we going to allow economics to control whether or not people are going to be bom in this democracy, this western society of ours? Do we as human beings have the right to make that decision? Some of us in this House would never be here today, if it was not for our parents wanting to bring us into this world.
I think of my own mother and father raising a family in the depression years of the 1930s. If economics had come into consideration, I certainly would not be here today and neither would my brother or sister. We had that kind of respect in our family. My mother and father took their duties as parents seriously.
Let us be a nation of understanding. Let us be a nation of love in the sense of respect and of help to others at all times. Common sense goes a long way in solving difficult problems.
May 24, 1990

I was not born in a hospital. I was born in a farmhouse during the depression years. The next door neighbour was the midwife. If economic considerations had been brought to bear at that time, I would never have been born and would not be here today.
I was born into a family that had no money. We could hardly pay our taxes during those years. However, there was love, caring, and understanding. I look back to my childhood days and I think of my parents. I consider them to be martyrs for what they went through. With no money they raised a family. They put three square meals a day on the table. They tried to give us guidance, and they gave us direction and encouragement. I well recall that if we did not take that guidance willingly, there were other methods of encouragement that persuaded us to take that guidance, and I do not regret that either.
If there is any side of economics that we should be looking at here, it is on the tax policies for young families. They should be given greater tax allowances. There must be some consideration given for the costs of raising a family today more so than we are doing.
I can remember when family allowances first came in. I was going to high school at that time. What a great thing that was for the family. To get a cheque at the end of the month for either $6 or $7-and eventually it became $8-was a real gift. We had never witnessed that before. It relates back to the situation where the economics of a family are indeed very important. If we are not going to help them out in that route with family expenses, then we should be helping them out through the tax system at their level of income.
Love at a time when young people become pregnant is a must. Love to people who experience unwanted pregnancies is a must. It is a time for understanding. It is not a time for self-righteousness. We must give them encouragement and no hypocrisy.
I know cases where mothers and fathers of young people have taken the daughter and the child and looked after them every day until they were on their own. I have every respect for people like that, because it shows that they are willing to face up to reality, that they have a great sense of decency, and that they accept the full responsibilities of parenthood.
The earlier or later stages of pregnancy do not really have anything to do with the rights of the foetus because
Government Orders
it is on its way to becoming a full-fledged individual from the day of conception onward. It does not matter at what stage you destroy that foetus, you are still destroying that child's right to be bom and to live a fair life.
My feelings are very strong on this issue because of personal experiences. I would just like to outline some of those personal experiences. I suppose in a way, as I said earlier, I have certain prejudices.
Our first child was bom on Mother's Day 1961. After a very serious and long period for my wife, the baby was stillborn. It was a very difficult situation for a mother going full term. It also turned out later that that baby and we as a family were one of the first victims of thalidomide. I do not know how many times I counted every square of concrete on the sidewalk that encircled that hospital during those many hours. It put real emphasis in my mind as to the protection of the mother when it comes to any legislation that we are discussing, whether it be this or any other legislation.
When our second child came along, perfectly healthy, it was a great joy. When the third one came along, it was another great joy. Quite frankly, my only regret is that we do not have five or six more like them.
The old law that the Supreme Court struck down on January 28,1988 was brought in with good intent in 1969. I was also here for that debate. However, the good intent of that legislation was not always followed in spirit over the years.
I get conflicting messages on the adoption of the argument: is there a real desire to adopt babies today? Some say that the system is working, and some say it is not.
There is one thing I want to put on the record, and it is that no father should be allowed to leave mother and child economically unprotected after having brought that child into the world. That father should not be allowed, simply because he lives in another province or territory, to fail to provide for that child's keep. He has an obligation.
In that regard, there is a real economic argument for this point. Part of this whole debate should be that once parents bring a child into the world, both of them are responsible. Certainly the father should not be allowed

to walk out and get off scot-free. I think that is what is building a lot of resentment in our society today.
In conclusion, I would like to see strong action taken at both the federal and provincial levels on that issue.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate on Bill C-43. I have been following this bill since the beginning.

I have been involved with this issue for several months, starting with the caucus committee where I was privileged to serve with the hon. members for Argenteuil- Papineau, Kitchener, Surrey-White Rock, and others. I was with the legislative committee studying Bill C-43 for many weeks and grappling with this issue. Now here we are finally before the House at third reading.
I believe that this very contentious, emotional, intellectual and human issue is one that challenges people in many ways and in many parts of our country. As is well known, it is one that divides Canadians in many ways. It is a many-sided issue. I believe that first and foremost the debate in this place is not about philosophy. It is not about morality. It is about governance. It is about law, legislation, and the administration of justice in Canada. It is with respect to those matters that I wish to address myself today.
This issue of abortion in Canada represents a challenge to Canadians, one of many challenges that we have had throughout our history. It is a challenge which charges us with the task of reaching consensus in a country of great diversity. Indeed, this week of all weeks, all members present and people from coast to coast are aware of the challenge to compromise that has been an inherent part of the history of this country since its origins: those days when people like John A. Macdonald, George Etienne Cartier, Charles Tupper, and others came together to try to find the compromise that would create this great and wonderful country of ours.
Here we are again, not undoubtedly for the last time, after several occasions in Parliament debating this very contentious, social, moral and philosophical issue. As I
said, I wish to address this issue from the context of what I believe is our role and function here, not as a group of moralists but rather as a group of parliamentarians, as a group of people who have been selected by our fellow citizens to come here and seek the compromises that are the basis upon which Canada can work.
During the course of my remarks I wish to make reference to my own personal views on this matter. In so doing, I say to this House that many of the things that I would say if debate was not limited have already been said by my hon. friend, the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock, who gave what I thought was a very outstanding, inspiring address on the subject. I look forward to hearing from the hon. member for Kitchener. I expect that I will be as well able to associate myself with his remarks as I wish to associate myself with the remarks of my hon. friend for Surrey-White Rock.
I wish to focus on the legislative and political aspects of this issue because, after all, we are here to govern. We are here to seek a resolution to a contentious issue that has been with Canadians for generations but has once again been with parliamentarians for a little over two years since the previous bill relating to this subject was struck down by the Supreme Court of Canada.
As parliamentarians our job is to legislate for Canadians. In doing so, we have to put to ourselves a series of questions. We have to ask ourselves: What is in the best interest of Canada? We have to ask ourselves: What do Canadians want with respect to this issue? We have to take cognizance not only of the processes of Parliament and the dynamics of having things pass this place and indeed the one down the hall, but we have to take cognizance of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, other legislation, and the Constitution of Canada which, like it or lump it, does impose limitations on what we can or cannot usefully do in this place.
We can stand and say that we should pass a law that says this or that or something else. But, in the final analysis, if that law does not meet the tests that will be applied when it is taken to the Supreme Court of Canada, we have failed in our responsibility as the governors and parliamentarians of this country who have been sent here to act in a responsible manner.
May 24, 1990

Dealing with contentious issues is not an easy task. Indeed, this country is faced with many challenges and contentious issues today. It is my judgment that the country is fortunate to have leadership that does not shy away from challenges, be they the economic problems of the country, the challenges of our Constitution, or a contentious social issue like the question of abortion and how it should be handled within the legislative framework of Canada. We are fortunate, in my judgment, to have the inspired leadership of the Prime Minister we have today. It is primarily through his leadership and his willingness to take on challenges that we are in the process of concluding a debate on the contentious issue of abortion.
When we began last fall to try to develop legislation, our responsibility as parliamentarians was to develop a bill that could meet the test of this House and be able to pass through Parliament. Otherwise, it would not be a useful exercise. Second, it has to satisfy the Supreme Court of Canada and, ultimately, meet the test of Canadian public opinion. That is the next question we have to look at.
I believe that the bill before us today will pass. I will vote for it and I urge all members to vote for it regardless of their personal feelings on this very contentious subject. There are people in this House, in all caucuses, who are of diametrically different opinions. Our responsibility, as a collective group of parliamentarians, is to come together and find the reasonable balance, which I think is reflected in Bill C-43.
I believe it will pass the test of the Supreme Court. There is no doubt in my mind that it will be challenged, in court but I believe it will pass that test and, ultimately, I believe it will meet the test of the people of Canada.
As the member for South Shore I can ask what the people of the South Shore want with respect to this issue. But we as parliamentarians must ask what the people of Canada want. I believe that the people of the South Shore reflect very well the views of the people of Canada with respect to this issue. There are people in the South Shore who are absolutely, unequivocally, opposed to abortion. There are people who are absolutely, unequivocally of the opinion that abortion should be
Government Orders
available on demand under any circumstances, at any time. There are people who have opinions that vary between those extremes.
I believe this bill represents a balance that will be acceptable to the overwhelming majority of Canadians. The people of the two extremes will not be satisfied and they have made that known fully, including those people, whom I admire, who stand out in front of this building every day as they have for months, fasting for life. I respect the courage, the commitment and the integrity of those people. But those people are not charged with governing Canada; we are. While I may share their sentiments, the fact of the matter is that a bill that reflects their position would be thrown out in a minute by the Supreme Court of Canada and we would have failed in carrying out our responsibilities.
I believe the overwhelming majority of Canadians want an end to the public chaos that has existed with respect to abortions in Canada. Last summer we in this country witnessed on television young people's lives in turmoil, young people going before the courts to fight out whether there should be or should not be an abortion in a particular circumstance. I think the Canadian public wants an end to that kind of thing. Canadians say that the role of government is to bring as much order as possible where there is chaos. That, I believe, is the challenge that the public has put to us. That, I believe, is what will be accomplished.
We will not satisfy everybody. We cannot satisfy everybody. Canadians are fundamentally reasonable people. That is why Canada has existed for 123 years. That is why Canadians met the challenge of the conscription crisis in 1944, the schools crisis in the 1890s, and indeed that is why I am confident Canadians will come together and resolve the constitutional crisis of 1990. That has been the essence of our history. Canadians are people who fundamentally understand the necessity of and indeed have the ability to cope with the need to compromise. That is what we have reflected in this bill before us here today.
I might take a moment or two to talk about my own feelings. When I became a candidate for public office early in the fall of 1988,1 knew that I would have to think about the issue of abortion and ask myself how I will be counted when the time comes.

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
I have never hidden my views on that subject. I consider myself a pro-lifer. I am one of those who believes, as was so eloquently articulated by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock earlier today, that life begins with conception. I believe that from the moment of conception, no matter what language is used, we are dealing with a life. I am one of those who believes that life should not be lightly taken away. I believe that one of the most basic human rights that exists in society is the right to life. Therefore, I essentially oppose abortions.
Frankly, there are circumstances under which abortions are appropriate. One has to look at abortion as an issue of conflict of interest, the interest and the rights of the mother on the one hand and the interests and the rights of the unborn child on the other.
If one is pushed to draw a line and is not constrained by things such as constitutions or charters or anything else, the appropriate line should be drawn where the self-interests of the one imposes upon the right to life of the other. If I were the draftsman or the technician, my line would recognize that where the health or life of the mother is threatened it may indeed be appropriate to have an abortion performed.
Inasmuch as you are dealing with that kind of conflict, in the final analysis I believe that abortion should not take place simply because somebody, as a matter of choice, does not wish to allow a baby to be born.
What is the best solution? There is no question that the way to deal with abortions is not through legislation. The best way to deal with abortions is to remove the need for them. It seems to me that a responsible government, in dealing with abortion, is not only going to address itself to defining a circumstance under which abortion can or cannot take place. Rather, it is going to ensure that education is in place so that unwanted pregnancies do not occur. It is going to ensure that appropriate birth control methods are readily available to those who have need of them. That is the way to deal with it.
We must ensure that the support systems exist in society so that if a young girl becomes pregnant she is not forced to give up that child because she is not in an economic circumstance where she can care for that child. Not only is she making a decision about that unborn child, she is making a decision that affects her. She may
prefer to have that opportunity but if the support services are not in place she is unable to take it.
A very good friend of mine has often said to me that there is no such thing as an unwanted child; there is somebody who wants that child. There are people in this country today who would like to have babies but cannot have their own. We have to come to grips with that as well.
In conclusion, I believe Bill C-43 achieves a balance that is reasonable. I believe it will meet the test of this House and, indeed, of the other place. I believe it will meet the test of the Supreme Court of Canada. Most important of all, I believe it will meet the test of the Canadian people. It recognizes the fundamental principle of life and when it begins. It recognizes that abortion should take place for some medical reasons. Personally, I would have preferred to have this bill more definitive, with a greater incumbency to demonstrate a medical necessity as opposed to what is, frankly, a fairly wide-open piece of legislation.
Nevertheless, the bill we have before us is unequivocally a step in the right direction. It is a piece of legislation that will serve the interests of Canadians. It is a piece of legislation that will bring an end to the chaos that has existed in this country.
Consequently, I am prepared to support this bill. I commend it to my fellow members of this House and urge all members to support it for the benefit of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I have a number of questions for the hon. member. The first relates to his analysis that this legislation is a matter of the "administration of justice". I put that last phrase in quotes because I think we have to talk about justice in a broader sense than just the legalistic term.
He also says that this a resolution of this contentious issue. I believe that he is fooling himself and fooling the rest of Canada with that analysis. There is not going to be a resolution of this contentious issue by recriminalizing abortion. The only means by which there is going to be a resolution of this contentious issue is to give adequate support, funding and understanding to enable women to exercise birth control and men to exercise responsibility in their relations with women. The Cana-
May 24, 1990

dian government should also participate in that in a really meaningful way.
The member talked about the public chaos of last summer. Once again, I think his analysis is totally wrong. This legislation would in no way stop injunctions of men wanting to use the court system to take control of women. There is no way that recriminalizing abortion will do that. His logic is rather strained.
I want to ask the member a question about his analysis that women are acting out of self-interest should they seek abortions. This type of logic speaks of the utter contempt in which some men in this House hold women. It makes me exceedingly angry. Women who have gone through this process and this painful decision have not done so out of self-interest. Abortion is always a tragedy.
I would commend the previous speaker to please have a little understanding. He has never experienced an unwanted pregnancy. He knows not of what he speaks. I would ask him to please address his comments with respect to Canadian women.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague opposite raises some very important points. I was taking notes to try to ensure that I address all of the points she raised. I will endeavour to do so.
Possibly she misunderstood my intent or I did not articulate my position adequately. I unequivocally recognize that an abortion is an option of the absolute last choice. I understood the hon. member to say that no woman has an abortion just for something to do, frivolously or otherwise. In no way whatsoever would I ever think that or suggest it.
I think, though, that it is incumbent on all people in Canada to act responsibly; men and women. As the member quite rightly points out, men are as much involved in the decision to create pregnancy as are women. However, the bottom line is that men cannot have abortions and I do not think it is a legitimate suggestion to therefore say that men have no interest in the subject whatsoever.
This is a subject that involves all Canadians because when we are talking about abortions we are not just talking about women. We are talking about an unborn child, about another human being. Where is the consultation process for that individual? Where is the choice
Government Orders
for that individual? That is why, in my judgment, we cannot lightly give away or abrogate the right of that individual to have his or her interest considered in the decisions that are taken.
With respect to the member's comments on the need for adequate support and funding, I believe that I addressed that point in my remarks. I feel very strongly, as I said, that the best way to deal with abortions is to eliminate them by making them unnecessary. The overwhelming number of abortions which are taking place in this country today need not take place if there was adequate support of the type the member speaks of, if there was proper education of young people. We have come a long way, but we have a long way to go.
The subject of criminalization has been a contentious issue from the beginning. It is important to recognize two things. First, people look to the Government of Canada to deal with this issue. The Government of Canada can only do so within the context of the jurisdiction provided it in the Constitution of Canada. The access to the Government of Canada came to this issue through the criminal process.
I should remind my hon. friend opposite that what is criminalized, if that is what is going on, is not abortions, but abortions held outside the law. This law, among other things, seeks to create an environment in which, in reasonable circumstances as defined in the law, abortions can take place where they should take place, under the authority of properly qualified medical practitioners.
Finally, as to the resolution of the issue, my hon. friend opposite is absolutely right. This bill will not end the debate on the subject of abortion in Canada. I never suggested that it would. I do not recall having suggested that. I doubt that any member of the House would suggest that this bill, or for that matter any other bill, would end debate on the subject of abortion in the country.
I suggested that this bill represents a reasonable compromise between diametrically opposite positions. It is a reasonable compromise that will be acceptable to the overwhelming majority of Canadians who fundamentally are not on the extreme of any given issue but are people who learn to understand. One might say it is the Canadian way of understanding, the way of reasonable compromise. That is what this bill is. For those people,

the vast majority of Canadians, this will mean a resolution to the issue, as I indicated.

Mr. Speaker, in a number of circumstances, the hon. member referred to the test of the Supreme Court and how, in his analysis of Bill C-43, it would meet the test of the Supreme Court.
Would the hon. member state for us what his view is of the test of the Supreme Court and how Bill C-43 will specifically meet that legal test?

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to stand here and pretend to be an expert in jurisprudence. Nevertheless, I will not hesitate to comment on the subject.
The lines were essentially drawn by the decisions that have been brought down in the Morgentaler case, the Daigle case, and others. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you do not want a 45-minute legal dissertation from me, which I would otherwise be delighted to present. But, essentially, those decisions stated, first, that Parliament should create a law. Second, they stated that, within that law, Parliament should make provision for women to have access to abortions in Canada and that the law should create an entitlement for women to have abortions in Canada. I prefer the word "entitlement" to "access". The access is something that is determined within the health services of the provinces.
At the same time, the decisions indicated that there is an incumbency on Parliament to take cognizance of the rights of the unborn. Therein it seems to me that the court has told this Parliament to find a middle road between the two positions. The courts have very clearly indicated that a choice on either of those extremes would not be acceptable to them. The courts have made it perfectly clear that we must find a middle road. That, I submit, is what we have attempted to do with Bill C-43.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate. At the outset I would like to state that I am opposed to this bill. I will persuade the rest of the House to take my position and I will give you the reasons why I will persuade them.
Even those who are opposed to abortion should understand that this bill is a political bill to deal with a social problem. It attempts to find a political solution to a problem that does not have a political solution.
If a member on either side of the House argues that in their opinion and moral conviction life begins at conception, then they cannot vote for this bill. It is sanctimonious cant to suggest that somehow this bill is a compromise and will allow them to abandon their principles and argument about the sanctity of life because the state somehow, with this piece of legislation, has defined when life is sanctified and when it is not. That is hypocrisy. It does not serve the debate that is necessary for the public to come to some acceptable resolution socially about this problem.
This government has set the debate back by using a political instrument to cover itself within the polls, rather than taking a responsible position as a government either for or against the right of a woman to make a choice as to whether or not she should have an abortion.
Those who hold to the argument-and I do not dispute their right to do it, I hold to a different argument-that life begins at conception cannot morally justify a vote for this legislation. It does a great deal of damage to those people who are sincere in holding their position-just as I am sincere in holding mine-that life begins at conception. It is a mockery of that argument to stand up in the Chamber and say they believe that and then allow themselves to vote for this bill.
Having said that, I want to outline why, after wrestling with my own conscience about this situation, I have decided to vote against the bill and why I am pro-choice.
There is indeed merit in the argument about when life begins. It is a human decision based upon the scientific and religious evidence in front of us. We have to make that decision in true conscience. I do not make my decision frivolously. It is based on true conscience because of an accumulated series of experiences I have had in my life through my chosen profession as a social worker.
I was 22 years old when I had my first caseload of children at the Children's Aid Society of Vancouver. In those days I was responsible for 78 children. This private agency hired me at the age of 22 to be, in a sense, a substitute parent for those 78 children. I had graduated
May 24, 1990

from university and it was presumed, because I had four years of university education, that I was somehow qualified to be a surrogate parent for those 78 children.
Nothing could have been further from the truth. I was not prepared to deal with the real problems of those children. All the book learning I had relative to the needs of those children was absolutely invalid in terms of the practical situation with which I was faced.
Most of the children for whom I was responsible had an absence of love. They were unwanted children. They were not desired by their mothers. It was an accident of fate as a result of a situation that existed in the country at that time.
You could not even buy condoms in a drugstore when I was a teenager. The attitude of the state at that time was to bury its head in the sand. Condoms were not even discussed. The only reason we discuss birth control or access to information on birth control is the threat of AIDS. What logic and reason could not do to our society, AIDS has forced us to do.
Now that we have had an open discussion about the problems of sexually-transmitted diseases, we are talking about preventing sexually-transmitted diseases without even putting it in the context of human sexuality and human physiology.
Those 78 children for whom I was responsible were disadvantaged from day one. They had no opportuntiy parallel to any normal child out there. My colleague made the bland statement: "Well, don't worry, there is somebody out there who will love the child". Would that be true!
Today, caseloads are not 78 children. They are 250 or 300 children per social worker and they are just as inadequate in dealing with those as they were in my day.
How many trained social workers with a Masters degree are in the line carrying a caseload? Very few. How many are there in the age group of 45 to 55, when they have accumulated at least some life experience to make some sensible judgments about the tremendous problems that are in front of them? Very few. We still have denied the fact that we reject children in our society. We reject those unwanted children in archaic
Government Orders
social systems that guarantee us a population in our prisons and in our mental institutions.
What chance does a child have if that child is unwanted and shuffled along to an agency with the hope that someone will adopt the child? In the argument of the previous two members I heard speak, economics has nothing to do with it. Like blazes, Mr. Speaker.
However, let us assume that economics had nothing to do with it and that wealthy people would be benevolent enough to embrace these children to their bosom and raise them. Money does not guarantee the raising of a good child. If there is an absence of love in a relationship between a man and a woman, it does not matter whether they live in a house with a dirt floor or in a mansion in one of the most expensive suburbs. That kid is headed for trouble.
Do we do any pre-marital counselling in the country? Not a whit. On a basis that the state says that we should-

I am glad I have their attention. In the province of British Columbia, we asked the religious community to make itself available on a voluntary basis for pre-marital counselling of those couples who chose to take it. They responded positively and we initiated a program. Then I said that we should delay giving marriage licences for a six-week period. If the state is going to give permission to people to get married, then the state should have some evidence that they voluntarily had pre-marital counselling.
What do we do with people who drive cars? The state requires not only that they take lessons in driving a car but that they pass an examination before they get behind the wheel. The state even goes further and requires that they drive on the proper side of the road.
What an interference of freedom of choice. Why in the heck does the state have the right to examine whether or not you can drive a car? Why does the state have the right to tell you what side of the road to drive on? Why does the state do that? It does so because it is in the role of social order, to ensure that there is a sense of public safety and discipline in the state.

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that if the state feels that secure about requiring a licence before you drive a car and telling you what side of the road to drive on, the state at least can make birth control information and pre-marital counselling available to make sure that we are not raising a generation of ignorant children who have no awareness of what human sexuality is all about.
When I grew up I was supposed to learn, as a male, about human sexuality by hanging around the street. When I was a teenager, every young man was supposed to be an expert in sexual matters and every girl was supposed to be a virgin. I never knew how, socially, we were to reach that desired goal in our male-female roles unless two people tangoed. There was a tacit admission in our society that sex did not exist. Yet, males were supposed to be experts and women were supposed to be virgins. The absurd hypocrisy of our society in dealing with human sexuality knows no limits and the progeny of that kind of ignorance fills up our institutions and mental hospitals.
I spent five years working in jails. In almost every single instance of young boys whom I worked with, there was an abysmal lack of information about human physiology and also an absence of love. They were bitter and hateful simply because they were not wanted. Now if the state says that you cannot have an abortion, then the state has a moral right to ensure-just as they do with drivers' licences or telling people what side of the road to drive on-that every child has the maximum opportunity to reach any potential level of success they can. We do not.
Look at our poverty rolls. Look at people on welfare. I have yet to hear a significant voice in the pro-life community demand a bill of rights for children in this country, and demand a guarantee of minimum services for those children. If they put the same amount of energy in their argument against abortion into the defence of those children who are already born, I would feel a little more comfortable.
The absence of child care in the institutions we provide, the scandals we see in the housing residences we have for young boys and girls, is shocking. In my own province, Willingdon School for Girls and Brandon Lake
School for Boys guaranteed a succeeding class of occupants for Kingston penitentiary and the British Columbia penitentiary. At one time 60 per cent of the occupants of the women's penitentiary in Kingston were graduates of the same Willingdon School for Girls.
There is a lot of hypocrisy going on and I want to address myself partly to that. Where in the world are those screaming battalions of voices and placards out in front of this building, demanding that basic child services be guaranteed by law for every child in this country? Where are they? Where are those screaming-meemies who are determined to tell every woman what she must or must not do about her body, or her choice? Where are those screaming-meemies when it comes to the number of children in this country who are going to school ill-housed and ill-fed?
I hear this pious clap-trap about love and understanding and commitment. It is b.s., Mr. Speaker. And you know what b.s. is? That's the Blarney Stone, Mr. Speaker-I do not want anyone to misinterpret what I am saying.
I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, there is an absence of commitment to children in this country.
Now I want to deal with the choice of some woman who finds herself with an unwanted pregnancy. Can you tell me what the hell the state has to do with the decision that she must make? Can you tell me what role this Chamber, a group of citizens representatives of all Canadians-and Lord help us, sometimes I think it is below the average of most Canadians-has got to do with telling that women, who is a victim of incest or rape, that she must carry the child to term? Fie on your head! Nonsense! Suggesting that any young woman, a victim of incest or rape, must carry a child to term is the most horrendous kind of scenario that one could possibly expect, and I think in this sense it is male-dominance visiting those attitudes on a woman in that situation.
I find it incredible that we are faced with this bill. I deeply respect those people in this House who say they are going to vote against it because of moral conviction and their belief that life starts at conception. I respect them deeply. And I hope that they, in turn, respect my point of view. But I do not respect the hypocrisy of those who are rationalizing that this bill somehow solves the problem.
May 24, 1990

Since you know my point of view and how I am going to vote and why, I make an appeal to this House. When this debate is over will we hear again about children in need in this country? When this debate is over will members get up and demand that the government set national standards for child care in this country? Will we hear a debate in this Chamber that no caseload of children in a child care agency, either private or public, goes over 30 or 40, just as we expect in classrooms? Will we hear a demand in this Chamber that never again will we set up community based and funded homes where children are placed in unsupervised situations and assaults on those children take place? Do you think this is new? It has gone on generation after generation after generation in this country and I dare say, unfortunately, it is probably still going on in some instances in this country.
We still jail children in this country, Mr. Speaker. Go and take a look at your own province's set-up for dealing with "juvenile delinquents". Check out what we do with children when they come into court. Find out what is going on day after day in a court system that denies children the same basic protection that any adult will get in any court situation in the country.
Hypocrisy reeks through this whole debate. Unless there is a guarantee that every child in this country is given some basic elementary human rights and protections from the law, the persuasion of my argument is going to fall on deaf ears. I have emptied the Chamber with my eloquence.
Having had the debate, it is incumbent on this Chamber, regardless of the side we take on this bill, to see that the government initiates legislation to deal with the companion problems of what is happening in our society. I appeal to members to understand that there are unwanted children in our society. Someone is responsible for them and that someone is us, the collectivity of the state that makes the laws. We are morally responsible to ensure that those children have a decent chance at life.
When this bill passes away, I would like to hear the sanctimonious voices that argue against it or for it, based on protecting their own political rear ends, focus on the leftover problem of the neglected children in our society who need our attention and care. I thank you for listening, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member speaks about sanctimony. He said: "Hypocrisy reeks through this whole debate". It is not often that I agree with the hon. member but, with respect to this particular statement, I agree.
Coming from a member of Parliament who belongs to a political party that speaks about choice and the freedom to choose, the member talks about choice. Yet, in his own political party-and you speak about hypocrisy and sanctimony-his colleagues do not have the choice to vote in this House according to their own conscience. The party says that if you are a member of the New Democratic Party, then you must vote in this particular way, regardless of what your own morality tells you, regardless of where you stand on the issue. Members of the New Democratic Party are not permitted to vote according to their own conscience.
The member speaks of hypocrisy, but he and others in his party participated in the capital punishment debate. I recall it well. The member was not in the House a few years ago when we debated that issue. I recall very vividly and specifically his colleagues standing up, one after another, talking about the sanctity of life, about how important it was to protect life and how morally wrong it is, for the Government of Canada to destroy human life through the process of capital punishment.
These same members-and you speak of hypocrisy-now argue a different point. Now they no longer argue how sacred and how much sanctity there is to human life, all of a sudden they approach it from a different perspective.
In view of the position of his party; first, can he explain why members of his party do not have the choice to vote according to their own consciences? Second, I would like to ask the hon. member to explain very clearly where he stands on the issue of when life begins? He took others to task for suggesting that life begins at the moment of conception. In his view, given his position-
Let him answer.

You will have a moment to answer. The hon. member says prior to birth. There ought not be a law in Canada to recognize life before birth. Is the hon. member arguing and suggesting that human life begins at the moment of birth? If not, how can he reconcile his

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
position on the issue of abortion with the fact that he must agree that life begins at some point before birth?

It is very hard to follow my predecessor's logic. First of all, I will deal with his question about the votes in my party. I want to make this very clear, I would never belong to a party that does not allow everybody, in true conscience, to make their own decisions.
That's nonsense.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member says that that is nonsense. I do not question the integrity of the members of his party. I believe every member who comes to this Chamber votes in true conscience. No party tells anybody what to do because, on that basis, it would hardly be worth our being here in the first place. If you presume that our party tells people how to vote, come to a caucus meeting some time and enjoy the experience.
Having said that, the next question is about the beginning of life. I do not believe it happens at conception. I spent six years in Catholic universities; I studied with the Jesuits; it was an incredible experience. Their position and my position are different. They worked on me for six years, I worked on them for six years. It was a draw, Mr. Speaker.
My opinion is different from that hon. member's. If he suggests life begins at the moment of conception then I have to accept, on the basis of that argument, that all those sperm that are being wasted are killers. All those sperm that have not performed their duty must be corralled by law and fined or locked up for not completing their job. We cannot have loose sperm running around this country, without completing their job. If life begins at conception, all those sperm are acting immorally by not performing their task, as predesigned under that theory. Now, I do not want to be a sperm rounder-upper, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to be a sperm counter, but if you follow that argument logically, then we can go into menopause as well and say that every month there has been a natural abortion, and save me from that argument. That rigidity is so stupid that it defies-
What is your position?
I am not God, neither are you. You have to make your own decision and at what point you make that decision.
What is your view? Are you afraid to state your view?
Mr. Speaker, if that member wants my view, rent me a hall, gather me a crowd, and I will tell him my view, how hypocritical it is to take the line of argument that member takes.
You're afraid to answer the question, Barrett. You're chicken.

Mr. Speaker, even the church had a different position 130 years ago. Read your own history, my friend. It is a man-made decision and man-altered decision. I do not tell you what to do, I do not play God and you do not play God either. That kind of sanctimonious camp, especially for women, telling them what they have to do, is frankly absurd.
I want to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for letting me participate in this debate and I want to thank my hon. friend who is so wrong but so sure of himself.

Mr. Speaker, I had difficulty in convincing my own colleagues in the House that legislation would be appropriate before issuing a marriage licence so I asked for voluntary participation. I asked the religious communities if they would participate, and they responded positively. We set up a family life council in the province of British Columbia that had the backing and the role of the religious community.
I am very sorry that my successor, the then minister of welfare, was the one who killed that program, the Hon. William Vander Zalm, the great spokesperson for family life. However, the program was reinitiated after public demand.
Referring to the consequence of it, it is not a question of asking people to write a test. It was a commitment from the religious community that I admire and respect on a non-sectarian basis to participate in encouraging and giving an opportunity to those people who had convictions or were seeking some guidance to discuss them with someone who was knowledgeable in that field. I was looking to cut down the number of divorces in our society. I am still looking for a way to solve that problem. I do not have the magic answer. However, I wanted to expand the options available to couples who were serious about their marriage vows to talk to somebody on a whole range of subjects before they went into marriage.
Furthermore, I would hope that such programs would be encouraged today. I conclude by making the same appeal. There are children out there who need basic services. Can we put the same emotion into an argument to ensure that those services are provided?

Mr. Speaker, I have struggled with how I should vote on this bill at third reading. As a legislator I accept my duty of legally
Government Orders
protecting the most vulnerable of all human beings within our society: the unborn.
Today, as I stand in this House, I appeal to my colleagues to contemplate the historical importance of this moment. We are doing what we have been elected to do: to make law. We have had no law since January 1988. For the previous 19 years we had a law that did not adequately protect the unborn. I have been a part of this continuing struggle since my involvement as a hospital board member in Kitchener for nine years and as a member of Parliament from 1979 to 1980 and again since 1984. I have submitted private members' bills on this topic and have participated in every debate on abortion and most recently as a member of the legislative committee on Bill C-43.
Earlier today we heard two excellent presentations by two other members of that committee. We heard a moving and inspiring speech by the member for Surrey-White Rock. We also heard an excellent address from the hon. member for South Shore.
Since the Morgentaler decision of the Supreme Court in January 1988 our country has been without a law on abortion. For many, the debate on what should be done about abortion has been based on the assumption that the only law which would be constitutionally acceptable to fill this vacuum is one that is based on the gestational approach. This approach would in effect guarantee abortion on demand for up to 16 weeks or 20 weeks.
The present bill is not what I would like it to be. To develop a law on the assumption of gestation would violate my fundamental understanding of life and that of the world-renowned scientists such as Dr. Jerome Le-Jeune who appeared before our committee.
My colleagues and I have worked long and hard to change the kind of bill the government would introduce into the House from one that permits abortion on demand for up to 20 weeks to one that protects life from conception.
I am pleased that Bill C-43 has implicitly accepted that life affirming approach to law and has rejected the gestational approach. After an all-party legislative committee examined the proposed legislation and after this House last night turned down amendments which would have strengthened the legal protection of the unborn, we are now faced with the key question of saying yes or no to

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
Bill C-43 unamended. Now I have come to this moment of declaring my position and my reasons for that position.
I will be supporting Bill C-43 as it stands at third reading. My reasons are as follows. First, if this bill passes it will signify an important shift in the debate since the Morgantaler decision of January 1988. The gestational approach, which even the Law Reform Commission in its 1989 study paper offered as the only way to reach a compromise, was rejected.
With the passage of this bill, arguments on the taking of the life of the unborn can no longer be based on the assumption that life before birth can be taken at will. Why? Because this bill has in effect rejected the proabortion ideology. If this bill is passed, future debates should focus on the reasons abortion should or should not be allowed.
Since January 1988 we have been forced to argue why the unborn should be protected. If this bill passes, the operative assumption is that life of the unborn is indeed deserving of some legal protection from conception. Now the burden lies with those who favour abortion to provide medically valid reasons it should be allowed. Therefore we have begun to build on the principle that life must be protected from conception.
Second, there is at least an attempt to deal with the very difficult challenge of protecting both the unborn child and the mother. While that attempt is incomplete the bill recognizes the existence of two lives. By so doing, the legislation recognizes a reality which cannot be and indeed must not be avoided.
The third reason I support this bill is that abortion is again in the Criminal Code and subject to a criminal sanction in the case of unlawful abortion. Let us not underestimate the value this communicates to the Canadian public. It makes a statement to our nation that abortion is no longer regarded by law makers as a simple or casual medical procedure. Abortion is again a criminal act unless it meets the requirements of the law and the standards of the medical profession. Law not only serves to contain unacceptable behaviour but also serves as a guide upholding values for all to see and to respect. As the Law Reform Commission stated:
The criminal law is our nation's fundamental statement of public policy-ultimately the criminal law is a mirror of what we are; it reflects our commitment or lack of commitment, to human dignity and equality. The law does not exist for the sole or primary purpose of punishing illicit acts. It exists, as an expression, in a broad sense,
of the kind of people we are. It does not merely regulate our behaviour, it articulates and symbolizes our values and beliefs.
Furthermore, the Supreme Court will be required to recognize the principles of justice reflected in this bill. As well, this bill calls on the medical profession to deal with the life of both the unborn child and the mother. Doctors are expected to exercise their professional responsibility to the best of their ability, recognizing that they must consider the human right to life of both patients.
Finally, this bill provides us with a foundation on which we can build in the future. By rejecting the assumption and approach of gestation and by implicitly recognizing the protection of life from conception, we now have a basis on which to build stronger protection for the unborn. We can then better balance the mother's right to the security of her person and the state's interest in the protection of the foetus. However, there is a very serious weakness in this bill. The definition of health is far too broad and far too inclusive. This major weakness created such difficulties for me, to the point of almost voting against the bill at third reading. However I have come to recognize that the bill at least points us in the right direction.
Many ask if this bill will save any lives. I believe it could. Cardinal Carter commented:
If the medical profession takes its new responsibilities seriously, if the attorneys general of our provinces apply the law as it is written, if our law officers, particularly our judges, enforce the prescriptions, we may save some lives.
Surely, if doctors took their responsibilities seriously under this bill individually and collectively, they could ensure that good medical practice according to their own medical standards and professional ethics would not permit some of their colleagues to disregard all that they have been taught. Through peer pressure and the enforcement of professional ethics, doctors could stop the vast majority of abortions that have absolutely no medical validity because they are socio-economic in origin, as they themselves testified and admitted before the committee.
For me, this bill is not a denial of my principles. I am not for a moment forsaking the principles which have guided and will continue to guide me in my ongoing struggle to protect the unborn. I am engaged in a long and difficult struggle for justice for the unborn. To vote for this bill is therefore part of a long-term strategy to
May 24, 1990

help bring about public respect for life at all stages of development.
In October 1989 my colleagues and I turned the Department of Justice and the cabinet from a gestational approach. Indeed, for me to vote against this bill now would be a compromise. It would be an admission of defeat, an opting for no law, and a cop-out. This would be an abdication of my responsibility as a law maker.
When Bill C-43 was debated at report stage my colleagues and I introduced amendments. Frankly, I am deeply disappointed that none of them passed. We pressed for at least three amendments.
The first one would have added the word "seriously" before the word "threatened".
The second one would have required the physician to first conclude that there is no other medically acceptable treatment to alleviate the health risk.
The third amendment would have stipulated that the definition of the word "health" specifically exclude psychological considerations which the Minister of Justice before the committee interpreted to include socioeconomic factors.
If these three amendments had been accepted they would have changed this bill into one which would have adequately responded to the Supreme Court's invitation to Parliament to balance the mother's rights to security of her person and society's interest in the protection of the foetus.
We are still making progress. In advising pro-lifers Dr. J. C. Wilke, President of the American Right to Life Movement said:
Their choice is either to be unrealistic and seek legislation they are sure to lose and then watch the holocaust continue, or realistically pass the best possible measure, stopping (some) of the killing now, and then come back another year and save some more lives-with the passing of years it has become painfully obvious that we are not going to stop abortion in one single step. All responsible pro-life leaders accept that it will have to be done step by step.
With this bill we are taking one small yet important step today for the unborn. My prayer is that many more steps will follow. To give up on the bill and to do nothing is to stand idly by as tens of thousands of lives per year are snuffed out. I personally do not see that stance as a
Government Orders
form of higher Christian integrity. We must work to restrain evil and save as many lives as we can whenever we can.
Some would argue that no law is better than this law. I believe they are mistaken for the following two reasons. First, we would be missing an opportunity to use the fulcrum of law to shift the influence of law toward justice for the unborn.
Second, it will be years before another government will attempt to write a law on abortion. As a legislator today, I cannot say: "Let's kill this bill so that hopefully in the future we can do better". That is compromising my task today by hiding behind the skirts of an unknown future and that, to me, is not leadership.
Furthermore, Cardinal Carter stated: "We are pleased that we will have a law, even one so imperfect".
Archbishop Ambrosic, who recently succeeded Cardinal Carter, stated on April 14, 1990:
Abortion is always wrong. We can never be at peace with a law that permits abortion. Having said this, I ought to add that in my opinion, some law is better than no law. As it stands, the proposed law at least criminalizes abortion although I would like to make it much more restrictive than it is.
Further, I agree with the Law Reform Commissions's testimony to the committee. I would like to quote from what Justice Linden said to us:
Bill C-43 does not solve all the problems of unwanted pregnancy. It is not meant to. It is just meant to solve a legal problem, a small aspect of this general problem. For a long-term solution, we need better education, better reproductive counselling, and greater social and economic support for child care. We need more help for women who get pregnant as a result of failed contraception, or because of incest or rape. We need to ensure that pregnant women have a real choice about their future, so that abortion does not seem to them to be the only answer. We need as a nation to be more compassionate and supportive of families, of mothers and their children. So let us recognize that Bill C-43 is only one step, albeit an important one, in dealing with this complex problem.
William Wilberforce fought for 19 years as a member of Parliament in England to end the slave trade, and for another 26 years to end slavery itself within the British Empire. Throughout all those years he never compromised on his ultimate goal and principles. However, he

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
