did make concessions in timing and he did vote yes to incremental improvements. He even agreed to pay slave traders money out of the public purse to provide an extra six inches of sleeping space on their ships carrying the slaves. But he did not compromise on his ultimate goal and principles.
Therefore, I say to my pro-life friends, let us keep our eyes clearly on the goal of achieving a real balance which recognizes both the mother's right to the security of her person and society's interest in the true protection of the unborn. In the meantime, let us say yes to whatever moves us toward that goal, even if the steps may seem very small indeed. At least they are steps in the right direction.
Today, we on the pro-life side of this debate, do not have the numbers, but we are strong enough to defeat any gestational law. We are strong enough to produce a bill that includes abortion in the Criminal Code. We are strong enough to make sure that there are some criminal sanctions against unlawful abortion and that the principle within that bill implicitly protects human life from conception or, more technically, from implantation.
We are also strong enough to ensure that by passing this bill we are taking the first step toward a stronger and better law in the future. Further, we are teaching that abortion is a serious moral issue and that society at large, and doctors in particular, should start acting responsibly. Our laws and our lives should express our commitment to compassion and justice for the lives of the unborn and their parents. This is my commitment. That is what I will work for as long and as best I can.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member and I happen to agree with respect to the issue itself and that life must be protected from the moment of conception. However, I have very serious difficulties in accepting the reasons why he and others who consider themselves pro-life are supporting this piece of legislation.
He speaks of incremental gain. He feels that it is better to have this bill than no bill at all. I suggest to the hon. member that if this bill carries, and it appears that in fact it will carry on Tuesday, then the likelihood of a new bill or changes to this bill being introduced in the foreseeable future are negligible in that the government
today, and perhaps future governments, will not feel the pressure necessary to address again the issue of abortion.
As well, I would like to say to him in all sincerity that when we are talking about rights surely he would agree that rights are rights. If we agree that life begins at the moment of conception, how then can he and others who consider themselves pro-life support a bill, which in my view is a fraudulent piece of legislation, that would allow abortion on demand, a bill that differentiates between life after birth and life before birth, in that if a life after birth is taken there follows a specific penalty?
In my view there is absolutely no adequate protection for life in this particular bill. The penalty is different for the taking of a life before birth, whether it be an hour before birth, a month before birth or three months before birth.
How can he reconcile his views with a bill that will, for all intents and purposes, allow abortion on demand? If one truly and sincerely believes in life and the sanctity of life, then how can one support a bill that treats life before birth differently than life after birth?

Mr. Speaker, I will be pleased to try and respond to the questions raised by the member for York South-Weston.
The comment he made about incremental gain is correct. I am saying that we are at least gaining something. We are gaming a law. In the first place it is in the Criminal Code. It has a criminal sanction. It implicitly recognizes that there is a need to protect the unborn child, from conception.
He said that the government may not feel the pressure now if we pass this bill, and therefore, we will not be able to do anything further. I know the member was listening to me. He will recall what I said about one example from the British Parliament concerning William Wilberforce who worked for 19 years to end the slave trade, then 26 years more to end slavery itself. That is a long, long time.
If someone had come to him after the first attempt and said: "You are not going to get it. Give up", or if someone had come to him and said: "You are making a slight concession here. You cannot do that. Go for all or nothing," would he have ended it? No. He had to keep his eye on the ultimate goal and keep working at every step possible to get something. That is what we have to do.
May 24, 1990

The member asked if the government was not going to feel the pressure. That never stopped him before the law was struck down, or since it was struck down by the court from bringing in his own private members' bills. It did not prevent me from bringing in private members' bills. It did not prevent any of us from speaking in support of those private members' bills. We will continue to do it. I hope that he does that. I intend to do that. We have to keep working at this.
The question now is whether or not we are really acting responsibly as lawmakers if we say that it is better to have no law with no restraints, meaning full abortion on demand for at least another four years, plus the two we have already just passed as a minimum. I say no.
However, if this was a gestational bill before us, then I would say its principles are wrong. At least the principles in this bill are implicitly going the right way. That is why I say build on the little bit of good that is there. Therefore we will have a law. Therefore we implicitly say something must be protected. Therefore we are teaching society, and there is value.
Let us start doing what we did in terms of smoking. For many years smoking was perfectly acceptable. It was legitimate. Then some of us started to learn in our health classes that it is not acceptable. As a health and physical education teacher I taught that. Then we worked hard. I worked hard as a hospital board member to get rid of it. Finally, everybody started to listen to the evidence. Then we finally started to see some change.
Let us bring in a law that says it is criminally wrong. Let us now use that to teach. Let us use all the information that people like Dr. Jerome LeJeune gave us. Let us keep reminding people that they are dealing with life from conception.
Just as we got society to turn around on smoking, maybe we will begin to get society to turn around on this issue and start doing what I know the hon. member wants, what I want as well.

Mr. Speaker, the member opposite made comments about a member of Parliament in the British Parliament who
Government Orders
worked for years to ensure an end to slavery. It was a laudable goal, and he was eventually successful.
I want to say that women in Canada have struggled for 20 years to get abortion out of the Criminal Code of Canada. Women have struggled long and hard to get abortion out of the Criminal Code of Canada.
I want to ask him how he feels about the majority of Canadian women who see this kind of legislation, and who see the kinds of remarks that he has made in this House today, as really insulting to them. Women do not take this decision lightly. Women struggle. Women search within their own souls and their own consciences before they make a decision to have an abortion.
How can he justify this criminal legislation and his attitude of the state and he having the right to decide when and if a woman will have a child?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby mentions the fact that there are women in Canada who do not want to see abortion in the Criminal Code. That is correct. There are also some men who do not want to see it in the Criminal Code. But there are also many other women who do want to see it in the Criminal Code. She did not mention that.
I presented in this House a petition with the signatures of women only-over 220,000 signatures-from across this country who wanted a law that would protect the unborn. What about those 220,000 women?
What about the many other women in Canada who say that according to all the available medical evidence we are dealing with two lives when we talk about abortion? We are dealing with the life of the mother and the life of the child within the mother.
I always find it incredulous to say that we have to balance those interests as though the mother somehow or other has to balance the choice of whether or not her own child within her has a right to life. My goodness, that is a denial of everything a mother wants. It makes no sense.
We know that in the sense of where there is a case of real threat to the mother's life, then there is a need to ask: "Is there a time when we take one life to protect another life?" There is then a legitimate role to play. The Supreme Court invited us to play that role. In fact, it said to us that the precise point in the development of that foetus is up to Parliament to decide. We have. This

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
bill, even in its weak form, states that it implicitly starts at conception. That is why I say, let us take at least the good in this bill and let us vote for it so that we can build on it and keep working in the future to improve it.

Mr. Speaker, in the brief time that I have to discuss Bill C-43 tonight, I would like to divide my remarks into three distinct categories.
First, I would like to state my position with respect to this issue. Perhaps a better way of putting it is to say that I will restate my position on this particular issue.
Second, I would like to discuss Bill C-43 and the inherent flaws that I see in it.
Third, I would like to make some responsive remarks to the speeches made by some other members and some of the points raised by them. I will then, of course, draw a conclusion.
My position is fairly clear. There is no greater right than the right to live. It is upon this right that all other rights rest. In that context, we have to look at what we are talking about when we speak about Bill C-43. Of course, we are speaking about abortion.
What is an abortion? With the greatest of respect, that is the question so many members of the House refuse to come to grips with. Precisely what is an abortion? If we look in the dictionary we find that abortion is defined as the procuring of premature delivery for the purpose of destroying offspring. I emphasize those words, "for the purpose of destroying offspring". That is the point. For me, human life begins at conception. Of course, if you have a human life and you have an abortion-a medical procedure designed to destroy offspring-you are clearly destroying human life.
Because an abortion kills a human being, it is wrong. It must be prevented, just as we prevent the killing of all other human beings, including convicted criminals. The reason the House is in this turmoil with respect to this issue is the overwhelming revulsion of society about the topic of abortion.
If we were not talking about the killing of a human being, but about something equivalent to cutting your hair or nails, or to mowing the lawn, no one would be upset. That is not what we are talking about. We are
talking about the destruction of human life. That is what gets people into the state in which they have to air their grievances and about which they feel that there is no position other than their own.
That is why we have to come to grips as a country and as a Parliament with the fundamental question. We have to admit to ourselves that an abortion destroys a human being.
Why would I say that there is a revulsion in society? Let us look at the medical profession. We know that the Canadian Medical Association has approximately 45,000 member doctors. Out of that membership of 45,000 we know that there are approximately 800 who will do abortions. That is 1.7 per cent of the doctors in the country.
We further know from the Canadian Medical Association that out of these 800 doctors only about 325 do the majority of abortions. That is 0.72 per cent of the doctors in the country.
I ask rhetorically: Why is it that an infinitesimal percentage of the medical doctors in the country will perform an abortion? I will provide an answer. It is because those doctors know scientifically, from medical school and biology class, that an abortion destroys a living entity.
I would like to move on to address the flaws, as I see them, of Bill C-43, and, in doing so, to speak directly to those members of Parliament who oppose the allowing of abortions and yet consider that it is appropriate to vote in favour of Bill C-43.
This morning the Minister of Justice declared that this bill protects the foetus. We heard the member for Kitchener say time and time again how this bill implicitly-and he emphasized the word "implicitly", not explicitly but implicitly-protects the foetus.
The Minister of Justice said that this bill protects the foetus. I would like to say two things in that regard. Why is it appropriate for our society to protect the foetus? It can only be because the foetus is a human being. If the foetus is not a human being, why protect it? Why should we be involved in this debate at all? Of course the foetus is a human being. It needs protection. The government
May 24, 1990

recognizes that it needs protection. The Minister of Justice says that this bill protects the foetus.
With the greatest of respect, I say that this bill does not protect the foetus. It will not stand the scrutiny of the Supreme Court of Canada. That is why I asked the member for South Shore what was the test of the Supreme Court of Canada. I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, what the test of the Supreme Court of Canada is.
I have in my hand the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in the Daigle case. I refer specifically to a section in which the Supreme Court is dealing with the Quebec Charter of Rights and the argument that a foetus is protected thereunder, and I quote:
In our view the Quebec Charter, considered as a whole, does not display any clear intention on the part of its framers to consider the status of a foetus. This is most evident in the fact that the Charter lacks any definition of "human being" or "person".
This bill lacks any definition of human being or person. Yet, because it is in the Criminal Code, the only definition of human being or person contained in the Criminal Code provides that one becomes a human being when one is bom. That is the definition of a human being in which this bill is being incorporated. How that protects the foetus is beyond me.
In any event, note that the Supreme Court finds that there is no specific definition of human being or person. The decision continues:
One can ask why the Quebec legislature, if it had intended to accord a foetus the right to life, would have left the protection of this right in such an uncertain state -If the legislature had wished to grant foetuses the right to life, then it seems unlikely that it would have left the protection of this right to such happenstance.
That is precisely the point. That is precisely, in my view, what the Supreme Court of Canada is going to say with regard to this bill.
There is a definition of health in the bill, a very comprehensive definition of health, but there is no definition of foetus, no definition of human being, and no definition of what it is that this bill is attempting to protect and why. That failure is a fatal flaw in this bill. In my view, it will not pass the scrutiny of the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court has stated clearly in the passages that I have cited that if you want to protect the foetus, Parliament has the right to do so, but you must do it explicitly. That is why the member for Kitchener, at least
Government Orders
four times in his speech, said "implicitly". The member recognizes that the test is to be explicit. This bill is not. In fact, as I said, there is no definition.
If this bill passes it will institutionalize abortion. It will, in fact, make the procedure of abortion legitimate. In my view, the respect for life which it pretends to try to engender, will be diminished.
The member for Kitchener was talking about step-bystep procedures. In the United Kingdom, there is an abortion law which allows an abortion up to 28 weeks. Simply dividing the four weeks that there are in a month into 28 weeks shows that we are talking about seven months. In England abortion is allowed up to seven months. That was passed on the basis of putting it into law, and then working backward. It has not happened. Not only has it not happened, but society has become desensitized to the respect for life.
The next step has already been played out. Because of the lack of respect for life, embryo experimentation has been authorized in the United Kingdom. The next step, of course, is foetal experimentation. Is that the kind of society that we can look forward to in Canada?
I will now quickly address a few of the points that have been raised up by other members. A statement has been made that a woman has the right to choose. The question must be, a right to choose what? The answer is, to terminate a pregnancy. Quite frankly, that is an antiseptic way of saying, the right to choose to destroy the living entity within the person. I submit that that is unacceptable in a civilized society.
Another statement which has been used is: "It's my body". The fact is that there are two bodies involved. There is the mother and there is the child within her. Both those bodies are entitled to respect. Both those bodies are entitled to protection.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I will have to ask the hon. member to conclude, please.

Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, I would like to quote Martin Luther King who said: "A law may not change the heart, but it will restrain the heartless."
What kind of law? The law must recognize explicitly civilized society's recognition of the right of the unborn to be alive. This bill does not do that. I urge members to defeat it for that reason. No law is better than a flawed law, because a flawed law will lend legislative legitimacy

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
to the greatest violation of human rights in history-the denial of the fundamental right to exist.

Mr. Speaker, when the member was stating his views on Bill C-43, he indicated that only a small proportion of doctors perform abortions in this country. He said it was because they knew or had scientific knowledge that when they were performing an abortion it was destroying a human life.
The truth of the matter is that only a small number of doctors perform abortions because they are harassed and because it is not a well-funded service for doctors. They find it a difficult question, there is no doubt about that, just as many of us find it a difficult question. But it has nothing to do with scientific knowledge.
I have a letter from the Canadian Medical Association. In part, it states: "We believe that, if passed, Bill C-43 will place at risk both the confidentiality and trust so essential to the physician-patient relationship. Further, we are convinced that this law will effectively limit access to this medical procedure resulting in greater danger to the pregnant woman's physical or mental well-being as the process for seeking an abortion becomes lengthier, one of the reasons the old law was struck down".
I would like the member to comment on the position of the Canadian Medical Association. I sat on the legislative committee. We saw no scientific knowledge from any of the scientific community, from the Canadian mental health community, or from the Canadian Medical Association, that supported his thesis. There simply is none. There was none. He is wrong.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague for her question. I believe that the answer that I can give is that there are divisions in the medical community as there are in this House, as there are in society. No matter what anybody says, less than 1 per cent of the doctors in this country do abortions. It is not because we do not pay doctors enough to do the abortions, it is because they find them distasteful. They find them
distasteful because they know precisely what they are doing.
Every obstetrician in this country knows that when he treats a pregnant woman, he is treating two patients, his pregnant patient and the child within her. Every single doctor who treats that pregnant woman is perfectly aware that there are two patients. We cannot deny simple biology. We cannot deny that there is a living entity within the womb that is growing. We cannot deny that biological fact.
To say that life begins at birth is to say that anything can be done before birth because there is no inherent human value to be protected. I do not accept that. I hope that our Canadian society does not accept that, but this is the forum to discuss those points. This is what we should be discussing, talking about when life begins, deciding those questions and not hiding from them and pretending that they do not exist. We have to come up with the facts and decide when human life begins. Once we decide that as a legislative body, then we will decide when, if ever, human life should be terminated.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I just wanted to let you know that the procedure on the government side of the House from now on will be that each member will divide the 20 minute time, so that each member will have 10 minutes, followed possibly by a five minute question period. From this point on, on the government side, that will be the procedure.

Mr. Speaker, first let me start off by offering to you my personal congratulations on the choice the Prime Minister announced in the House the other day. I think you and I have spent have spent time in this House together and at different committees, and I was absolutely thrilled with the announcement. I wish you the very best and look forward to working with you and being recognized as time goes on.
I am not going to enlarge on the substance of what I have said in this House on two other occasions on this very important subject, those dates having been October 30 and November 22.1 have some hesitation in getting up again today to speak on this subject but I found I
May 24, 1990

should get up and speak from a procedural aspect rather than from a substantive aspect of the abortion bill.
Let me quote from the comments I made on November 22, as reported at page 6016 of Hansard:
- it is the duty of every member of this House, to address these very important issues. We have now come to the point where decisions should be made. The decisions that are before us are: When do we terminate a pregnancy, what rights do individuals have in our society, and what are the rights of the unborn child from the moment of conception?
These are awesome questions that sometimes we have difficulty in answering. The reason that I rise today to address, not the substance of that issue, but some procedural aspects is that, prior to this first debate and as we get on to the situation of voting on this issue tonight, there is a group in our society that is determined to put an end to all abortions.
Unfortunately, in their zeal to protect the rights of the unborn, they often contravene, infringe upon, and fail to respect the rights of the living. They fail to respect the most fundamental right of all Canadians under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the right to free speech. On a personal note, this has happened to me and, as a result, I have some hesitation in getting up and speaking about it, not about the substance or because of the substance-I cannot change from my original position-but from the procedural aspects and the type of tactics they use in order to get you to change your position.
They use letters and magazines. The one that I am going to refer to is Vitality, Volume 3, No. 8. It says that, despite the fact that I had issued no new statement and had made no public statement calling for full legal protection of the unborn, which is absolutely wrong. The article reads, "Joe Comuzzi won in this election, a man who has made no public commitment to work to protect the rights of the unborn". That again, is wrong. What they were looking for in that statement is for me to sign some document which I could not sign. I had given them the reasons why I could not sign that document. It was not acceptable, it did not fit their very tight philosophy and, as a result, they were trying to blackmail me into signing. I refused to do so and these were the tactics they used.
The other modes of trying to coerce people into adopting position are letters to the editor from people
Government Orders
who are obviously in the pro-life movement. They try to embarrass you in your local community. I consider these types of procedures to be unacceptable and they are the reason for my rising today to make these statements.
Despite our personal beliefs, the subject we are discussing today must be approached with compassion, tolerance and understanding. Only through this reasonable dialogue between reasonable men and women can we attack and expect to resolve this very difficult societal issue that is before us today.
In my analysis of what we have heard and what we have seen, I particularly liked the speech that was given by the Governor of the State of New York, when he was addressing the convocation class in 1984 at Notre Dame University. I thought it would be interesting to quote from Governor Cuomo's speech where he said: "It would be tragic if we let the dialogue that we are involved with today become a prolonged and divisive argument that destroys or impairs our ability to practise and to love one another, to practise any part of our morality, to practise our sense of touching and healing our fellow human being, and to affirm that great life that surrounds all of us in this country".
In that quote I think is the compassion which I referred to earlier in my speech. I am afraid it is a compassion that has been missing in the procedural movement of those people who claim to be pro-life and use the tactics I referred to earlier to get people like myself to change our minds or be more adamant in our positions.
I think there was no more compelling meeting in this whole process than the meeting in my office in Thunder Bay, when I visited with the people of the pro-choice movement. They came into my office and for the first time I listened to them intently. They said that they are not on the other side of the fence. They are not against life because they oppose those principles and the philosophy that the other side chooses. That was the most sincere statement I heard in this whole process. I do not think anyone in this debate is against life. I compliment and thank the people who took the time out in the area I represent, Thunder Bay-Nipigon, and all those people throughout Canada who have taken an interest in this very important topic, people who came and expressed their views and helped us make our decisions as politicians, in a reasoned and compassionate way. As I said,

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
Mr. Speaker, it was the best lesson that I had heard, and the best lesson throughout this whole process.
At the outset I made my views known on this topic very clearly. I reconfirmed my position. I did not want to leave anyone uncertain as to where I stood. The result the pro-life movement has tried to accomplish is where I really stand on this issue. My position has not changed. Substantively, I am with those people who are against the termination of pregnancy and I am certainly against the procedural issues that the pro-life movement stands for and how they approach the problem. I reconfirmed that position in the House today. I intend to vote against the legislation.
Philosophically, I am on their side but, personally, I separate myself from any association with that group which fails to exhibit the compassion towards our fellow human beings which this sensitive subject demands. I think I have made my position clear. This group that represents the substantive issue that I represent fails to exhibit the compassion, it fails to listen to a reasoned approach, it fails to acknowledge that there can be another side to an issue, and it fails to respect the freedoms that all of us in Canada have come to enjoy.
There is a group which in their zeal attempts to protect the life and rights of the unborn but they fail to protect the rights of those of us already here.

Mr. Speaker, I extend to you my sincere congratulations in assuming your very high position. I also thank you for recognizing me during this critical and emotional debate for so many Canadians.
I will be brief as I make my position clear one more time, as I have done debate after debate, vote after vote, election after election, and Parliament after Parliament.
I believe that life begins at the moment of conception, period, full stop. I believe that nothing should interrupt that life if we are truly trying to protect the rights of the unborn.
While I can modify my anti-abortion stand in a couple of ways, and I will refer to them in a moment, I must stand on my own personal beliefs, whether or not there is a consensus among the people I represent, whether or
not I am adhering to the government line, as expressed by the Prime Minister and the Attorney General of Canada, both of whom know exactly where I stand.
On that point, I want to commend the Right Hon. Prime Minister, his House leader, and my friend from Calgaiy West, the chief government whip for allowing a free vote according to the individual conscience of members of Parliament. I exercised that opportunity to vote freely during a number of amendments to Bill C-43 and a motion of concurrence last evening.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot tell you, or anyone who is looking in, or listening to, or reading the transcripts of this debate, how agonizing, how emotionally difficult this matter of abortion is for any member of Parliament, regardless of the party that he or she represents. Here is what I said in my weekly, or in my semi-occasional weekly column to my constituents in the Flambouroulgh Review of July 20, 1988:
Abortion is an extremely volatile issue. It is philosophical. It is
emotional. It affects everybody, deeply and personally. I will
therefore exercise my vote conscientiously and responsibly.
I said earlier that I could soften my pro-life stand in a couple of obviously difficult circumstances: first, in the case of rape or incest and, second, in the case of a medical emergency. This comes down to a fundamentally important point which some of our colleagues have touched upon, but I want to reinforce it. I am not equipped to play God. No politician is. Any politician who thinks she or he is equipped to play God had better not be in this business.
Only when there is a really true medical emergency which affects the life of the mother to be should the matter become a case between the woman and her doctor. In that case I can certainly support the medical side of this issue.
As an adjunct to that, I also soften a little in terms of the psychological aspects if there is severe mental distress or harm to the mother and/or to the foetus. Then I think that again it becomes a matter between a woman and the appropriate medical authority to make that decision, but that is where it stops in my view.
I have one very deep regret about some of the signals I have been sending on Bill C-43, and that is my profound respect for women, not only for my colleagues on all sides of the House but for the women's movement in
May 24, 1990

Government Orders
general. I truly admire those women who have wrestled in physical, psychological and legal ways with this issue.
I do not want any of my female colleagues in this place to think for one moment that my very deep and proper conscience votes on the amendments have anything to do with my respect for the women colleagues in this place who vote the other way. Not in the slightest do I acquaint my affection for women with the direction that my votes take on the abortion issue.
We are talking about life itself. Male and female foetuses are at stake here. We respect life. We spare life. I see no way that I can support this bill next Tuesday, May 29, unless there is some recognition of the protection of the unborn. There may be some. I am willing to withhold my final decision in terms of how I vote. There may be some of that protection. Maybe some law is better than no law at all, but I ha'e me doubts.
I really feel that I cannot support the legislation, not because my constituents feel that I should do so, not because I have received countless letters from across the country in support of my stand to vote against this bill unless amendments are passed, and certainly not because anyone on this side has ordered me one way or the other how to vote on this issue. No, sir.
I do not respond favourably to write-in campaigns or orders from above anywhere. I am simply voting according to my conscience, as I have said, the Prime Minister has graciously allowed members of Parliament to do.
I sympathize with those who want to vote pro-life according to their consciences. I heard very clearly, as we all have if we have been listening to this debate, the opposite arguments so very eloquently stated by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca, both distinguished representatives from British Columbia. I found their arguments fascinating, and in the case of the former premier of British Columbia, great theatre. It still does not change my mind. I owe it to my constituents and my fellow believers across the country to promote the sanctity of life and the protection of innocent unborn children.
Some will tell you, Mr. Speaker, that some compromise law is better than no law at all. As I said earlier, some do not want any law regarding abortion. As I said, I am not God and, certainly the former premier of British Columbia said the truest words that I have heard from him, neither is he.
This is a non-partisan debate. This bill in my view does not strike a balance between the rights of the woman and the rights of the foetus. I want a law which truly protects the rights of the unborn children who have no right or chance or opportunity to speak in this chamber as we do today. I will be keeping my own counsel about how to vote on Bill C-43 at third reading.

Mr. Speaker, I must say to the member for Hamilton-Wentworth that I think that was truly one of the better speeches I have heard in the House. It was one of the better speeches because it came straight from the heart. I said earlier today that many times we are engaged in rhetoric. This is one of those rare occasions in the House where the rhetoric has lessened and the emotion and humanness of the members of this place is shown to be at its best.
I do not know whether the hon. member heard my speech earlier, but I find myself in almost the same position of trying to grapple with that balance which in the Supreme Court decision said that parliamentarians had a right and should by right look at the societal interest and the rights of the foetus. I firmly believe, as a reasonable, rational individual such as my friend from Hamilton-Wentworth is, that the bill simply does not go far enough.
I guess I do this at some risk, and I hope I am not putting the member at some risk, but many times in my position of trying to find that balance with the societal rights of the foetus, people will say: "You are against women". Absolutely nothing could be further from the truth in my case, and I know in the case of the hon. member. TTie hon. member mentioned something that I have not heard in this debate before. It is that when we are dealing with the rights of the foetus, we are dealing with the rights of the foetus, male and female, so we are indeed dealing with the rights of women which must in my view be protected under any law. I want to commend him for striking a particular note with me on that

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
remark. I would hope that others who find this debate to be divisive would see the compassion and the deep reflective thought the hon. member put into his remarks.
I want to ask a question. The hon. member mentioned that he had been looking in the bill for some better definition of what "at risk" means when an abortion would be permitted under law. I am wondering, not to put words in the hon. member's mouth, if he is as concerned as I am and as some members are that the definition of when an abortion would be permitted under this legislation is just a little too loose and a little too open to interpretation. In a legalistic sense when those things happen, sometimes we err on the side of leniency and expansion. That is a great concern that I have.
Could the member elaborate a little more about the type of amendment he would have liked to have seen which would have better defined "at risk" and "health"?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my friend across the way for his kind comments.
One of the problems that I and a number of us on this side have about the current legislation is that one could drive trucks through the legal definitions of what at risk is, what health is, whether health means physical health, mental health, psychological health, or whatever. That is one of the things that will ultimately have to be resolved once we in this House decide what to do about this legislation.
I am being persuaded that some law, some foot in the door, some restriction on the Morgantaler-type mentality on abortions, is better than no law at all. I am being persuaded that maybe we have a chance in this House of Commons to do something which some Parliaments down the road may never have a chance to do. We have got a pretty good consensus kind of legislation. As I say, one can drive trucks through some of the phrases and the points such as at risk, for example.
All I can say to my hon. friend is that it is something that all of us are wrestling with. When I talked about male and female foetuses I thought that maybe I should draw attention to that end of the spectrum, because male and female members of Parliament are debating this issue and yet this issue is perceived to be strictly a woman's issue. It is. It is veiy much a woman's issue. None of us men have to go through abortions, but I still think that because we are talking from one end of the spectrum to the other we are talking about the need for
all members of society to take a very serious look at this question and at this bill.

Mr. Speaker, as my friends have previously outlined, this is obviously a matter that causes us a great deal of concern. All of us have wrestled with the various aspects of the matter. As was previously mentioned it is also a balancing of rights.
In looking at the evidence before the parliamentary committee, the balancing of rights was mentioned quite a bit in term of various rights such as the foetal rights and the rights of the mother. It was a thread that seemed to go through the evidence all the time. Obviously that is the result of the Morgentaler decision and the striking down of the previous Section 251 because it infringed upon Section 7 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and affected a woman's security of her person.
In looking at what type of law can be drafted, we look at the decision and we see the remark that society has an interest in the foetus which has to be balanced with the rights of the mother.
How do we do that? Obviously it is very difficult. Bill C-43 is an attempt to reach that balance between the woman and the security of her person and society's interest in the protection of the foetus. When we are drafting the law we have to realize that we are within those parameters and have to deal with that particular aspect of the matter. Otherwise, if we have a law that is too restrictive, it will be struck down.
In looking at that, as well as looking at the woman's right to security of her person and also other matters under Section 2A of the charter, her equality rights under Section 15 and also her sexual equality rights under Section 28, we realize all those matters have to be taken into account in drafting the law.
It would not be easy to take a stand that would say no abortion ever, but if we decided to pass such a law we know that it would be struck down immediately. Are we being true to ourselves or am I being true to myself if we do that? I do not think I am. Where does that leave us?
I noticed in the evidence before the committee there was some indication that we could use Section 33 of the charter in order to make whatever law we produced valid for five years. I cannot accept that. I cannot accept that. We have a Charter of Rights and Freedoms and our country has evolved to the point where we feel confident enough that we can use that charter. Our laws should be within that charter. In that respect, I cannot see using
May 24, 1990

Section 33 in order to validate any law that we put forward.
If we wanted to go even further, to say that life begins at conception, this would require a constitutional amendment, with the obvious difficulties we all know that entails. But that also introduces a legal regime for the foetus itself. We do not even know the implications of that legal regime.
After a decision regarding foetal rights in the United States, and I do not mean to be frivolous, an action was launched by individuals claiming that nine months should be added to everybody's age, showing how that would affect individuals. There is also the question of accidents, and what happens in that matter. It is something that has not been thought through and I cannot go in that direction and I would not like to see the country go in that direction. So I reject Section 33 and I reject any constitutional amendment.
That leaves us with a framework as set out in the Morgentaler and Daigle cases in order to try to balance the rights of the woman under the Charter of Rights and balance the rights of the foetus. It is obviously a difficult task, and we have heard people make comment here that it has not occurred in this legislation.
This is something that is obviously going to change over a period of time. It is not going to remain static. I think that we all realize that the matter is not going to end in this particular chamber once this bill is dealt with. If the bill is defeated, we are faced with the reality that there will be no law in place. Although the Daigle case speaks to it, we do not want to see the events of last summer repeated, with the degradation of people and their emotions and private lives being exposed on the televisions of the nation. We need some law that will give us stability in this area.
This legislation is the best attempt at finding a a balance of the rights of the woman and the rights of the foetus. Many of the aspects of the Morgentaler decision in terms of access have been removed. One doctor is involved in this particular law. We see a definition of health to deal with previous concerns about that definition. Those are a couple of matters that seem to deal
Government Orders
with the objections in terms of access that were raised by two or three of the judges in the Morgentaler decision. The attempt is being made to try to deal with the defects that were found in the previous Section 251 in this particular law.
The gestational approach originally proposed by the Law Reform Commission as a way to balance the rights of the foetus and the rights of the woman has been rejected. I have to agree with that decision because that approach could raise many difficult questions.
The Daigle case indicated that rights begin at birth. Looking at that particular aspect of it, it seems the Supreme Court did not want deal extensively with the legal aspect of rights of the foetus. I have my own personal views on the subject matter, but I do not feel that I can force them on to any other individual.
As I say, I start with the premise that we have a Charter of Rights and we must have a law that fits within that. To be true to myself and to ensure the inclusion of such a law, while recognizing the woman's rights, I think the balance provided within Bill C-43 is the best that can be achieved at this time.
I did not vote in favour of any the amendments that were put forward last evening. If any of those amendments were passed, they would have made the bill too restrictive.
If this law is passed, we are going to have a determination on it, I am sure, and this matter will not end here. But for those reasons, I feel that this is the best that we can do at the present time, in balancing the rights of the woman and the rights of the foetus. That is why I will be supporting this bill on third reading.

Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to what the member on the government side of the House had to say. I think that he has tried very hard to be sensitive to many of the issues that people in the House and people from coast to coast in this country are struggling with on the whole issue.
I did, though, wonder when he said that part of his rationale for supporting Bill C-43 would be that he felt that this bill would prohibit or stop the kinds of horrific spectacles we saw last summer when the most personal

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
and intimate details of the life of a young woman, Chantal Daigle, were displayed across the country.
The anti-choice people, the anti-choice zealots, have already indicated clearly that if Bill C-43 becomes law, they will take that law and use it as a new legal tool in order to harass doctors and women who are seeking abortions. They have made that very clear.
I want to ask the hon. member to reconsider the idea that Bill C-43 will stop that. It will not stop that. What has stopped those civil injunctions has been the Supreme Court of Canada. It has been very busily going about its work shutting down these legal avenues to estranged boyfriends and others who would use the legal avenues to harass women.
However, these same people have indicated that if this bill becomes law they will use it in order to harass women and doctors. I would like him to comment on that, please.

Mr. Speaker, I would submit that the harassment, if there is any, will not go on too long. I share her concern and I do not want to see that sort of thing start up again.
By the same token, society's interest in protecting the foetus has to be recognized, as well as the woman's right. It has to be done through the mechanism that is set out here, with a doctors' opinion which is arrived at using generally accepted standards of the medical profession. I am sure that no court is going to allow a frivolous application to come forward. You are going to have to deal with that particular matter. You are going to have to show that that has not been taken care of.
I see my friend shaking her head. We disagree on that particular point. It is set out and the definition is there and a frivolous matter, I know, will be quickly taken care of.

Mr. Speaker, as you know, last evening Parliament was called upon to decide on a series of amendment that were introduced. Each of the amendments were defeated and the bill itself was concurred in at report stage by a significant number of members of Parliament. I believe the number was 132. That would suggest that when the final vote is
called on Bill C-43, the legislation will, in fact, become law. I find that extremely regrettable.
When this bill was introduced into the House of Commons and debated at second reading stage, I voted for Bill C-43, not because I agreed with the bill. I indicated at the time that I had very serious reservations about Bill C-43, but I supported the bill at second reading simply to allow the bill to proceed to committee in order to enable members of Parliament, including myself, to present amendments in order to more accurately reflect my particular point of view with respect to this subject matter.
In their wisdom, the members of the legislative committee who considered Bill C-43, did not accept any amendments to the bill in the form that it was presented to them and given first reading on November 3, 1989.
In spite of the fact that the Prime Minister indicated to the House and to the country that it was a free vote, that members of Parliament in his caucus, the Conservative caucus, would be permitted to vote according to their own conscience, we know that in reality it was not a free vote. Members of Parliament were not free to vote according to their own conscience. In fact, the Prime Minister said that members of his cabinet were not free to vote, that they would all have to toe the party line and endorse Bill C-43. The message went out very clearly to the Conservative back-benchers that they should support Bill C-43.
At this point, I would like to salute those Conservative members of Parliament who broke with their party and rejected to date Bill C-43.1 have great respect for them, knowing the possible consequences that might follow as a result of them not supporting the Prime Minister and cabinet on this particular issue.
This bill will become law on Tbesday. As I indicated at second reading stage, and I have since indicated time and time again in speeches that I have given across the country, this bill is the most fraudulent and hypocritical piece of legislation that I have seen in the six years that I have been in Parliament.
Bill C-43 resulted from the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada over two years ago that declared Sections 287 and 288 of the Code unconstitutional.
May 24, 1990

For a long period of time the government dithered, delayed, procrastinated and hoped that somehow the issue would disappear. It waited for the Morgentaler follow-up decision on the Borowski case. It then wanted to test the will of Parliament by introducing a multiple choice type of resolution.
Then, finally, it introduced amendments to the Criminal Code in the form that we have before us, Bill C-43.1 submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the government would not have introduced Bill C-43 had it not been for the so-called pro-life members of the Conservative caucus who decided to compromise on the issue and support the bill.
I am convinced that, if those members of Parliament had stood by their views and stood by their convictions and insisted on a piece of legislation that would accurately reflect how they felt about the issue, then the government would not have introduced this bill. It would not have perpetrated a fraud on the people of Canada by suggesting somehow that this bill was a compromise, a common ground, a bill that would try to bridge the gap between those who believe there ought to be no law at all and those who believe there should be a law protecting life from the moment of conception onward.
The only redeeming aspect of Bill C-43 is that it is legislation that would amend the Criminal Code of Canada. In effect, it would reintroduce the subject of abortion back into the Criminal Code of Canada. That is the only redeeming aspect of it.
Members of Parliament will know that the only jurisdiction that Parliament has to deal with this issue is the Criminal Code of Canada. The only place that a law could be dealt with is within the criminal law jurisdiction. The health jurisdiction is within the powers of provincial governments. So, if the government wanted to deal with this issue, it had to deal with it in the Criminal Code of Canada.
Why is this bill hypocritical and fraudulent? Prima facie at the outset, this bill states that, because they are introduced into the Criminal Code of Canada, abortions are illegal and contrary to the Criminal Code. That is what it says at the outset. The government thought that those who believed that the innocent unborn must be protected from the moment of conception onward would be happy and rejoice and say: "Thank you, Prime
Government Orders
Minister. Thank you, Conservative government. You have recognized the sanctity of life."
The bill then defines the circumstances under which abortions could be obtained in such a broad fashion as to allow abortion on demand, abortion on request.
I would like to read the operative clause. It is a short bill, a page and half of text, two sections of the Criminal Code. The operative section would be 287(1) which states:
Every person who induces an abortion on a female person is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, unless the abortion is induced by or under the direction of a medical practitioner who is of the opinion that, if the abortion were not induced, the health or life of the female person would be likely to be threatened.
What does all that mean? First, it means that the abortion does not have to be done by a doctor, a medical practitioner. It simply states that in order to be legal, the abortion has to be done by a doctor or under the direction of a medical practitioner. In other words, as long as the medical practitioner or the doctor directs the person, a nurse, a clerk-anybody-can conduct an abortion. The doctor does not have to be present. The doctor could be elsewhere in the office, elsewhere in the city, or elsewhere in the country. All the doctor has to do is form the opinion-and I will get to how he forms that opinion in a moment-and that opinion could be formed as a result of a telephone conversation with the woman. Once that opinion is formed, the doctor could direct a nurse, a clerk, or anyone in the office, to perform that abortion.
How does the doctor arrive at the opinion that the abortion ought to take place? The doctor has to form the opinion that, if the abortion were not induced, the health or life of the female person would be likely to be threatened. The latter part of that is clear and straightforward, "the life of the female person would be likely be threatened". That is specific. Although it uses the word "likely", we are talking about the life of the female person.
But where the bill becomes totally broad and open is with respect to the word "health". Health is defined in the bill itself in subsection (ii) as including physical, mental and psychological health. In effect, under every circumstance, the doctor could form the opinion. There is no restriction. Mental, physical and psychological

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
health-that is the definition of health by which the doctor could form the opinion.
The likelihood of any doctor ever being prosecuted for an offence under Bill C-43 is extremely remote, to say the least. How could any doctor ever be successfully prosecuted? How could any prosecutor ever decide to prosecute under this particular section? It would be impossible and the government knew that. The bill is hypocritical in that it purports to be all things to all people.
Yesterday, I supported each of the amendments that were presented to the House that would make the bill a more restrictive bill. I regret that the motions did not cany, particularly Motion No. 10 which was introduced by my colleague and friend, the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. That particular motion would have allowed abortions only in the circumstance in which the life of the mother was threatened.
The amendments were all defeated. It is my intention to vote against the bill and to encourage and urge other members of Parliament to vote against the bill, because I believe it is a bad piece of legislation.
I believe it is bad, not only because of its nature, in that it tries to be all things to all people, but because it does not address the central issue which somehow politicians in this place are afraid to deal with and which the government was afraid to deal with, and that is the issue of when life begins.
The Supreme Court of Canada in the Morgentaler decision did not have the courage and backbone to render a decision in terms of when life begins. How can the issue of abortion be dealt with, and all the consequent considerations of the issue of abortion, without deciding first when life begins?
I put a question to a member of the New Democratic Party earlier today. I asked him when life begins, in his view, and he refused to answer. He made a joke about the issue. That is where the argument of the so-called pro-choice element of this debate completely collapses.
According to the pro-choice-those who would have no abortion law at all-the logic of their position is that life begins at birth. They are saying that they want no law at all, absolutely, under no circumstances. In effect, they are saying that life begins at birth.
That position cannot be reasonably argued because any reasonable person must conclude that there is life before birth. We know that as a scientific fact that there is life before birth. When that life begins is the question. Some might ask, who am I to try to decide when life begins?
We are all mere mortals. We are all mere human beings. We are called upon as parliamentarians and as legislators to make difficult decisions and to make tough decisions. Yet, the government and members on the government side and on this side of the House refuse to deal with the question of when life begins.
We all agree, or at least the overwhelming majority of members of the House agree, that life is sacred, that life is sacrosanct. I participated in the capital punishment debate a few short years ago. I listened to members of the New Democratic Party, members of the Conservative Party, and my colleagues in the Liberal Party. Notwithstanding the views of the overwhelming majority of Canadians, the House said no to capital punishment. The House, in a very significant vote, said that life is sacred, life must be protected, and life cannot be taken by the state under any circumstances, regardless of how criminal that life may be. It was the right decision. It was a day to be remembered in the House of Commons.
Those arguments somehow are lost when we are dealing with life before birth. They are equally as applicable. We heard the arguments about the sanctity of life and how life must be protected, and surely that must be extended to life before birth. Yet, the argument or the debate has not centered around the issue of life before birth and when it begins.
The position that I have taken, as a member of Parliament and as an individual, is that life begins at conception. To my mind, there is no other logical place where life begins. How can it be reasonably argued that in the nine-month span that life begins at some point other than conception? I state, and I have stated before, that in my view life cannot begin after birth, that there is life before birth. What argument, what medical-legal logic can be applied to determine when life begins before birth, other than at conception?
If one concludes that life begins before birth, at any point before birth, or that it begins at conception, surely that life must be afforded every protection that we have
May 24, 1990

as living, breathing, human beings. Who are we to distinguish between life?
As parliamentarians, we do not distinguish between a disabled person and an able-bodied person. We believe that all life is sacred after birth and must be protected. Who are we to say that that life before birth somehow is less deserving of the protection of law as life after birth? That is the central issue. It is not a question of choice and denying women the right to choose, or anything of the sort, in my view.
Yes, it is a difficult issue. No one likes to see the situations in which women find themselves with an unwanted pregnancy. We would all like to see that every pregnancy is a wanted pregnancy, but that is not reality.
Unless there is protection in law for life, from the moment of conception until natural death, I cannot support any legislation. I urge members of Parliament to defeat this bill and to encourage and force the government to bring in a more restrictive bill and allow the debate to carry on in a free and unfettered fashion in order to recognize the sanctity of life and the protection of the innocent unborn in our country.

Mr. Speaker, this is the third time that I have spoken on abortion during the debate on Bill C-43.
I am probably one of the more fortunate members of Parliament because, from my arrival in the House a couple of years ago, there has been no question in my mind as to how I would vote on this matter. I made it known publicly two years ago or more now that I am a pro-life member of Parliament and that I intend to stay. Because of that, I do not have to put myself through the mental turmoil that many members of Parliament have to in grappling with this issue. I am pro-life and that I will remain.
Bill C-43 is simply not a pro-life bill, not at all. It is a compromise piece of legislation which compromises human life and because of that I cannot support it.
The last time I spoke on this bill, in the fall of 1989,1 concluded by reiterating a conversation I had with my son. I want to continue with that conversation. My son Christian, who is eight years old, asked me one evening: "What is abortion?" To answer an eight year old child in a way which does not disturb the innocence of that child is very, very difficult. If all members of Parliament had to stand before a classroom of children, whether they be six year olds, seven year olds or ten year olds, and describe
Government Orders
to them what abortion is, the reality of what we are talking about would come home to them.
In the course of conversation with my son I attempted to explain to him what abortion actually is. In that process I was attempting to disguise my words. I was trying to protect the innocence of a child without distorting human values. Immediately that child begins to ask questions: "What is abortion, Dad? What happens to that baby inside the mother, Dad? Does the baby actually die, Dad?" That is what we are talking about. That is coming to grips with what abortion really is. It is not an easy subject to talk about with a child or in front of a group of children because that is exactly what it is, it is the destruction of human life.
As the member who spoke just previously mentioned, if you are pro-life, if you are for human beings, you have to act on the premise that life begins at conception. If we believe that life begins at conception, and if we believe that a human being exists at the moment of conception, we have to believe that when that life is destroyed a human being is actually killed. The reality of abortion is simply that. It is the taking of a human life.
Bill C-43 does not address that reality. Every member of Parliament can ask him or herself this simple question: If Bill C-43 becomes law, will we be preserving human life? In other words, will there be less abortions after Bill C-43 is enacted? The answer is simply that there will not be. It will not make one bit of difference. We will still have abortions in this country and they will still be legal. We will not have done what we have to do as parliamentarians-protect the life and innocence of those unborn. We will not have dealt with the reality of the situation and this is masking that reality. We have to honestly ask ourselves whether we are protecting the lives of the unborn with Bill C-43. Obviously we are not because, again, we are attempting to compromise human life.
It is not a question of being holier than thou because, I am just a human being. I am not a constitutional lawyer or a doctor, but I am a human being. Those are the kinds of people whom I represent. Certainly there are doctors in my riding. There are doctors in this House. There are lawyers in my riding. We can get into the nitty-gritty of when life begins. We can have doctors debating doctors as to when that magic moment of life actually begins. We can have constitutional lawyers arguing whether Bill C-43 is constitutional or whether a solidly pro-life bill would be constitutional. Some argue that it would be, some argue that it would not be. Others argue that if we are going to bring in a pro-life bill we would have to change the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, in other

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
words, change the Constitution so that it does protect the life of the unborn child.
Some lawyers argue that that would be an impossibility. Some parliamentarians argue it would be an impossibility to change the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in this country. Maybe it is an impossibility, but unless we strive for the ultimate, that is the protection of the human being, we have not fulfilled our roles as parliamentarians.
We are talking of the most defenceless of all human beings, the unborn child. That, in essence, is what this debate is all about, whether we as parliamentarians can come to grips with that reality. I say we are not doing that with Bill C-43. It is, in a sense, a classic Canadian compromise, but it is not doing what we set out to do as pro-lifers. It is not protecting the life of that unborn child.
From the first vote onwards I never supported Bill C-43. I attempted, through the amendment process, to make Bill C-43 a pro-life bill. That was not successful. We tried. I tried. Many of us have tried but we have not achieved that pro-life bill that we attempted to achieve since many days ago. We have failed.
With that, we are left with a bill that has not achieved the desired objective, that is to protect the life of the unborn. Because of that, I cannot support this bill. Again, I will only support abortion when the life of the mother is clearly endangered. I cannot support a bill that does not support the life of the unborn child. For that reason, I will not support Bill C-43. Human life cannot be compromised.

Madam Speaker, I would like to congratulate my colleague on a very passionate speech, with which I agree. I would like to get his reaction to something that I heard from one of the earlier speakers today who was also a strong pro-lifer. He said that with this bill we are making an incremental gain and therefore we should take this opportunity. He meant, I guess, that at some point down the road there would be some more gains made and eventually society
would look upon this in the way it should be looked upon, as taking a life.
Would my colleague like to comment on the thought that if we miss this opportunity to make Bill C-43 law, we will miss the opportunity for incremental gain toward reaching the long-range goal of having total and complete respect for life in all stages?

Madam Speaker, I think that we have already missed the opportunity to do what we should be doing. It is strictly hypothetical to look down the road to what might happen based on something which did not happen.
Again, this is the classic compromise. Maybe in some cases a compromise is good enough, but unless we strive for perfection, unless we strive for the ultimate, which is protection of the foetus, I think we have done ourselves an injustice.
I believe that the hon. member who posed this question believes the same thing. I think we will have done ourselves a disservice if we look down the road to what might have happened. The opportunity is now and we have to seize it now, not later.

Madam Speaker, many positions have been put forth in this debate on Bill C-43 showing the wide diversity of opinion that exists in Canada with regard to the matter of abortion and the degrees of respect for life. It is my privilege to join in this debate and to give a point of view which I believe is held by many Canadians.
Yesterday members of the House of Commons dealt with the amendments. I regret that some of the amendments that I thought were so vital and so important did not carry, in particular, Motion No. 10 which dealt with the life of the mother.
Let me make it clear from the outset that I have always had and continue to have the utmost respect for human life from conception to natural death. It is a matter of conscience that I must speak out in the strongest possible terms in favour of the preservation of the life of the unborn. One of the marks of a civilized society is the high regard in which it holds life and the

right to life of all humans, especially those unable to defend themselves.
The more society advances in its civilization, the more the various countries realize that too many lives are being wasted by the permissiveness that has allowed so many human unborn babies to be sacrificed. In Great Britain, the leaders are striving to chip away at the present laws to cut down on the number of abortions. The President of the United States and his predecessor both made it clear that laws must be changed to stop the great number of unborn children being killed.
A recent survey showed that almost two-thirds of Canadians are not even aware that one million abortions have been approved in Canada since 1969. Half of those surveyed did not know that medicare paid for most of those abortions. That same survey showed that a majority of Canadians believe that abortion should be illegal unless the mother's life is in danger. Surely we in Canada are civilized enough, Christian enough and caring enough to take measures to stop the slaughter of so many innocent victims. As a man of conscience I cannot and I will not accept any legislation that does not protect the sanctity of human life. I urge my colleagues to take the same stand.
We are told that abortion is a very complex matter. There are some who feel that it is not that complicated at all. For example, Mother Teresa sees it as a very simple matter. Abortion is the taking of a human life, and it is wrong. That is all. Of course saints are very uncomplicated people, which makes it so difficult for journalists to interview them. There is no way they can twist her words or the meaning she puts across. When they say that some women do not want their baby, she replies: "Give it to me. I want the child". We know she means exactly that because she has taken so many unwanted children.
I believe that abortion is the destruction of an innocent child. I frankly do not think that anyone, no matter on which side of the argument he or she may be, wants to see the destruction of an innocent child. That is why I call upon my fellow parliamentarians in this House to make sure that their decision regarding abortion is an informed one.
Government Orders
When does life begin? Does abortion really solve social problems, or does it create them? These are the questions I would like to help answer.
When the United States Senate conducted an extensive hearing on this subject in 1981, over 50 international authorities testified. The official report reads as follows: "Physicians and scientists agree that conception marks the beginning of the life of a human being-a being that is alive and is a member of the human species. There is overwhelming agreement on this point in countless medical and scientific writings."
It is clear then that it is not the time of birth that represents the creation of a new human being. Actual birth is only a change in the place of residence of the already living, active person.
Abortion is the violent killing of an unborn. Others have described it in various ways. I do not want to go into a description of the grisly details with regard to abortion, because others have. Suffice it to say that whether we refer to abortion as killing or as an induced death, it is largely a question of semantics. The effect on the child is the same: it dies.
Dr. Bernard Nathanson, who once was the director of the world's largest abortion clinic and is now a staunch pro-life supporter, has stated that there is seldom any purely medical indications for abortion.
We can go on to raise questions with regard to the safety of legal abortions. Very often we do not hear very much said about that. In a book written by David Reardon, he points out that of the 252 women surveyed, approximately half of them complained of suffering from at least one type of physical complication following abortion. The facts are clear that the so-called health problems during pregnancy are not a real factor. Rather, the true health problems exist after the abortion. The post-abortion syndrome is a very well-known phenomenon which is becoming more and more known as followup is being recorded.
This fact was made abundantly clear to the committee when Ms. Beverly Hadland, executive director of the Abortion Crisis Centre in Toronto, appeared and shared with the committee her considerable experience.
The natural order, regardless of one's religious belief, is a law which must be respected by all. A person of religious convictions has an even greater reason to

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
uphold the sanctity of human life. It is the law of God. These same principles have been enunciated over and over again by Pope John Paul II.
I want to conclude with a couple of other remarks about the role of society with regard to this matter because I believe there is a social issue that must be addressed.
We live in a society that is becoming more and more permissive, a laissez-faire society where moral values have been shoved aside. I believe that the school and the home have a very important role to play in the education of our children. Should a pregnancy occur, what then? Good counselling must be readily available. Too many of the so-called counselling centres only offer information on where to get an abortion. These pregnant women need love and understanding, comfort and care. The killing of a baby is not the answer.
Where needed, society should provide housing and day care assistance for these pregnant mothers so that they can make the choice of whether or not to have the child. At the time of the birth of the child the mother would decide whether to raise the child or to give it up for adoption.
Why is it that couples wishing to adopt a child have to wait years? There is a need to examine our adoption procedure with a view to speeding up the process.
I firmly believe that society as a whole has a role to play in providing more education, improved counselling, housing, and day care availability. I urge all Canadians to join together to resolve a social problem. I believe that as parliamentarians we have reached a point in time when we must make a choice and that choice is clear: whether we stand for life or stand by idly and surrender to a philosophy of death. I will be voting for life against the bill.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity at this late hour to be discussing Bill C-43, the abortion legislation, at third reading. I want the House to know that I also oppose Bill C-43 and will be voting against its passage at third reading, but perhaps not for the reasons that some of those who have just spoken have enunciated.
I believe that this bill goes some distance toward criminalizing abortion. As the member for Kitchener has outlined, it is part of a transition toward criminalization
of abortion in Canada and a reversal of the procedure that has been happening in this country over the past several years.
Part of the problem with this legislation is that it is going to create an untenable situation for doctors and an untenable situation for mothers who have made the decision to have an abortion, in that they will have both disgruntled boyfriends and so-called pro-life agencies looking over their shoulders and questioning in the courts and otherwise whether this was done for the reasons permitted under Bill C-43.
This is going to create an absolutely untenable situation for those women and those doctors, and it is going to make it more and more difficult for people who seek abortions for legitimate reasons to obtain abortions.
That is not to say that I have not listened carefully to the arguments that have been made by members on all sides of the House. I think members have made those arguments in good conscience and good faith. I do not think we should question the integrity, the agony, or the study that has gone into the speeches that have been made in this House. Members speak out of strongly held beliefs. There are some who believe that life begins at conception and therefore that the extension of the law of this land to the foetus while in its mother's womb is a legitimate extension of the laws of this Parliament.
I reject that position. I think it is going to create a very difficult situation with respect to the balancing of rights. I believe that extending the law of this country into the womb of a mother makes that women a second-class citizen and undermines the rights she enjoys as an individual who is due all of the rights of a Canadian citizen. It is going to create some serious difficulties by imposing the rights of two individuals on the body of a single person. Again, that is untenable for women and this would be a very difficult piece of legislation to implement and uphold. It is going to be very difficult.
The argument about when life begins seems like a very abstract argument, very distant from the situation of a woman who finds herself with an unwanted pregnancy agonizing over whether to give birth to another mouth to feed or to give the child up for adoption. Those are decisions which many of the people who are making that argument, and certainly myself, have never been compelled to make. It is very easy to be abstract, theoretical, dry, and scientific on this issue and to discuss it as if it is
May 24, 1990

nothing more than the usual dry debate we hear on legislation and scientific abstractions.
For many people faced with this decision, it is a very real and terrifying decision which the majority of us in this room are so remote from that we cannot possibly bring ourselves close enough to understand it, other than from an abstract point of view.
Over the years, having examined the subject and having had discussions with people who were presented with the decision of whether or not to abort, I have come to the conclusion that I support the pro-choice position. This piece of legislation is so antagonistic to that prochoice position that I am compelled to vote against it.
I have had some experience with the issue of abortion. I used to work in the criminal justice system of the province of British Columbia. I worked in the prison system at a time when abortion was illegal under the Criminal Code. Consequently, on those occasions when an abortionist was captured and ended up under my control in the prison system, I was introduced to the people who cany out this process under a criminalized regime, how they act, and what type of people they are.
They are not the type of people you would want yourself, Madam Speaker, your daughter, your granddaughter or your nieces ever to come in contact with. The abortionists whom I met are looking at this legislation and rubbing their hands in glee because they have reason to believe that their profession is now going back to what it was before and that it will be as lucrative as it was before, with very minimal risks involved, because people who go to such abortionist do not go to the newspapers and tell tales about them. The only times it comes to the attention of the media is when these people fail and mutilate or kill their clients. That happens time after time.
It is a very lucrative profession. Those people whom I kept in jail under the previous regime saw prison as a holiday before they went back to their work, which earned them a great deal of money with very little risk at all.
