I can see them now, rubbing their hands together, as the Parliament of Canada is talking about supporting life and arguing abstractly about when life begins. For these people this is when their business begins and then they
Government Orders
can get back to work in the back alleys of Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver and every city of any size in this country. This law is going to guarantee them customers.
I hear people talk about the concern they have for life, and I mentioned this in my previous speech on second reading. I recall reading a magazine about UNICEF, the United Nations Children's Emergency Fund, and the work that UNICEF does around the world. In our discussion we talked about the abstractness of when life begins, whether it begins at conception or at some other time, or at birth. There are children who are bom in this world who do not live, who starve to death. I am told by UNICEF about the number of children who die every single week in the world because they have inadequate food, or because they have inadequate protection from disease, or because they have inadequate sewage and clean water supplies, or inadequate shelter. That number of children is a quarter million a week. They die before the age of five years.
When we are talking about life, somebody in this debate has to give some consideration to the quarter million children who die around this world because we in this Parliament, by the way we handle our foreign aid, have made sure that many of those children will die before the age of five. Those children die of humiliating diseases, like dysentery, things that could be easily cured with a very small expenditure of money, money that we have cut back in our foreign aid program in this country.
I talk about a quarter million people around the globe dying before the age of five. According to UNICEF statistics, every two days more people around this world die before the age of five than abortions are done in Canada in a year.
Really we are not talking here about respect for human life, because if we were talking about respect for human life, at the top end of the priority list would be that quarter million children around the world who are dying, having been bom, and having lived to the age of five. Those children were the hopes of their parents, their aspirations for the future, children as loved as any other children in this country or anywhere else in the world. Yet they have to go through the agony of seeing

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
those children die of terrible diseases prior to the age of five.
Here we are talking about when life begins. Does it begin at conception? Does it begin at birth? A quarter million people will die before this week is out and this legislation is passed.
I do not believe that the pro-life movement has given itself a name that it is justified to have. It is a movement around the world that has been seeking to outlaw abortion, to outlaw access to abortion. It has been successful in a number of countries. It has been successful in Ireland for example, and in Ireland I am told that the rights of a foetus are enshrined in the constitution of that country. Ireland is the country my ancestors come from.
In Ireland the rights of a foetus are enshrined in the constitution of that country, yet it has been demonstrated in WHO statistics that Ireland has the highest per capita abortion rate of any developed country. Some are wealthy enough to be able to go to England to obtain an abortion, or to the continent of Europe. Those who are not wealthy enough either go to back-room abortionists or else attempt to perform the operation on themselves. But Ireland, where the foetus is protected in the constitution, has the highest per capita rate of abortion in the world.
I would like to quote statistics from Brazil because I just came back from there a few days ago. In Brazil abortion is also frowned upon by both the church and the state. I am told that in Brazil there are abortion clinics where one can obtain an abortion for something like $100 to $1,000. Most women in Brazil cannot afford to pay that kind of money for an abortion and so they perform abortions on themselves. As a result, an estimated three to five million clandestine abortions take place eveiy year in Brazil, a country with a total population of 145 million. This gives Brazil the leading share of the world's 65 million abortions, according to the World Health Organization. Research in Brazil estimates that 10,000 Brazilian women die each year from self-induced abortions. World-wide, 150,000 to 200,000 women die annually as a result of complications related to abortions.
Thirty to forty per cent of the half million pregnancy-related deaths that are estimated by the World Health Organization to take place each year, are the result of
botched, clandestine abortions. The statistics indicate that another 200,000 Brazilian women are put into hospital each year because they have been mutilated by or suffered complications from abortions.
What I am suggesting to members of the House of Commons is that we should clearly think about what we are doing here today. Why are we passing this legislation? What we are doing to doctors is making sure that the public and the anti-abortion activist groups can look over their shoulders to determine whether they are making the right medical decisions. I am not sure that that is the right thing to do.
What we are doing is making sure that disgruntled boyfriends, spouses or organizations that have taken it upon themselves to protect foetuses are going to examine every single abortion operation that takes place in this country and perhaps drag it into court in order to prevent abortion, disqualify doctors or make abortion much more difficult.
I am against the number of abortions that are taking place in this country. I think at roughly 65,000, the number of abortions in Canada is far too high. But I think there are ways of dealing with that problem without going through the process of criminalizing abortions. As I said before, you do not do away with abortions by criminalizing them, you simply create a lucrative industry for a criminal element in this country that mutilates your wives, your mothers, you daughters, your nieces and your granddaughters; you do not do away with abortion by this kind of legislation.
The way to do away with abortions or reduce the number of abortions is to make it possible for children in this country to be wanted children and to make it possible for children to get information about birth control and contraception so that they can understand the nature of their own sexuality and how to prevent pregnancy when, at a certain age, they begin to experiment with their own sexuality.
I recall a statistic from the American Medical Association. Doctors who were members of the AMA were saying that the highest number of cases coming before them were girls in the age range of 15 years whose first question they asked of their doctors was about pregnancy. The second question they asked was about acne. This is a serious problem when girls of that age do not even understand the basic elements of their sexuality and end
May 24, 1990

up in their doctors' offices wondering if they are pregnant or not.
Surely, this is a failure of our educational system. If this government wants to do something to stop unwanted pregnancies and therefore to stop abortions, what it should be doing is making the kind of education available to our young people and to adults that will assist them in understanding their sexuality, understanding the process of contraception and understanding what their options are.
The second thing the government should be doing is making it possible for families in this country to see all children as wanted children and having children as something exciting, expected and anticipated. I have two children, and my wife and I looked forward to having these children, to bring something into our lives which we did not have before. They were wanted children. There was no consideration on our part, ever, to see those pregnancies terminated because these were wanted and loved children, and they are to this very day.
Not all families look upon a new child that way. To some mothers a new child is an absolute terror. How is she going to feed this child? If she is married or partnered with a husband or boy-friend who is abusive, or is likely to sexually or physically assault this child, how can she feel good about bringing this child into the world?
There are 1.3 million Canadians in a country as rich as ours who live below the poverty line. How can families who find themselves living below the poverty line, through no fault of their own, have any hope and expectation? How can they want to bring a child into the world who is the result of an unwanted pregnancy?
What this government must do, and what this Parliament must do, is support families across this country, to make sure that children can be brought up in decent, happy and hopeful surroundings, free of poverty and abuse. That is the kind of thing that this government should commit itself to if it wants to reduce the number of abortions that are taking place in this country.
I think we can reduce the number of abortions in this country, but we cannot do it by recriminalizing abortion. The only way we can do it is by making it possible for
Government Orders
Canadian families and Canadian people to bring up their families in healthy, happy, hopeful surroundings, free of poverty and abuse.
The reason I am voting against this legislation is because it does not do that and it does not provide any hope for that to happen. I would like to see members of the House defeat this legislation and defeat it overwhelmingly.

Madam Speaker, the abortion issue has two views that divide our population into opposing communities of thought. Unlike most difficult issues, this one is characterized by the unique fact that neither side has much, if any, capacity to understand or appreciate the views of the other.
What makes a political resolution most difficult is the fact that the pro and anti-abortion persons both hold to their views for moral reasons in an environment charged with emotion, while asserting that their views are logical. Unfortunately, on this issue, I am no different than anyone else. With my vote I will make roughly one-half of my constituents happy, the other may feel somewhat abandoned.
At the outset, I want to indicate that I do not believe that the issue of criminalization of abortion lends itself to the kinds of compromises that would allow for overwhelming public support in light of the range of public attitudes that exist.
Just as importantly, I want to extend my regrets to those whose views are different from mine and at least to allow that while we differ in our understanding of a deeply moral issue, I do not conclude that these are amoral persons, but rather, individuals who have, for whatever reason, come to understand the question of abortion from another perspective.
If there is a correct view, and I believe there is, then its resolution will not be found in law at this time. Likewise, the passage of Bill C-43 will not conclude the national debate. Society will continue to change, and one day a law will likely exist that reflects a significant majority position. In the interim, it is incumbent on those to whom this issue matters most to do what they can to influence society.
My views are pro-life. Therefore, it is only natural that I would, in a perfect world, seek to restrict and limit abortion.

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
As an ethic, I believe that every human being is duty bound to uphold the sanctity of life. If life is to be precious then it must be precious in all stages. By contrast, if one stage of life can be deliberately diminished, can any other stage be reasonably assured?
At the root of this debate on abortion is the fundamental question of when does life begin. There are those who argue that an embryonic foetus is not yet human. I have asked such persons on frequent occasions: "Is it wrong to abort a nine-month old foetus just prior to natural partition?" The answer is a universal yes. Therefore, if it is wrong to abort a child just prior to birth, how can we back up through the gestational period, one second at a time, and find the moment when this developing person is not human?
Mr. Speaker, are not you and I persons who are still developing today? Is not aging a stage of development?
Some have argued that a foetus is not human until after the cerebral cortex is fully developed. They claim that this development is what distinguishes mankind from animals. However, if this to be an accepted standard, then what is to become of those persons who develop Alzheimer's disease?
Those who base their human evaluation of a foetus on the mere question of reasoning power also bring into question the value of those less privileged adult persons whose reasoning powers are, unfortunately, sub-standard. A caring and loving society embraces all persons, with all of their failings and at all stages.
With respect to human value, when any one person is allowed to be restricted from reaching their potential, we are all, in turn, diminished. Our challenge is to seek an ideal world and such a world is one in which each and every human has the opportunity to achieve fulfilment by maximizing their potential.
Now, we come to the matter of the bill that is before us. I believe the bill is an important improvement over the 1968 legislation.
First, it proclaims that abortion is wrong and can only be obtained with the support of a trained medical opinion. Moreover, the bill defines abortion to be wrong to the extent that a breach of condition is considered to be a criminal act and defined as such in the Criminal
Code. Finally, the notion of an arbitrary gestational time period in which abortions are allowed is abandoned in favour of a definition that proclaims it to be wrong to have an abortion at any time except for medical cause.
For all these reasons, I agree with the bill. My single concern is that the medical requirements for the protection of health are too loosely defined. There is a part of my analysis that encourages me to vote against the bill on principle. Abortions will still be allowed, and from my perspective that is wrong. Therefore, a negative vote might be justified.
The counter balancing analysis is, however, more compelling. We must recall the process by which we came to be in this situation.
In the summer of 1988, the Supreme Court ruled that Canada's existing abortion law was unconstitutional, largely because of unbalanced access in various regions of the country. In their judgment, the members of the court effectively ruled out the possibility of a new law that absolutely protected the foetus at all stages for all causes. At the same time, the court indicated that the Parliament of Canada had the right to limit, through law, the basis upon which an abortion could be obtained.
The House was given an opportunity to seek out, from a range of options, a perspective upon which the law could be designed and drafted. What proved to be the case was that there was no more consensus on this issue in the House of Commons than there was in the nation. The House was then faced with the dilemma of accepting a less than perfect law or living in a vacuum of no law.
I recognize that law alone cannot transform a human heart or soul. Law is an important ingredient in the process that involves other institutions and other persuasions.
What I have had to consider is, what kind of society would we have, what kind of protection would there be for the unborn, and what are the possibilities for improved legislation if this bill fails to pass? I am convinced that we need a law, even if the present Parliament cannot grant the law that meets my ideal.
The proposed law does underline the view that human life has unique value. It does make a wrongfully acquired abortion a criminal act. It does avoid an arbitrary
May 24, 1990

judgment about the value of a human being at various stages of gestation.
The single fact that a medical definition is, in my view, imprecise would be the wrong reason to allow society to live for an untold period of time without influence of law on this issue. If the bill were defeated, there would be an absence of a signal for the guidance of society. Moreover, an imperfect law can be built upon and changed over time. The absence of law could propel society into a set of attitudes from which we might never recover.
It is incumbent upon me to express my deep gratitude to the literally thousands of constituents of Crowfoot who have helped me comprehend and resolve my position on this issue. The issue is not concluded. The case is not resolved. However, Parliament and society must walk together for a while longer until a stronger consensus is acquired.
Finally, I want to say that it is not merely a question of abortion. It is also a question of our attitudes towards each other as human beings with respect to sexual relationships.
Sex is not a dirty or smutty issue, or a subject to be hidden from conversation. Rather, it is a matter upon which Canadians everywhere must become more comfortable. Sex education does not mean abandoning responsibilities to the school system and certainly it does not imply that the subject be dismissed in silence.
Too often, pre-school children are given a lesson in sex relations when what they wanted to know was, "Where did I come from?". Likewise, and unfortunately, frequently, teenagers are given lessons in biology when their curiosity is about interpersonal relationships. The matter of "how I am to behave with another" or "what am I to do about these powerful feelings that I have" cannot be answered by showing charts and graphs of the human reproductive system.
We must seek to achieve a society that embraces sexual respect. Sex must be thought of as an instrument of communication in relationships. Sex cannot be an object, exclusive and apart from all other obligations. As a society, we have to mature in the nature of our human relationships and, as a society, we have a long way to go.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Questions or comments? On debate, the hon. member for Wetaskiwin.
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, I too welcome the opportunity to express my concerns on Bill C-43.1 supported the bill on second reading so that we all could be afforded the benefit of a committee addressing this complex and highly controversial issue. That has of course occurred. Unfortunately, no amendments were recommended to support more fully my pro-life views. Consequently, I tried to move specific amendments. Again, unfortunately, all were ruled inadmissible. Last night's votes now leave me and all of my colleagues in a very serious and difficult predicament. As others have said this is a very personal and emotional issue.
To begin with, I would like to quote from Mr. Justice Bernier who, on July 26, 1989, in the unreported Daigle case stated:
The child conceived but not yet bom, whatever the definition of his civil status, is a reality which we must acknowledge. He is not an inanimate object, he is the property of no one, he is a living human entity, different from the one of his or her mother who carries him; he is an entity who exists because of two human beings who gave him life, who procreated him; he, to begin with, has a right to life and to protection from those who conceived him or her.
I concur with Mr. Justice Bernier. I too believe we must acknowledge the child conceived but not yet bom. This was the major reason for my moving amendments: to protect specifically the unborn child and to define what in law is a foetus.
The Supreme Court of Canada has clearly requested of Parliament to state its intentions. In the Morgentaler case the justices unanimously were of the opinion that the protection of the foetus was a worthy legislative intent. I believe that the majority of this House would agree as well that the protection of the foetus is a worthy legislative intent. Many of my constituents have clearly indicated that the foetus must be protected. This protection is a duty of the state; just as it appropriately is the duty of the state to protect others who are unable to protect themselves, such as perhaps the mentally ill. However, its intent must be clearly stated. As the Supreme Court of Canada in the Daigle case stated:
One can ask why the Quebec legislation if it had intended to accord a foetus the right to life, would have left the protection of this right in such an uncertain state.
One can ask the same question of Parliament.
The other side of the issue, the rights of women to the security of the person, guaranteed under Section 7 of the charter, cannot be ignored either. We as parliamentari-

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
ans must pay heed to the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada.
The intentions of government which guided this new legislation as stated earlier are: first, balancing the woman's constitutional rights with society's interest in the foetus; second, ensuring that fair and reasonable access to abortion is not denied; and, third, ensuring that all abortions are performed by qualified medical practitioners based on a health ground.
The first of these intentions, balancing the woman's constitutional rights with society's interest in the foetus, is one aspect of the present bill that is lacking.
Some have argued that to amend Bill C-43 in any way renders it unconstitutional. I am of the view that the Supreme Court of Canada would not ask Parliament to legislate for the unborn specifically if only to strike it down as unconstitutional.
Mr. Chief Justice Dickson in the Morgentaler case stated:
I agree that protection of foetal interests by Parliament is also a
valid governmental objective.
He adds later on page 75:
-state protection of foetal interests may well be deserving of
constitutional recognition under section 1.
Madam Justice Wilson also stated:
I believe that the main objective advanced to justify a restriction
on the pregnant woman's section 7 right is the protection of the
foetus. I think this is a perfectly valid legislative objective.
Others argue, and it may be true, that the criminal sanction does provide for some protection for the unborn by implication. But, this is not adequate. It is inadequate by virtue of the fact that abortions may be performed for any reason falling under mental, physical or psychological domain. An abortion may be performed by virtue of any of those reasons, which is an exhaustive list, a woman may desire to have an abortion, including as a method of birth control.
It is the latter with which I am not at all in agreement. This has not balanced any societal interest in the foetus, no legal personality has been given to the foetus, nor have any rights been confirmed upon the foetus. But most importantly no specific intention has been made by Parliament to protect the foetus.
Such an intention must be clear and unequivocal in the eyes of the court. To this end, last night I expressed my support for several amendments of this bill which I felt would have accomplished that. If the pro-life amendments had passed, I would have no doubt been able to support the bill at third reading. Only then would we have shown an intention to confer rights on the unborn, a measure which is clearly appropriate for Parliament to take, as stated by the Supreme Court of Canada Justices. In my view it is also the duty of Parliament to protect those who are unable to protect themselves.
The question now becomes, because there have not been any pro-life amendments passed, based on my conscience, am I prepared to support the bill at third reading. Madam Speaker, I do not think one can compromise with life and therefore I will not be supporting BUI C-43.

Mr. Speaker, I once again rise to speak during third reading of Bill C-43, an act respecting abortion. I voted for this bill on second reading in the belief and optimism that the government would welcome amendments to clarify and strengthen the intent of the bill.
I must now speak against this bill because, despite the sincere efforts of a good number of my hon. colleagues in proposing amendments to make the bill a viable and meaningful one, to be truly an instrument of protection for the unborn, the government for the most part refused to allow the necessary changes. Therefore, the bill remains unacceptable. It neither promotes, protects, nor preserves fundamental Canadian values such as respect for human life, particularly the lives of unborn children who will be the women and men of the future.
It does not defend the most vulnerable and defenceless. Let us remind ourselves that unborn children can only articulate their aspirations through our own feelings, love, sacrifices and compassion.
Also, the bill does not address the rightful concerns and needs of women. It does not provide for a balance of rights, not even a compromise. Rather it is a capitulation of both the unborn's and the woman's rights.
On January 28, 1988, the Supreme Court of Canada declared Canada's abortion law unconstitutional on procedural grounds and not, I repeat, not on the basis that abortion is a constitutional right. In fact, the
May 24, 1990

Supreme Court clearly indicated the state has a legitimate interest to protect the foetus, the unborn child.
Also, the Chairman of the Civil Liberties section of the British Columbia branch of the Canadian Bar Association has noted:
Careful review of the decision reveals that far from vesting an untrammelled right to abortion, the court has left Parliament leeway to change the law in ways that are significantly more favourable to the preservation of foetal life than the law which the court struck down.
Regrettably, the bill now before us is more permissive than the law which was struck down.
Indeed, there is no constitutional right to abortion. The Charter of Rights and Freedoms specifically mentions voting, religion, language and minority rights. It does not contain anything about the right to abortion. I will therefore never fathom, and I am confident all Canadians are with me on this sentiment, that the infliction of death on innocent human lives in the wombs of their mothers would ever be a legitimate exercise of anyone's right unless there is a compelling, serious and substantive medical reason or reasons for that given pregnancy that imminently threatens the life and health of the pregnant mother and for which medical condition no alternative treatment exists.
As Mr. Justice William McIntyre pointed out when the Supreme Court of Canada rendered the old law ineffective, there has always been a clear recognition of a public interest in the protection of the unborn. There has been no evidence of any general acceptance of the concept of abortion at will in our society. In fact, public opinion polls have consistently indicated that roughly 70 per cent of Canadians oppose elective abortion, suggesting that some type of genuine medical threat ought to exist before abortion is allowed.
Admittedly, some of the defeated amendments would probably be violations of security of the person under Section 7 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, but this would not have rendered such amendments unconstitutional. Chief Justice Dickson explained this in the Morgentaler case:
I wish to reiterate that finding a violation of security of the person does not end the inquiry on Section 7 of the Charter. Parliament could choose to infringe security of the person if it did so in a manner consistent with the principles of fundamental justice.
Government Orders
Indeed, the protection of the foetus is a concern that outweighs the woman's right not to carry the foetus to term, unless genuine medical threats exist.
We must protect the most defenceless of us if we are to maintain a strong foundation to protect the rights of all of us.
During its appearance before the legislative committee that examined this bill, the family and friends of the handicapped made the following observation:
Bill C-43 represents an attack upon the efforts of the disabled to obtain equality in society and win the dignity and respect to which they are entitled. The Bill would allow for abortion for the widest possible reasons. It would enshrine in law a principle that the lives of some may be destroyed for the convenience of others.
It continued:
It is true that the Bill does not make any explicit reference to handicapped children. However, it does allow abortion where psychological health is threatened. The Law Reform Commission Report of last year made clear that such a clause can be used to authorize aborting disabled children.
This is a major flaw in the bill. We have to recognize that the unborn are human beings. For centuries the English common law of property has recognized unborn children as autonomous human beings and their property rights have been protected by law. In 1795, an English court interpreted the meaning of "children" in a last will and testament to include a child "in the womb" of their mothers.
Under tort law, learned authorities have maintained "that the unborn child in the path of an automobile is as much a person in the street as the mother". How then can we as Canadians and parliamentarians accept that such an unborn child becomes less a person when instead of an automobile, a physicians's forceps, suction machine, a salt or hormonal solution is used to cause that unborn child's death?
The proclamation by the Supreme Court of Canada that the state has a legislative interest to protect the foetus is a tacit admission that once human life has commenced in the womb of the mother the state not only has the right but the duty of safeguarding that unborn human life, and through this protection, protects and preserves society itself.
What do we have in this bill? Health is defined as including:

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
For greater certainty, physical, mental and psychological, health. In common language this in effect is abortion on choice.
Why? When the Canadian Medical Association appeared before the legislative committee, it said:
It is recognized that 85 per cent to 95 per cent of induced abortions are done for psychiatric reasons, but there are very few absolute psychiatric reasons that are a threat to life-
The Canadian Physicians for Life, also appearing before the committee, confirmed that 96 per cent of abortions are performed for non-medical reasons.
The National Action Committee on the Status of Women also testified before the legislative committee:
Women have abortions for many reasons. Most of them are social and economic in origin.
Indeed, the loose definition for health would make this bill a legal prescription for abortion on demand.
In introducing this legislation, the Minister of Justice stated:
This bill has been carefully drafted to achieve a delicate balance between the conflicting views on the abortion issue.
The minister is only partly correct. In defending the government's approach to rejecting all amendments the same minister said:
Any amendment to the bill could be perceived as unfairly favouring the state's interest in protecting the foetus to the detriment of the woman's constitutional right to security of the person could endanger the legislation's constitutional validity.
Only the Supreme Court of Canada can make a definitive determination of the constitutional validity of any law passed by Parliament. Both the Minister of Justice and the Law Reform Commission agreed to this view during their appearances before the legislative committee. Hence, the government should have allowed amendments to clarify and insist that only genuine medical threats to the life and health of the pregnant woman could constitute valid indication for abortion. That I attempted to do. Unfortunately, my amendments were defeated. This government chose not to make that choice.
Many submissions to the legislative committee supported the necessity for many amendments.
Indeed, this bill, unamended, is tantamount to abortion on demand, which is a perversion of the purposes of both law and medicine. Law in a civilized country is meant to preserve justice and to protect the weak from abuses by the strong. Medicine is meant to protect life. When legislation permits abortion on demand, it violates both.
Modem science and medicine are much too far advanced to permit the fiction that the being which inhabits a pregnant woman's womb is not a human being. From the moment of conception the foetus has all the necessary genetic material which makes it a distinctive individual, coded into its own DNA which is different from anyone else's, and unmistakably human. While still in the womb, the foetus is a doctor's patient, just like its mother, and with science at its present stages, can be operated on and treated while still in the womb. That is why we have departments of obstetrics in schools of medicine and in hospitals. That is why the discipline of perinatology has evolved in medicine. Any argument which does not recognize the human nature of the foetus is becoming every day more patently untenable.
Like any individual living outside the womb, the foetus must be granted the same rights to life and liberty as any other human life. In any society which strives to maintain liberty, limits must be drawn. No liberty is absolute in this world; instead, each person's liberty is limited by the liberty of others. It is largely unquestioned that the law is right to lock up thieves and murderers, to breach the security of their persons, to deprive them of their personal liberty of movement because it has been used to violate the liberty of other individuals in the society.
In the same way, the foetus' right to the most basic liberty, the liberty to live, should not be overruled by the mother's right to choose in the absence of genuine medical threats. Abortion on demand violates this basic principle. It claims the woman's liberty to be limitless vis-a-vis the liberty of her unborn child. The liberty of the foetus to live and exercise further liberty must be protected only if the mother so wishes. This in effect is a denial of the individual humanity of the foetus because it is a denial of the rights which belong to human beings by virtue of their humanity. Any denial of the humanity of the foetus is simply untenable.
May 24, 1990

The problems to which abortion seems to be the solution must be addressed. Although some women use abortion simply as a matter of birth control, a tragedy which must be stopped as soon as possible for we cannot as a compassionate and caring society continue to condone some 70,000 deaths of unborn babies every year, there are many who would appeal to such an answer only in the case of severe problems. A simple prohibition of abortion is not a sufficient or compassionate answer either.
The most clear-cut of these problems occurs when the mother's life is physically threatened by her pregnancy. In such extraordinary circumstances, the same exception which is made for self-defence in other circumstances can be applied. The chances of death of the mother must be weighed against a genuine concern for the foetus as a human being in its own right. Once the medical profession is convinced that the risks to the mother's life are great enough to warrant the use of abortion to save her life, then in such circumstances the mother should be persuaded to agree to the medical procedure.
Such cases, however, occur comparatively rarely in the context of the many abortions which are performed. Other cases involve a wide range of less clear-cut considerations. Among these are societal problems which have both economic and psychological ramifications for a prospective mother.
More provisions to deal with these problems must be made, such as homes for single mothers during pregnancy, financial assistance, child care centres, educational programs, and other services as may be helpful. Governments are duty bound to provide them to solve the causes of why some pregnant women consider abortion.
Most important, perhaps, better counselling must be provided so that individuals are truly able to decide what to do both in order to avoid unplanned pregnancies and in order to deal with them without sacrificing the child. Many women who choose to undergo abortions have not been acquainted with the other options including adoption, nor with the devastating physical and psychological trauma on them of having an abortion. These were startling revelations made before the legislative committee that examined this bill.
Government Orders
A law restricting abortion only to medical indications is not punitive to women. It is in a very real sense a guide or a legal tool to protect their interests during their hours of need. Both child and parents have needs and both must be addressed, neither one being sacrificed to the other. Abortion on demand effectively addresses neither in that it fails to deal with the root problems, making a pregnant woman opt for abortion and may cause further damage to her at the same time as her child is killed.
Some of my colleagues in this House have argued against placing the subject of abortion in the Criminal Code of Canada. In reply, I would like to quote from a legal scholar, Mr. Joseph Maingot of the Law Reform Commission of Canada, who said:
The criminal law can make a significant contribution by addressing the issue of abortion. Criminal prohibitions on abortions are desirable for both functional and symbolic reasons. Functional, because criminal prohibitions will reduce, although not eliminate, abortions. Since foetal life deserves legal protection, it follows that a reduction in abortions is a net social benefit. The symbolic function of the criminal law is our nation's fundamental statement of public policy. It is the instrument by which the community draws a line between the tolerable and the intolerable. Criminal law defines those whose interests are worthy of respect and protection and in my view, they should include all members of the human family. Ultimately, the criminal law is a mirror of what we are; it reflects our commitment, or lack of commitment, to human dignity and equality.
That is why we have laws directed at degrading pornography, against hate, against child abuse, and laws on affirmative action programs. The state has a key role to play in the development of a collective conscience to sustain social peace and respect for citizens of different viewpoints. Any law shapes and reflects the collective conscience of any society. We should have laws that will continue to preserve, promote, and protect Canadian values.
In conclusion, Bill C-43 could make legitimate, even noble, the performance of abortion outside the tradition of medical practice. I deeply believe that we need to rethink Canadian values as I stated at the beginning of my debate. We must protect the most vulnerable and defenceless in our society, epitomized by the unborn children whose aspirations for life can only be realized when we adults in Parliament, men and women alike, sensitively reflect their aspirations by passage of a law that truly protects the lives of the unborn in the wombs

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
of their mothers. Let us say yes to life at all times and no to abortion on simple choice.

Madam Speaker, I want to make it very clear that I totally disagree with the orientation of the previous member. I think that a woman has every right to reproductive choice.
I want to ask him a couple of questions of a little more technical nature, since he takes the stand that a woman has no right to reproductive choice. Would he comment, first of all, on whether he opposes the use of IUDs or the morning-after pill, both of which are a form of medical treatment that allows a woman not to carry through a pregnancy after fertilization takes place?
If he feels that a woman has no choice in reproductive matters, does he support her right to birth control, to use both chemical and mechanical forms of birth control, or does he feel that a woman is in a position where the only time she is permitted to be involved in intercourse is when conception is to take place?
I think that those are the logical extensions of what the member is saying, that a woman has no choice in terms of her reproductive capacity.

Madam Speaker, it is a fundamental principle in cross-examination even in a court of law that you do not answer your own question because you are likely to be wrong in the answers you will give yourself. That is exactly what happened. The hon. member asked a question. He assumed I had answered it, but completely wrong.
As to the question of whether I believe in reproductive choice, I do not even know whether we agree on the definition of reproductive choice and what is reproduction.
Reproduction is when you begin from nowhere, from nothing. Once you have that something, you have reproduced a product, and that is what I call reproduction. If what he believes I am asking, and it is a big if, is that after a product has been produced you can destroy this product, human life, then of course my answer definitely is no. Whether a woman should marry and reproduce, that is her ultimate and paramount right. Whether a woman should have birth control or not, that also is her right.
Once a human life has been created, created by the Supreme Being, that human life must be protected. Let me remind my hon. colleague that even the Charter of Rights and Freedoms of the Canadian Constitution, invokes in its preamble the supremacy of God and the rule of law. Invoking the supremacy of God indicates that no more shall we have a law which violates the principle of God. Incidentally, I once heard the same sentiments from the lips of a justice of the Supreme Court of Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have heard the hon. member for Surrey North. Somebody else is rising in the House whom I will recognize and then come back to the hon. member. The hon. member for Dartmouth.

Madam Speaker, I listened to my hon. colleague from Winnipeg North espouse his convictions and views on this very delicate, contentious and difficult matter. There were a few things said on which I would like clarification.
Quotations were made from submissions to the committee of which he was a member, and I assume that he was there for most or nearly all of the presentations. The statistics quoted by the hon. member for Winnipeg North indicate that the vast majority of abortions that are obtained are for social and economic reasons.
Is it the hon. member's belief that if this bill is passed as is, without the accompanying regulations or companion legislation, it would clearly indicate that the government through its agencies and departments is prepared to address those social and economic reasons that many women have to go and seek abortions?
Is it his belief that this bill will lessen the likelihood of this government, or a subsequent government, revisiting the issue and putting in place those very programs which would be necessary so that women who find themselves pregnant do not have to seek abortions for social and economic reasons? Our social programs would be expanded and targeted so that would no longer be the case.

Madam Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague for his thoughtful questions. Yes, indeed, I was with the legislative committee for most of the time, and yes indeed the vast majority of the bases for abortion as indicated by the Canadian Medical Association and the Canadian Physicians for Life have been the result of social and economic difficulties. It is my belief, which is shared by many Canadians, that if we allow this bill to pass as is, unamended, the words "psychological health" could be used-and the Minister of Justice has indicated
May 24, 1990

that-to include social and economic difficulties as a consequence of poverty.
Could a government of the day be complacent and not address real issues of poverty, real need for assistance for the needy? Yes, I believe that that is a real possibility; in fact I would submit a real probability. That is why I am very concerned that the bill, unamended, is unacceptable both to me and my constituents of Winnipeg North.
Jim Karpoff (Surrey North): Madam Speaker, I asked the member whether he agreed that a woman had the right to use two forms of birth control, IUD and the morning-after pill. He neglected or refused to answer them.
I ask him again: Does he believe that the woman has the right to use an IUD and the morning-after pill?
Madam Speaker, my answer is that I do not believe in the morning-after pill. In terms of the IUD, I think there are better forms of birth control than that. That is fraught with dangers.

Madam Speaker, I know that by now everyone in this House knows my intense and deeply felt opposition to this legislation, Bill C-43. My party position has been brought to question in this House of Commons. The position of the New Democratic Party seems to be thought of as extremist by some members here, trying to rationalize their illogical support for this bill.
I stand for family planning education. I stand for research into safe and effective contraception. I stand for support for pregnant women and for families. This is a social policy approach to the abortion issue, rather than an ineffective criminal law approach.
Some people then may find family planning to be an extreme position. Some people seem to find support for families extremist. Some people seem to find equality for women, the need to be able to make decisions about our own bodies and our own lives extremist.
Government Orders
No one wants to face an unwanted pregnancy. The solution is to eliminate or at least reduce the number of unwanted pregnancies, not to criminalize abortion.
It is a national tragedy that support and equality for women are considered to be extremist views in this country, and seen in the same light as wishing to give a zygote full legal and social rights as a human being. It is an appalling contradiction.
In British Columbia and in Ontario women entering clinics are harassed and intimidated. The Everywoman's Health Centre in Vancouver was broken into and the medical equipment there worth thousands of thousands of dollars was vandalized and destroyed.
Some of my colleagues and I have received threats of physical violence from an organization. This is what is really extreme, not views that support women, children and the family. Equality for women, the right to decide our own fate, is not extremist.
When members here talk about a balance of rights, they should consider what we are really talking about. The Tories are being pressured by cabinet to vote for this criminal bill, something which was so evident last night.
Pro-choice Tories are told this bill will have absolutely no negative effects on women. Anti-choice Tories are told that it may not be everything they want, but that it does encompass the principles that they stand for-criminalization from conception onwards.
To believe that the bill will have absolutely no negative effect on women is to ignore Canada's top legal experts, Canada's medical authorities and the majority of the women in this nation from coast to coast who know this first-hand. It is to ignore what they are saying.
If this bill is to have no effect and there will be no prosecutions, as the Minister of Justice would have us believe, then it is an improper use of the Criminal Code. If it will have an effect and charges will be laid, as under every other criminal abortion law we have had in Canada, then the effect on the women and the doctors will be profound.
Not only is Bill C-43 a bad law because it is a lie, it is simply a bad piece of legislation according to a majority of respected legal experts in this country. Of 18 constitutional lawyers at the most respected law schools in this

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
country, 17 of them seriously challenged the validity of the justice minister's legal arguments in support of Bill C-43. They have called it "legal nonsense".
Professor Ryder from Osgoode Hall law school states:
-it creates no entitlement whatsoever; -Bill C-43 will do nothing to remove the provinces' ability to place restrictions on funding and access to abortion.
The purpose of criminal law is to punish, deter and stigmatize conduct that is inimical to the public interest. Criminal law takes the form of a prohibition coupled with a penalty. Given these characteristics of criminal provisions, it is an oxymoron to speak of a criminal law entitlement. Indeed, recriminalizing abortion will place the procedure once again under a shroud of immorality, and consequently will deter women from seeking access and will deter doctors, hospitals and governments from providing services. This suggests that the true basis of Bill C-43 is the government's accordance of a moral status to the foetus that transcends and is independent of women's priorities and aspirations.
He goes on to state:
The Justice Minister has claimed that "by occupying the field" of abortion regulation with Bill C-43, the doctrine of federal paramountcy will prevent the provinces from further restricting access. With all due respect, the Justice Minister is relying on a long abandoned conception of federal paramountcy.
Two University of Victoria law professors say that the minister's legal arguments are: "untenable" and "simply wrong". They say the bill does not create entitlement. They say she "does not provide a convincing rationale for the enactment of a federal abortion law".
Two University of Ottawa professors concur that the minister's arguments are "totally without merit from a constitutional point of view". They say it does not create any sort of national standard for abortion.
They wrote:
It is clear that the federal government has several statutory mechanisms available to regulate abortion standards at a national level. There is therefore no factual basis for the claim that a Criminal Code provision is necessary to create a national standard for entitlement to abortion services.
They go on to state:
The absence of federal criminal legislation in relation to abortion does not in any way modify or expand the provinces' legislative authority over abortion.
Bill C-43 will have a detrimental effect on access. Doctors and women told the legislative committee this over and over again.
Doctors who came to us from the Province of Quebec said that up to one-third of the doctors in that province who are currently performing abortions will stop if this bill becomes law.
There is only one doctor in all of Newfoundland who performs abortions.
I think it is important that we look at what the situation is like in this country right now, today, with no law.
This doctor is based at the St. John's General Hospital in Newfoundland. The General's policy is to provide only early abortions and to require approval by a gynaecologist, a psychiatrist, a social worker and counselling by a registered nurse. These access barriers are in no way contradicted by Bill C-43.
In fact Bill C-43 encourages these types of referrals because of its health criteria.
Bill C-43 does not provide any kind of national standard. The St. John's General will continue to have these built-in delays and referrals, while the Morgental-er Clinic in Montreal will continue to place no barriers before women to abortion. Thus there is no national standard.
No hospital in Prince Edward Island will perform abortions today. In P.E.I. the province will not pay for an out-of-province abortion unless a five-doctor panel approves the woman's reasons for having one. Few applications are approved and costly travel expenses are never reimbursed.
Bill C-43 will not change things for the women of Prince Edward Island. Criminal law does not change stringent and restrictive provincial health practices.
In Nova Scotia, a law was passed to outlaw health clinics that provide abortion services. C-43 will not outlaw this Nova Scotian law. In fact, doctors who provide the only legal abortions in Nova Scotia at the Victoria General Hospital have said that if this bill passes, they will cease to do so. We have that from the hon. member for Halifax. She released a letter from a doctor there who has said that. This would leave no access in Nova Scotia at all, directly because of Bill C-43.
May 24, 1990

New Brunswick requires the approval of two doctors before it will pay for an abortion. Bill C-43 does not touch this requirement in any way.
Under Bill C-43, if a province wanted a 25-doctor panel to approve an abortion, it would still be legal and perfectly valid under this bill.
Bill C-43 has no effect on provincial health regulations, other than to make them more stringent in order to comply with the health requirements of Bill C-43.
In my province of British Columbia, the right-wing Social Credit government tried to withdraw funding for abortions. It did withdraw funding for abortions for a time after the Morgentaler decision came down, and then was made to stop that by the courts. That province is spending $20 million to try to discourage abortions.
Bill C-43 will have no effect on this other than to encourage the abuse of the law in provinces where the anti-choice movement or the government in that province is strong and rather bizarre, as in my home province of British Columbia.
Anti-choice zealots have chained themselves to clinics. They have defied injunctions. They have risked jail. They have been in jail. They have been fined. They have risked injury. These are the very people who will be using Bill C-43 against women and against doctors.
I am not making this up. We have press reports which state that the anti-choice people themselves have indicated that when this bill is passed they will use it as another legal tool to harass women and doctors. They have made promises to do that.
I have to say that as a woman I really did feel betrayed last night when my amendment, the only pro-choice amendment proposed to this bill, was defeated by such a wide margin. It was defeated by more votes than the regressive anti-women, anti-choice amendments were defeated.
Some women have believed that simply by voting for women candidates their views will be represented in this House of Commons. The votes last night on the amendments to the abortion bill proved that that theory is sadly mistaken.
Government Orders
I believe that the Tory women on the other side of the House really sold out the women of Canada, along with the government. Not one woman on that side of that House supported the only pro-choice amendment.
I do want to thank the members in this House who did support the amendment for women's rights to decide for ourselves just how many children we will have and when we will have them.
Every member of my caucus, man and woman, who was here voted for the pro-choice amendment. Five Liberals out of a caucus of 84 voted for the pro-choice amendment. Only two Tory members in this House of Commons voted in favour of choice. This government has a huge majority in this House of Commons and yet only two members on that side of the House voted in favour of the only pro-choice amendment. Those two were men. Not one Tory woman stood up for choice.
The commitment of these individual Liberal and Tory women for choice who did support my amendment is strong. Unfortunately, those Liberals are a minority in their caucus and the Tories were facing incredible pressure to vote against choice.
When Canadians are at the ballot box they will know that if they want to vote for choice, if they really want to vote for the fundamental equality issue for women, then they must vote for the New Democratic Party.
This bill does not define entitlement. It is a bill of disentitlement.
It states that women are not entitled to abortions unless they meet criteria unrelated to their own goals and aspirations and unless they meet the criteria set out by the state. This is supposed to be a government that is opposed to state intervention. This is a government which keeps telling us over and over again that it does not believe in state intervention in the marketplace, in rent controls and all those kinds of social programs that my party says the state belongs in. Yet this government wants to be involved in and have state control over the most intimate, personal, and agonizing decision that a woman is ever forced to make. It is absolutely bizarre.
The justice minister said today that "criminalization" is an emotional word and that it was misleading. It is an emotional word and it brings out strong emotions. Unfortunately, it is deadly accurate in this case.

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
This bill makes abortion a crime. You bet it is an emotional word to those doctors who will now have the possibility of criminal charges hanging over their heads. You bet it is an emotional word to a physician like Dr. Henry Morgentaler who spent time in jail, who was convicted under the last criminal abortion law. It is certainly an emotional word to the millions of Canadian women who thought that, finally, after the Supreme Court threw out the last criminal law on abortion, they would no longer be criminals for deciding the number and spacing of their children, that they were now free to choose what to do and what decisions to make about their own reproductive health and about their own lives.
We have seen demonstrations right across this country because the recriminalization of abortion is an emotional time in our history. It seems as though we are going back to the 19th century.
It is a sad time in our history. It is a time when we are turning our backs on women and children. We are ignoring family planning by cutting down on the social support network that makes it easier for women to bring children into this world. This a time when we have taken the regressive step of putting abortion back into the Criminal Code, instead of the progressive step of making this a society in which women feel that they can bring children into a society in which women have real choices.
Other people have said that this criminal bill is a matter of values. I agree. I think that recriminalizing abortion says a great deal about what we really think about women.
This bill needs to be defeated on principle and because of the real effect it will have. The minister has said many times that society has an interest in protecting the foetus. Instead of criminalizing abortion, which is an ineffective way of protecting the foetus, why is the government not concerned about reproductive health hazards in the workplace? Why is this government not concerned about the environment and poverty? These are the real threats to the foetus.
In poor parts of Montreal the incidence of low birth weight babies is comparable to that of the Third World because their mothers were malnourished during their pregnancy. It is appalling. The minister can best advocate the protection of the foetus and of women's health through social policy measures, not a criminal act that
will jail doctors for up to two years and make women liable to aiding and abetting sections of the Criminal Code.
There was a time not long ago that the minister was advocating women's rights rather than foetal rights.
I want to quote from an editorial which appeared in The Vancouver Sun of February 11, 1988. This goes back to just after the Morgentaler decision was handed down in the Supreme Court. Before the minister came out against her former leader, Premier Bill Vander Zalm, The Vancouver Sun wrote:
It was quite a sight, a sight I will never forget, to see Cabinet aspirant Kim Campbell do a crab-like scuttle from the television reporter who asked her if her opinion on abortion coincided with the Premier's. Regardless of her views on abortion, Ms. Campbell is too smart to elucidate them. A woman tangibly eager for power, ambition cloaks her like a mantle. Ms. Campbell will keep her trap shut.
The current Minister of Justice read that. It must have had an impact on her because she then called The Vancouver Sun columnist Nicole Parton and, with courage, she put her career on the line to stand up for what she believed in.
She told Parton that the Socred caucus was unwilling to break ranks with Vander Zalm because of caucus solidarity and that it was essential to the government, but that she was now willing to break that caucus solidarity.
She is in the same position now, except it seems that her ambitions have been realized. She is now in cabinet. It is ironic that her name is now on the bill that will put abortion back into the Criminal Code. Where is that courage that we all admired a few years ago?
Yesterday, at my constituency office, after I had spoken on the amendments in the House of Commons, a call came in on my answering machine. It was a call from a young woman. She was crying. I want to take a moment just to let you know what she said. It was a very emotional message.
I will read to this House exactly as she said it, because I think this is what we are talking about. This is the kind of situation and the concern that women have:
Hi Dawn. Thank you very much for speaking out in Parliament in favour of pro-choice. When I was 17, the child my father gave me when he raped me, he forced to have aborted. He drove me to Washington State and I had no say in the matter. I am pro-choice because that decision was mine to make and not his. How I feel about it is my choice, my decision and no one has the right to take that away
May 24, 1990

from me-certainly not a bunch of parliamentarians who hang around and get paid $65,000 a year to spout their-
I will leave that word blank. She then said:
I am being abusive. I am sorry. Good-bye.
I think those comments from that young woman tell us exactly what we are talking about here today. It is an emotional debate. It is an emotional issue. It is not going to go away. It is not going to go away when this bill passes. There will be challenges.
I urge all members to think carefully again, to re-examine their position and vote against Bill C-43.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBIanc (Cape Breton Highlands- Canso):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the issue of abortion is a matter that has caused great distress and concern among many people, women and men, in my constituency of Highlands-Canso in particular since the restrictions on this practice were removed as a result of the Supreme Court decision in 1988.
There is no question that I have received more mail from my riding on this issue than on any other issue. I want to quote a few letters from some of the constituents who have written to me expressing their views that legislation to restrict this practice and to prevent this tragedy from occurring be re-introduced.
The first letter comes from Sister Theresa LeBIanc of Antigonish who writes:
Surely in a country such as ours, where human rights are respected, the most fundamental right, the right to life, will be guaranteed and protected by Canadian legislation to the most helpless of all, the unborn.
Another woman from my riding also wrote. She is Mrs. Vera Landry of River Bourgeois, and she says:
I am upset and ashamed that as women we would even consider claiming the right to kill another innocent human being in an effort to further our own equality. The quest for justice for women must not be accomplished by denying justice to others.
A third person, Mr. Duncan Maclsaac of Judique, writes:
The divisive issue of abortion is a tremendous test of moral leadership for those who seek truth and desire to uphold life.
The debate we are involved in tonight is about life and about rights, fundamental human rights for all human beings from the moment of conception, from the mo-
Govemment Orders
ment that we can define their possibility as human beings. It is that which must not be forgotten. That is what this debate is all about.
Bill C-43 was an attempt by this government at a law to legislate on abortion. At second reading I said that this bill, as drafted, was deeply flawed. I pointed out areas in which I thought the bill was vague and ambiguous. Yet, because I know that Canadians abhor the current legislative vacuum and want legislation that would express our desire for restrictions and would support Canadians so that abortions would be reduced, I voted for this legislation at second reading. I voted for it so that it could go forward to the committee stage to be clarified, strengthened, and improved.
Unfortunately, despite the testimony of many distinguished interveners, Bill C-43 emerged from committee unchanged. Amendments were proposed which were considered yesterday at the report stage which would have improved this bill, which would have strengthened it in many respects. I voted for many of these amendments. In fact, I even introduced one myself. I voted for these amendments in the hope that we could have legislation on the books which would reflect the views of society that abortion is not a practice which we in this civilized society condone.
I voted for several of these amendments in the hope that we could strengthen this bill, so that it would convey that message to Canadians. Unfortunately, none of those amendments were accepted and it is with regret that I must say tonight that I will be voting against this bill at third reading. I will be voting against this bill because it does not accomplish what the majority of Canadians want, which is legislation that will be a reflection of Canadian society at this point in time.
Bill C-43, as presently drafted, is a divisive bill. It drives an even larger wedge between already vehement opposites in this debate. It encourages the kind of debate which has taken place in Canada recently, a debate which ignores the shared ends of each side and concentrates on the differences. It concentrates on the extreme positions which have been advocated by those who proclaim themselves to be pro-life and those who proclaim themselves to be pro-choice. The pro-choicers accuse the other side of being anti-choice and the

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
pro-lifers accuse the other side of being pro-death, extreme labels which have polarized Canadians.
Unfortunately, Bill C-43 has contributed to and promoted that kind of negative debate. The tragedy of the debate is that is focused on the means and not on the ends. Nobody likes abortion. What is required is a policy and program of the government to bring down abortions. That program has to include an abortion law which conveys that message, but it has to be broader than an abortion law.
No one is naive enough to believe that by itself legislation on abortion is going to accomplish a reduction in abortion. If there is a commitment toward this, it has to be part of a much broader program of support and policies by this government, a program of policies which affirms life, which affirms values that we share as Canadians, including family values and values that respect life at all stages.
We must reduce the number of unwanted pregnancies through value-based sex and family planning education. We must be open and up front with our children so we may be able to face the overwhelming pressures of adolescence and adulthood. We must use education in our homes, our churches and our schools to instil in our young adults a clear sense of sexual knowledge, morality and responsibility.
We must address socio-economic concerns facing pregnant women today. Child care must be addressed by this government now, not at the time of the next election. Equal pay and opportunity remain huge obstacles. The recently released report of the task force on barriers to women in the Public Service confirms this. Stricter enforcement of support agreements is another urgent requirement. The recently established Family Orders and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Act is a step in the right direction, but it must be strengthened. Affordable housing is desperately required, especially in cities with a high living standard and a low vacancy rate.
Of course we must go beyond legislation and programs of government to work toward changing the social attitudes we express as a society. On this point the Catholic Conference of Bishops, in their testimony before the committee studying Bill C-43, was particularly eloquent. Let me quote a passage from that testimony. The bishops said:
Government reforms are not sufficient. They must be accompanied by social changes throughout society. Communities must be more responsive to families and women in need. Adoption needs to be promoted as a solution to an unwanted pregnancy but with greater compassion for the agony of giving up a child. Educational, cultural and other institutions, including the Catholic Church, must be more active in promoting the equality of women and respect for them as persons. Some male attitudes and behaviour have to change radically if there is to be an end to violence against women, more coresponsibility in parenting and more respectful inter-personal relationships.
These are challenges for us as a civilized society. They are challenges we will constantly be required to meet, and a legislative framework that includes legislation respecting abortion is part of that support mechanism for fostering the kind of attitudes that we need to foster in a society that protects rights for everyone.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I would like now to ask the hon. member to conclude, please.

This debate will continue long after this vote and long after we have been replaced as members in this chamber. Let us be able to say, though, that in our debate we have furthered not our own agendas but the cause of Canadian women and their children.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday I rose in this House and spoke on report stage and I said that I was sad about what had happened, about how 25 years after the first go-around on this issue we were back again arguing the same points and discussing the same things. Tonight, however, while I am still sad, I am also angry. I am angry because last night I saw, as the hon. member from New Westminster said in her eloquent comments earlier, the way the votes went and the lack of comprehension by so many in the House about this issue and the all too strong comprehension by too many others.
The root problem here is that true equality for women does not exist in our country, no matter how many women MPs, cabinet ministers, deputy speakers, party leaders, leadership candidates, vice-regals, and onward and upward women in positions of prominence we have. It does not exist, and there is not a woman who sits in the House or in the country who does not know in her secret soul that equality does not exist.
May 24, 1990

The term "reproductive choice" has become synonymous with the word "abortion". It should not be. It should mean a range of choices which would preclude the necessity for abortion, but that range of choices is not available for women in this country or indeed any country in the western world.
Regarding the kinds of reactions to women that we have heard over the last several days, I compliment the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso on his most reasoned remarks and for his support for social programs, despite the fact that we disagree on the most basic issue. Yesterday, when speaking against some of the amendments, I talked about the fact that the problem can be solved only by fostering equality and the kinds of social support networks necessary to make this society friendly for women and children. "Friendly" may be too strong a word. The word I really mean is basically "decent". It is not, and again, every member knows it is not for far too many women and children.
I have a good friend in Halifax at my old university, Mount Saint Vincent, who is an historian and a feminist. I remember her once saying to a class in women's studies that the women's movement is the most cataclysmic movement in social history, certainly since the Industrial Revolution, and possibly even more cataclysmic than the Industrial Revolution. All I can say-I do not say it with humour but with deadly seriousness-is it is amazing that women have managed to achieve this kind of cataclysm given the leg irons that are on them because of this want of equality in our society.
What we see here-I almost hesitate to say this, but I have felt it for a long time-with far too many people in this Chamber who oppose a woman's right to choose is truly a reaction to the women's movement. I do not say that this is the reason for all those who oppose a women's right to choose, but I say it is the reason for a frightening number. Mr. Speaker, if you do not believe me, you should have been at the study of Bill C-43. You would have heard, and I think it would have struck fear into your heart.
We hear, and heard, from men saying: "Women cannot be allowed to do this. Women cannot be allowed to do that." Women are coming to the point where the question of what we are and are not allowed to do will no longer be acceptable.
Government Orders
Over the past two days, I have listened in the House to some things that truly astound me. For example, I have heard that most abortions take place for socio-economic reasons, as if the socio-economic reasons being cited were mere fripperies and women resort to abortion because a pregnancy is merely inconvenient. Do these people live in the real world? Do they live in modern-day Canada where one million children go to food banks? Do they live in real-life Canada where women are subject every day to violence and to death? Do they live in the Canada that less than six months ago saw 14 young women cut down in the prime of their youth and their scholarship because they were women who dared enter a formerly male-dominated profession?
Socio-economic reasons are not fripperies. I suggest to some of my colleagues who sneer at socio-economic reasons that they should perhaps do some visiting in some of the housing projects in this country, in some of the community clinics and in some of the women's centres, those that are able to remain open, to find out the lives of fear, poverty and desperation that so many women live.
Mr. Speaker, I will tell you another thing. Many of the women who suffer this way are not, by any means, living in the physical poverty that we can identify in our cities and towns. Many of them are living in an equal poverty of spirit and poverty of choice in some of the finest addresses this country can provide. The enslavement and the enchaining of women goes on, in many cases, undeterred.
We are going to see this bill pass on Tuesday and we are going to see the criminalization of women. We are going to see the criminalization of abortion, which for the past two years has gone on in this country without any law and without an opening of the floodgates, without the moral fabric of the country falling apart and without, God knows, even women managing to take over the political spectrum. This law is unnecessary and it is a fraud. It is an insult to the intelligence and the morality of the women of this country, and also to the intelligence and the morality of the men of this country. Those of us who advocate a woman's right to choose do not say that men have no right in a family decision. Again, when the situation is optimum, when the question to be decided is between two equal partners who take full responsibility for their actions and for the results of their actions, that is one thing. But too many women in Canada face these

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
decisions alone because they have been left and deserted physically, emotionally and morally by their partners.
In my one remaining minute I would like to say that I am tired of the threats I have received. I am tired of being called a baby-killer. I want to say that I received a call today from a young woman from Manitoba who told me that doctors there are already beginning to cancel appointments, so that access in Manitoba is going down. I want to say that I sympathize with the people my colleague from Cape Breton Highlands-Canso mentioned. I have had letters from those people too. I want to say that I wish I had the luxury to hold those views, because it would be a luxury to say there is no need for abortion in this country. All of us in the women's movement live for the day when that will be so, but until we root out the causes-poverty, ignorance, violence and fear- the need for abortion will continue. Until we do that, nothing-no law, no government-will stop abortion. It will only drive the practice into the nether world of criminal activity and turn desperate women and sympathetic doctors into fugitives from so-called justice.
Is that what Canadians want, Mr. Speaker? I do not think so.

Mr. Speaker, before I launch into a full discussion of Bill C-43, I will see if I can get away with a minor bending of the rules by making a comment on the other issue that is before the country. I can tie the two together by saying that I think both the issue of the constitutional crisis that this country faces and the issue of Bill C-43 deal with the same underlying principles. That is the question of whether we, as legislators and parliamentarians, can provide the leadership to develop in this country a sense of tolerance, understanding, compassion and a real belief in the rights of others.
On the issue that others are meeting in this city tonight to deal with and try to come to grips with, I want to offer the wisdom of Dennis Lee. A friend of mine, Elicia Scott, sent me this poem which she found in a book of Dennis Lee's called Garbage Delight. It is called "A Pair of Pants". It reads:
Johnny came from England. Jackie came from France. They went to see a wise man about a pair of pants. One said they're too long. One said they're too little. The wise man took the pair of pants and ripped
them up the middle. Now each one has got a pant leg, each is freezing,
too. And yet it seemed the only thing that anyone could do.
Turning to Bill C-43,1 would like to confirm that along with the other members of my party, I intend to vote against Bill C-43 on third reading. I believe this bill offends the rights of Canadians and, in particular, the rights of women. I believe it is a bill which imposes on doctors a responsibility which is not properly theirs to have. It is a bill which makes a criminal act of an act which should not be seen as a criminal act. It is a bill which will not do its stated purpose of protecting the foetus.
As a Christian and one who has held a position in the Anglican Church of Canada as Vice-Chancellor of the diocese in which I live, I want to make it absolutely clear that I do not speak for the church, and I do so from that perspective and from the perspective of understanding, I believe in the sacredness of human life. I believe an understanding of the sacredness of life cannot lead to the conclusion that abortions, in virtually every case, should be made criminal. Those cases, which are to be exceptions, are to be decided by doctors. This is really not a medical decision.
An attempt to squeeze into this law an idea that the decision in individual cases of whether or not to have an abortion is a medical one is a perversion. I believe, as earnestly as I can, that this bill does not provide a principled answer.
