It denies the principles enunciated by those who believe that the foetus is a matter of human life, and those who believe that until the foetus is bom, the predominant right is that of the woman. The extent to which the foetus has rights is a matter to be determined in the final analysis by the conscience of the woman who bears the child.
Let me take my time to focus on the comments of the Minister of Justice. The minister has had the responsibility of introducing this bill and seeing it through the House. She has made a number of speeches and comments on the bill. Let me deal with her comments on report stage because I understand that, and having reviewed her comments this morning, I appreciate the fact that this embodies her rationale for what is a profound change in her position. I believe it is not too strong to say it is a betrayal of the position of the rights of women in this country and, therefore, the rights of all Canadians. In her speech to the House on May 22, she first raised the canard that somehow the Supreme Court of Canada imposed an obligation on this House to act. That is simply wrong. Any careful reading of the Supreme Court decisions confound the proposition that she
May 24, 1990

makes that the Supreme Court of Canada in the Mor-gentaler case in effect called on the House of Commons to come up with a law that allegedly balanced the rights of women as guaranteed by the Charter of Rights and as enunciated by the Supreme Court of Canada with the alleged right and the societal interest in the protection of the foetus. The fact is the Supreme Court of Canada said no such thing either in the Morgentaler case, in the Borowski case, or in the Daigle case.
The minister says on page 11666 of Hansard:
It is our role as parliamentarians to bring forward legislation that reasonably reflects the various views and interests of Canadian society in a manner acceptable to that majority of Canadians, and that respects constitutional guarantees.
This bill does not deal and respond to those responsibilities. I suggest on an even higher plane it is critical that the first duty of Parliament in an area of sensitivity such as this, it is our duty to respond to principle and to try to deal with the rights of Canadians irrespective of the majority. As it happens, the majority favours the position of choice. That is an irrelevant argument to the argument of principle which is that surely now as we approach the 21st century the time has come for us as a civilized society to understand that women have the right to choose and make the decision in this most difficult of all decisions.
The Minister of Justice went on to say that the highest court of the land recognized this responsibility by stating in the Morgentaler affair that it was its role to examine the laws and it was the role of Parliament to achieve this balance. Again there is the implication that the court was imposing a duty.
That simply is not consistent with the language of the court's decision. Let me read from the decision of Chief Justice Dickson in the Morgentaler case: "I conclude that the procedures created by section 251 of the Criminal Code for obtaining a therapeutic abortion do not comport with the principles of fundamental justice. Simply put, assuming Parliament can act, it must do so properly." Assuming Parliament can act, and the Chief Justice added emphasis to those words in his decision.
Government Orders
There is no direction by the Supreme Court for Parliament to act. It is an entirely proper position for Parliament to take that there must be no criminal law in the area of abortion; that the issue of abortion is a matter of conscience and of right. It is a difficult decision but it is one which must be left to the women.
In her speech the Minister of Justice went on to talk about the legislative committee. She proclaimed the myth that following months of hearings, including testimony from many individuals and groups expressing strong views at either end of the spectrum of opinion on abortion, the committee recognized its duty to attempt to strike a fair balance between the rights and interests of women and society's concern that the foetus be protected. Over 90 per cent of the briefs and evidence received by that committee were against the bill and called on the committee to reject the bill.
From day one the majority on that committee had its mind made up and was determined to endorse the political solution to the political problem that the government and so many members of the Liberal party had, a solution which is not principled, a solution which will divide this country in the longer run and will destroy lives in the long run.
The minister concluded her remarks by saying: "It would be my hope that these members do not condemn this bill for not reflecting their own personal positions, but recognize its ability to respond to the concerns of their fellow Canadians in a matter that is understandable, workable and fair."
Let us look at the bill and see whether it is understandable, workable or fair. Let me remind the House and the country what this bill provides. It sets out new wording to Section 287 of the Criminal Code, which reads as follows:
287.(1) Every person who induces an abortion on a female person is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, unless the abortion is induced by or under the direction of a medical practitioner who is of the opinion that, if the abortion were not induced, the health or life of the female person would be likely to be threatened.
The bill goes on to define "health" to include physical, mental and psychological health.

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
First, this bill clearly makes the inducement of an abortion a criminal offence, except in certain circumstances. Those circumstances affect the opinion of a human medical practitioner who must exercise an opinion. We already know that medical practitioners are going to have different opinions on individual sets of facts. They are asked to form their opinion on the question of whether the abortion, if it were not induced, would put the health or life of the female person in jeopardy. It is expected that the medical practitioners will pass judgment on whether a failure to induce the abortion would cause a threat to physical, mental or psychological health.
What we have here is a disguised failure of this Parliament to make a decision. Instead, it is turned not back to the person who ought to be making what is a moral decision, but instead to medical practitioners who are asked to make it on the vague test of physical, mental or psychological health.
Those from the anti-choice side of this House, who moved amendments last night, were perfectly correct when they said that the language is not certain and not clear. It is doubly not certain and not clear when it is turned over to a medical practitioner who, after all, is not a lawyer. He is asked to express a medical opinion.
The bill is not understandable. It is not workable in that it imposes an onus on those who seek to escape the effect of the criminal law to demonstrate the onus, and it is far from fair. There is no question that there are going to be different views of medical practitioners. Access to abortion is going to vary across the country. There is no distinction made on the basis of age or condition of women, and it is going to be taken outside the realm that it ought to be in in determination.
One set of legal issues, which have been raised by the minister, have been put to the test of law professors and lawyers across the country. In her attempt to justify this bill, the Minister of Justice offered the propositions that, first, there was at law a requirement for a medical justification for legal abortion and that that would create a national standard of entitlement to abortion for Canadian women. The minister secondly argued that it was necessary for Parliament to use its criminal law power to restrict the ways in which provincial legislatures can restrict access to abortion.
Those were two critical arguments that the minister used to justify this legislation and to attempt to persuade, as she apparently has successfully done, her colleagues in the Conservative and Liberal parties to vote for the bill.
A series of legal opinions were sought and there were 17 opinions returned from professors and other experts across the country. Before I get into the detail of them, I just want to read what the Minister of Justice said about these distinguished constitutional experts.
When it was put to her in the Justice Committee on May 10,1990, the Minister of Justice said that she first of all had not read any of the opinions. However, she proceeded to pronounce that their arguments were utterly without foundation. She then went on to say that she did not recognize any of the leading luminaries in constitutional law in Canada in the list of people named in The Globe and Mail article.
The minister appears not to have either taken the trouble to ask for a comprehensive review of the opinions, but she proceeded to dismiss the opinions as coming from those who were beneath her dignity to know.
Let me tell the House about some of the opinions. First of all, may I offer the opinion from the Faculty of Law at the University of Toronto of seven professors, one of whom I had as a professor and so did other distinguished members of this House, if I can include myself in that category. However, apparently they failed to get through to the Minister of Justice. I am thinking here of Professor Risk. I include Professors Duclos, Macklem, Rogerson, Colker, Grant and Roach, seven professors from perhaps the most distinguished law school. I hesitate to get too comparative in this, but it is my Alma Mater.
All of them took apart the minister's arguments limb by limb. At the end of this six-page letter of opinion, there is nothing left of the arguments.
On the question of a national standard of entitlement, these professors, as did others, Professor Bruce Ryder from Osgoode Hall, Professor Andrew Petter from the even more distinguished University of Victoria, Martha Jackman, professor of constitutional law, and Sandra Rodgers, professor of medical legal issues at the University of Ottawa and on and on, all make the point, first of all, that this inept bill, Bill C-43, does not create any national entitlement to abortion. Quite the opposite. It
May 24, 1990

makes abortion, in most circumstances, a criminal offence.
Mr. Speaker, I see you waving your finger of one minute at me, so I am going to ask my colleagues if they feel so minded to put a question to me. I will give them, when the time comes, an opportunity to learn even more about the opinion of professors at the various universities on the inadequacies of the Minister of Justice's opinion.
Let me just finish by saying that people across this country do not want this bill. They do not want abortion to be a matter of criminal law. They do not wish the matter turned over simply to doctors to decide. Women across Canada do not want this bill. The courts have made it very clear that this bill, by making abortion illegal, intervenes in one of the most difficult decisions that a person can make.
Let me conclude by quoting from Madam Justice Wilson who said: "This decision, that of having an abortion, is one that will have profound psychological, economic, and social consequences for the pregnant woman. The circumstances giving rise to it can be complex and varied. There may be and usually are powerful considerations militating in opposite directions. It is a decision that deeply reflects the way the woman thinks about herself and her relationship to others and to society at large. It is not just a medical decision. It is a profound social and ethical one as well. Her response to it will be the response of the whole person".
This decision about the future of a foetus is one which is a profound social and ethical question. It is not one that Parliament can make, a Parliament, predominantly, as has been noted, of men who will never face this decision. It is not a decision which doctors can make. It is a decision which women make, and I urge the House to vote against the bill.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It seems that at least two members have listened to your suggestion for questions and comments and I recognize the hon. member for Mission-Coquitlam on a question or comment.

Indeed, I am taking up the suggestion of the hon. member because I am very interested in hearing what is the legal analysis from the 17 law professors. The women in Canada have a
Government Orders
right to have spelled out for them what the analysis is. I would ask the hon. member if he could, in the time allotted for questions and comments, provide me and the women of Canada with that information.

I thank my friend for the very perceptive question. I do appreciate it. It does give me a chance to add some remarks which I had hoped to squeeze in in the main part of my speech.
It is perhaps clear on the face of it that the question of national standard of entitlement is not established by this bill. That is a specious argument. Let me go to the second of the two arguments that the minister raised in which he stated: "It is necessary for Parliament to use its criminal law power to restrictive the ways in which provincial legislatures can restrict access to abortion".
There are a number of flaws with that, but the main one is that all of the cases demonstrate clearly that the provincial legislatures operating within their areas of jurisdiction, and in this case probably the area of health, could enact even more restrictive legislation than this Parliament enacts and that such legislation would not be deemed to be in conflict with validly enacted federal legislation.
In the case of car accidents, for example, or car offences, the federal Criminal Code applies one standard. In provincial legislatures which have enacted additional standards, that legislation has been upheld by the courts.
In the justice committee the minister pronounced herself and dismissed all of these arguments as not knowing what they are talking about. She said that they were talking about the paramountcy principle and then proceeded to demonstrate that she did not know anything about the paramountcy principle at all.
The only case that the minister could even refer to was one decided in 1896 on the paramountcy issue, subsequently completely changed and developed in a different direction by courts. The paramountcy issue is the following. If there are conflicting, validly enacted federal and provincial legislation, then the federal law will prevail. But first there must be a finding of valid provincial legislation and then there must be a determination of conflict. It is that point which the minister fails to understand but she demonstrates in her discussion of the

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
Westindorp case, which she completely misunderstands and misquotes.
This legislation does not so occupy the field in the area of abortion that it would prevent more restrictive legislation be enacted by provinces. This law does not establish national standards. This law is not something that is required by the courts.
As we watched the votes unfold last night, the vote by the Liberal Party brought me great sadness. This is a difficult issue to make partisan. Yet by their votes, both the Conservative and Liberal parties demonstrated that when the crunch really comes the talk about women's rights is just talk. A mere handful of Liberals stood up, 5 Liberals out of a caucus of 83 or 84-some of them are off running for leader right now-and voted for the position that abortion should not be a matter of criminal law at all; a handful.
Women across Canada and men across Canada who are concerned about the profound issue of women's rights are going to have to ask themselves, as they move towards future elections, whether it in fact aids the cause of women's rights to have more Liberals in the House. Last night demonstrated beyond doubt that Liberals, as with Conservatives, cannot be counted on to stand with women when it really matters.

I was
pleased to hear my colleague from Victoria's comments. It is almost a breath of fresh air to hear from a man in this House articulating the position of choice for women in such a clear and forceful manner. It is also a pleasure to hear him look at the legal ramifications of this bill. That leads me to one of the questions that I have.
One of the rationales that we have heard around this place for bringing in criminal legislation has been the Chantal Daigle case last summer, when Canadians from coast to coast were horrified to see this young woman's life displayed across television sets from coast to coast, to have the most intimate details of her life spoken of in cafes, in barber shops, on street comers, in all the places in Canada. People did not like that spectacle. They wanted to ensure that it would not happen again. One of the rationales we keep hearing is, if Bill C-43 passes that will stop that kind of display.
I would like to ask my colleague, how will Bill C-43 stop civil injunctions? Will it, in fact? Or will we continue to see this kind of display, this kind of action by some of the more reactionary, more forceful, more nasty antichoice people in our society?

The answer is that the bill will in fact encourage legal action. It will make abortions in most cases illegal. The lines, when they are not illegal are vague. That is an invitation to legal action. It is an invitation to injunctions. The Supreme Court of Canada in the Daigle case made it very clear that it frowned on any law which put women through the court system during pregnancy. I am quite convinced that, in due course, this bill, which we are agonizing through here and which the countiy is agonizing through, will be ruled unconstitutional by the Supreme Court of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I was interested to hear the hon. member from New Westminster-Burnaby refer to the legal analysis that we have just heard from the hon. member for Victoria and the thoughtful and articulate way in which he has expressed his concern for the legislation that is before us.
I will find it very difficult under the circumstances to be able to put forward the thoughtful, rational words that are necessary. I am afraid that after listening for hours and hours this week to women being denigrated, I am rapidly getting to the point that it is going to be very difficult to maintain rationality, to maintain dignity, or even to maintain the respect that is necessary to speak in this House.
In an article in The Vancouver Province, the Justice Minister stated that the criminal law has two major purposes. First, the preservation of the peace and protection of the public, and secondly, the safeguards of equality, fairness, and a guarantee of the rights and liberties of the individual against the state".
This bill will not preserve peace on the question of abortion. Indeed, the outrage expressed by both sides on this question ensures that the legislation will ensure an ongoing inflamed debate.
With regard to the protection of the public, just what public is the minister suggesting must be protected by this legislation, and from whom?
May 24, 1990

The second purpose, she said, was the safeguard of equity and fairness and a guarantee of rights and liberties of the individual against the state. How does Bill C-43 safeguard and protect equity and fairness, and how does it guarantee the rights of women in Canada?
This is not a compromise bill. This is a bill that recriminalizes abortion. The Liberals want this bill to pass because they would like to have the issue laid to rest in anticipation of forming the next government. The Liberals anticipate that once the bill is in place they will not have to deal with it if indeed they do become the next government.
To those who watched the votes last night it became very clear to Canadian women where the hearts and support of the Liberals are on issues as they pertain to women. The verbal rhetoric will escalate as we go into an election campaign, but unfortunately the Liberal Party has neither the policy nor the will, as evidenced last night, to ensure that Canadian women's rights and justice for Canadian women will prevail under their governments.
For the Tories, this bill, in my view, is a sacrificial offering to the radical fringe, the fringe that does not like turbans, that opposes pay equity and that in many ways has demonstrated that it very much dislikes women. The government is offering up on the sacrificial altar of expediency the right of women to choose.
The Minister of Justice, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, parted ways with Bill Vander Zalm and his Socred cronies in Victoria because of his interference on the question of abortion in British Columbia. Women in the riding of Vancouver Centre trusted the Minister of Justice. They believed that she would stand with them on this most basic of rights. They were thrilled, as were many women in this country, when the hon. member was made the first woman justice minister.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre, the Minister of Justice, has broken ranks with her sisters, the women of Canada, the women who supported her, the women who celebrated her appointment with her, and has turned her back on them. She has stood in this House and offered an arrogant rationale implying balance in a bill that devastates the rights of women in this country.
Government Orders
I have a letter addressed to the Minister of Justice that was sent to me by a constituent of mine and that I would like to put on the record. It reads:
Dear Minister,
Re: Proposed Recriminalization of Abortion
I would like to be able to congratulate you on your appointment as Justice Minister, since the appointment of a woman to that position is an historical event and should be one that all women wish to celebrate. However, I believe that the Prime Minister's decision to appoint a woman to the Justice portfolio was neither made in a spirit of commitment to women's equality nor in recognition of the potential contribution that a woman incumbent could make to all women in Canada. Rather, I believe that your appointment is a thinly veiled attempt to counter all the bad press that the federal government has received over its recent decision to cut federal funding to women's programs across Canada.
Further, I believe that your appointment was intended to cloud the fact that the proposed abortion bill will recriminalize abortion. I believe the Prime Minister considered your B.C. reputation as a supporter of a woman's right to reproductive choice and decided that he could rely on that reputation to reassure Canadian women that the hon. Minister would be fair in her representation of women on this issue. I believe the Canadian women are not that easily fooled-
and it gives the minister's name.
Those same women who applauded your position on choice are now wondering why you have turned away from them to endorse proposed legislation to recriminalize abortion. I know why. It is politically expedient for you to abandon the wishes of the majority of Canadian women on this subject at this time. That is nothing for us to celebrate.
The majority of Canadians support a woman's right to choose whether or not to have a child. I demand that you, hon. Minister, act on behalf of the majority of Canadians in opposing the proposed abortion bill. I must advise you that if you do not, I will do everything within my power to ensure that Canadian women know that you favour political expediency over the rights of women, and I will be encouraging them to ensure that you are not re-elected to the House of Commons.
Yours truly,
Linda Tosac
This past year, January to December 1989, provided a long list of rude awakenings for Canadian women, women who thought we had won the right to make our own reproductive decisions. Women in Ontario were shocked when the Supreme Court of Ontario judge granted Barbara Dodd's former boyfriend an injunction preventing her from having an abortion. The decision followed a hearing at which neither Dodd nor her lawyer were present.
Women in Quebec were shocked when Chantal Daigle's former lover persuaded a Superior Court judge

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
to order the young woman to cany her pregnancy to term. The province's highest court upheld the ruling.
Women in Nova Scotia watched helplessly as Premier John Buchanan's government passed a law to prevent Dr. Henry Morgentaler from operating a Halifax clinic that was to facilitate safe, timely abortions in the underserved Atlantic provinces.
Women throughout the country looked on with amazement and shock as this government introduced a new criminal abortion law that could lead to the imprisonment of both women and their doctors for abortions performed for reasons other than health.
All this in spite of the fact that in 1988 the Supreme Court ruled and came down with a decision that struck down Canada's abortion laws because they forced women seeking abortions to meet a criterion that is unrelated to their own priorities and aspirations.
Now we are in 1990, and now we have listened through this long week to member of parliament after member of parliament get up and, in the most sanctimonious terms, vilify the women of this country.
Part of the argument that was put forward was an argument for women to carry children to term and for the government, I assume, or society as a whole, to provide to those women the kinds of support that are necessary for them either to bear the children and keep them or, as some might suggest, to bear them for another, which is an option I am sure those who have suggested it have not thought about in terms of the person who is doing the bearing.
Having said that, in the last 18 months since this parliament began I have not seen one shred of evidence from the government to show that there is any intention on the part of the same government that brings forward such regressive, cruel legislation-not one shred of evidence that that government in fact plans to provide the support necessary for women to be able to bear these children and raise these children with the support of the community.
In fact, it is important for us to note that the number of working families in this country has steadily increased between 1973 and 1986, and in fact is up by 19 percent. There is a disproportionate number of working-poor families residing in western Canada. Often these include families with two incomes. Roughly 60 percent of working-poor families consists of couples with dependent children.
Has the government provided any kind of assistance to these families? No. The government has put a cap on CAP in western provinces. The government has clawed back child allowance. The government has failed to deliver on the child care that was promised and, to top it all off, the government is throwing in a 7 percent goods and services tax. This lack of support is totally unrealistic.
In 1966, a minimum-wage worker who supports a family could earn 46 percent of the poverty line income. Those are 1986 figures, Mr. Speaker. The minimum wage has not increased in this Parliament since 1986. Even if both spouses were fully employed at the minimum wage, they could only earn 92 percent of the poverty line with both of them working. I do not know if this government expects that they should run out and steal the other 8 percent. I do not know how this government plans that they should find the 7 percent to pay the goods and services tax, but I do know that this kind of policy is not going to help those mothers and fathers face poverty and deal with additional children if in fact their choice were one that is abortion.
There is a failure by this government to set an example for the rest of Canada about how it will provide this wonderful support that it keeps saying we as a community must provide. It is easy to get up in this House and say that we as a community must provide support to the women of Canada.
I will tell you something: if you start looking at the statutes that have come into this House to be debated in this House about supporting women, not one of them will help a woman who is faced with these kinds of choices.
I could go into detail on the legislation, but I do not intend to because I think it has been amply described by my colleagues from the New Democratic Party.
This is a sad week for women in Canada, and it is going to be a sadder week next week when women return to the life of a chattel, being subject to male analysis of the decisions we make and to being threatened with jail if those decisions are the wrong ones in the view of those men. In fact, the minister, as the hon. member for Victoria says, used as her paramountcy a decision from the last century. There are generations of women who have been born since the last century who remember, and who will continue to remember, their sisters, their
May 24, 1990

neighbours, their mothers, their friends, without the right to have a legal safe abortion, who helped each other in desperation, knowing they were breaking the law, watching some die or suffer horribly, but willing to make that sacrifice because there was no alternative.
Women will continue to have abortions in this country. The ante will go up tremendously if this bill passes. I am finding it very difficult tonight, as I said at the beginning, to make a speech that gives the dignity to this House that it deserves. I am absolutely devastated at the thought that in 1990, 50 years after we women became persons, we are faced with the fait accompli of Bill C-43, the recriminalization of abortion.
The hon. member for Victoria drew a parallel between the constitutional crisis Canada faces and this bill. I agree with him totally, not only does this bill parallel the constitutional crisis, this bill is the Meech Lake Accord of women in Canada.
I condemn this bill for its lack of fairness, for its lack of equity, for its lack of justice. I condemn it on behalf of a great number of women in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would first like to thank the member for her kind words. I would also like to take this opportunity to congratulate the member for New Westminster-Burnaby for her fight on this bill. It has been terrific. I am proud to be sitting next to her in this House and to be associated with her in this battle.
As I was listening to her and to the member for Mission-Coquitlam I noted a sadness, particularly among women, in this debate and in the vote. It is a sadness with which I empathize. It is not a pleasant thing to see the society in which you live a lesser place than you would like it to be. I think that is the perception of what is happening.
I happened, for quite different reasons, to go into the reading room tonight and I found a book called The Long Distance Runner, the autobiography of Michael Harrington. Michael Harrington is an American socialist. He told a joke that William Buckley told on him in introducing him. He said: "That is like being a skyscraper in Desmoines".
Government Orders
He tells the story in this book of his life as a democratic socialist in the United States. He describes it as the long distance run. Part of it is the evolution of his thinking as the years went along, part of it is an account of the joy of accomplishment and the despair at the losses and the difficult times. He concludes, as it happened just before he died recently of cancer, to say that he would not have traded his life for any other, that the struggle for social justice is important and worth it. Whatever the short-term loss tonight, it is a fight that must go on.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for Victoria for what he has just put before the House. I think it probably reflects the sentiments of many Canadian women. Many of the women who have spoken in this House believed, I think, that we were part of the last generation of women who would have to face unwanted pregnancy with no alternatives but to break the law. In fact, we find ourselves part of a generation again facing those alternatives. That is the legacy we have to give to our daughters.
I too want to draw a little bit of a comparison. There was a black and white film put out years ago. It is still around in some places. It was put out by the International Ladies Garment Workers and is about the organizing drives in New York at the turn of the century. There is a song which closes the film. The chorus in the song says: "Every generation has to win it again". I guess that is what we are facing here.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak very briefly at the third reading stage of Bill C-43 and express my reservations about the legislation tabled by this government.
Jesus Christ said something I think is very apt in this case; "Forgive them, for they know not what they do". I think these words are a very good description of this government, which has tabled a bill that does not in any way deal with the problem facing our modem society.
In fact, neither pro-life nor pro-choice supporters can identify with this bill. Both groups are disappointed by this legislation. I fail to see why the government refused to pass legislation similar to that which exists in most of the world's industrialized countries. I am referring to legislation that clearly specifies that in the early stages of pregnancy, it is exclusively up to the woman to decide whether or not she will keep her child. In most modem

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
countries, the legislation provides that this decision may be made by the mother without any intervention by the State, and in a totally decriminalized context.
In most of these countries-I am thinking of France in particular-there is a provision that in the second quarter, the decision is a matter between the mother and a physician. In other words, the decision must be medically approved if the abortion, if that is what the mother wants, is to take place.
In the last three months of pregnancy, most industrialized countries provide that to have an abortion is a criminal act, except in cases where the life of the mother is in danger.
I think the legislation before the House today might, in the opinion of those who support the pro-life movement, open the door far too wide to abuse. If we read the wording of the bill very carefully, it is indeed a possibility. Conversely, and this is where the situation gets rather confused, we have had both on second reading and at the report stage of this bill and now on third reading, parliamentarians who said that in fact, the bill was far too restrictive and that in the final instance, the whole bill should not be subject to the Criminal Code.
I think the amendment proposed by the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby (Ms. Black), who suggested repealing sections 287 and 288 of the Criminal Code, had some merit. I did not vote in favour of the amendment because personally, I think the decision, at least in the early stages of pregnancy, should be entirely up to the mother and certainly not subject to the Criminal Code. Personally, I think that in the final stages of pregnancy, abortion would constitute a crime, just as a mother who cuts her child's throat in the days and weeks following its birth would be committing a crime. If we apply criminal sanctions to the mother who commits such an act in the weeks following birth, I don't see how we could not do so when an abortion is done in the weeks preceding birth. There would otherwise be a double standard.
I think it is unfortunate that the bill ignores the various stages of pregnancy. The medical profession has very clearly addressed the whole question of deciding when life really begins. Is it at the time of conception, during the first few weeks, or during the first few months? I suggest that this still has not been resolved at
the medical level. But it seems to me that after a number of weeks, there is undoubtedly a living being in its mother's womb and to carry out an abortion at that time could be accepted by society only under very stringent conditions and on the basis of a clear decision of the medical profession.
I can say this with the utmost conviction because my father was a general practictioner who probably delivered a few thousand babies in his lifetime, operating for many years in such rural areas as the Lower St. Lawrence, near Riviere-du-Loup, Kamouraska, Saint-Pascal, but especially in Kamouraska, and later on in Charlesbourg, a suburd of Quebec City. He is no longer here to discuss with me and tell me how I should have voted on this bill. I am quite sure that he did not cany out many abortions. And if he did I am sure it was clearly to save the mother's life.
As several other Parliamentarians, I took it upon myself to seek opinions. This is a bill on which hon. members may vote freely, irrespective of their party affiliation or party line, according their conscience. I have been able to realize to what extent Canadians are divided on this issue, for having sought the opinion of my own children-I have two daughters and two sons-I know what they think, and I can tell you that if one of my sons is pro-life, the other is pro-choice, and that if one of my daughters is pro-life, the other is pro-choice. They are, like the rest of the Canadian people, deeply divided on this issue. Unfortunately, the bill we have before us does not help in any way. I hope that the bill will pass on third reading. I think it will. We just have to refer to the final votes on the report stage and see what happened then to conclude that Bill C-43 will very likely pass on third reading.
I hope that this law will not have as much trouble in the courts as the previous law because in reality, it is no longer possible, I think, to successfully prosecute a doctor who performs an abortion. The experience of the criminal courts in recent years clearly shows that when a physician is taken to court, a trial with judge and jury is automatically requested. In today's modem society, it is impossible to bring together 12 jurors who are unanimous on this question. That is why I find it rather unfortunate that the government decided to maintain this as a criminal matter. I am convinced that when it comes to trial in court, this question, again, will never be settled. I do not see how we can find 12 jurors who will
May 24, 1990

unanimously convict a physician for performing an abortion.
I also find it regrettable that so much emphasis is put on the physician's responsibility. It seems to me that doctors practise their profession in conditions that are often very difficult in our modern society. It is not the doctor's duty to pass a legal, much less a religious, judgement. Therefore putting so much emphasis in the bill on the physician's responsibility seems to me to be fundamentally wrong. I am quite disappointed to see how determined the government is to pass its bill in its present form.
Personally, I will vote against this bill on third reading because I think that it does not meet the needs of the day.
For sure, the Canadian government cannot legislate in this area without using the Criminal Code, since it is possibly the only law that allows it to legislate.
But it seems to me that this issue, which I think ought to be decriminalized, should be strictly regulated by provincial and medical authorities in each Canadian province. Had we been able to get the agreement of the ten provinces to put the matter of abortion under civil law to allow abortion during the first weeks of pregnancy, as I said earlier, I suggest we might have had a piece of legislation which would have been much fairer and much more serene, but which could have provided stricter sanctions for abortion in the latter phase of pregnancy.
I voted for an amendment introduced by the member from Fraser Valler East (Mr. Belsher). His amendment had to do with the physician who concludes that without abortion the life or health of the mother might be seriously threatened. I thought that adding the word "seriously" would in a way restrict the open-door approach to abortion on demand which seems to be a characteristic of this bill. I am very disappointed that the government did not see fit to accept this amendment from one of its own backbenchers.
I vividly remember the words of Mgr. Lebel, president of the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, who expressed strong disappointment when he learned that the parliamentary committee on abortion did not accept

This is something I have been concerned with personally in the sense that I have seen it primarily not as a legal issue but as a moral issue.
My wife and the rest of my family and I have discussed this frequently over the years. My wife and I have seven children and a number of grandchildren, and we are glad of every one of them. My wife and I have never tried to prevent the birth of one of our children. We not only reverence life, but we enjoy and value it. I am encouraged by a large part of the brief that the United Church of Canada presented on this subject earlier this year. I may not agree with absolutely every detail of it, but it is one of the best statements I have found of the moral and religious issues at stake in this matter.

Some of us who decided years ago to join the Canadian Armed Forces were certainly deciding to try to take lives, since that is what has to be done in war. the general point that there are times when we have to make very grave decisions relating even to life itself.

Family planning, including vasectomy and tubal ligation, is a Christian duty. During my life, particularly during my married life and my life as an active member of the church, at present the Anglican Church, I have not been able to understand why some people teach that contraception is wrong. Some people seem to place contraception almost on a level with abortion in their scale of evil. I cannot for the life of me understand it because I believe it is true that the restriction or hindrance of contraception or a discouragement of contraception has in fact been responsible in part for many abortions.
The United Church goes on to says:

The United Church does not say that abortion is good. It does no say that abortion is neutral, neither good nor evil. It says it is wrong, but it does not take an absolutist view of that. It goes on:
We affirm the inherent value of human life, both as immature in the foetus-

Mr. Speaker, quite frankly, the abortion debate is one that I welcome.
I welcome this debate because it is an opportunity to focus attention not just on life, but on our whole attitude toward caring and sharing, attitudes New Democrats and their predecessors hold and have held very dear. It is a matter of understanding life, with all its important parts, and how we as individuals within a diversified society can best serve each other, not just in times of need but in everyday life when positive interaction prevents problems and stimulates development.
I state outright my support for life, life within the womb and later as the child grows to adulthood, aging, I would hope gracefully toward a natural death. In so doing, I express my understanding of our current society where children and adults die in poverty, without friends, without family and often without dignity.
Words are important. Definitions shape perceptions, and we have to be careful in our understanding of these definitions. We are all pro-life, and to suggest otherwise is nonsense. There is no other way to describe someone who bears concern and consideration for another's life, opportunity and future.
Some things enter into all this. The well-known Canadian Laurier Lapierre said it well not long ago, speaking at a convention that I attended in Saskatoon. The former television personality said that there is great
support among Canadians for the sanctity of life. Then he added: "until after birth".
The North American society we have created through economic decisions taken by governments is responsible for thousands of deaths every year.
There are suicides. The farmer about to lose the land that he inherited from his father feels that he has failed. The worker laid off for the third time in 10 years feels he can no longer serve his impoverished family. The student whose strife-tom home life is affecting his grades and social interaction with others feels he has no future worth living. This is a society in which crucial individual life and death decisions are based on one's interpretation of one's own future. Desperate decisions to take one's own life or the life of one yet to be bom are not taken lightly.
These are decisions reached in reaction to situations often created by others. They are decisions reached from deep within their souls, personal, private and often illogical. They are decisions not easily understood by you or me.
There are more than 60,000 abortions every year. We have to ask: Why? Are these the acts of indecisive women, uncaring women destined for hell? I think not, Mr. Speaker. A decision to take any life is one reached with much suffering, regret and guilt. Very often if there were alternatives, there would not be a decision to have that abortion. Community and local church support in this regard is very important.
As parliamentarians and members of this society, our goal is to reduce the number of abortions in Canada. It is a most admirable goal, one that I believe to be of utmost importance. However, if our society is going to achieve that goal or other goals such as the reduction in the number of suicides, the number of child or wife abuse situations or the number of crimes committed by juveniles, we are going to have to correct the social and economic problems that are the root cause of each. It is an admirable challenge, one we have to adopt as our own.
What all these problems have in common is that no law in and of itself will stop them. Young men and women will continue to commit suicide. Husbands will continue to beat their wives. Children will continue to commit crimes against person and property. People will continue to consider abortion as an alternative for their own futures regardless of well-placed words from wellmeaning individuals, speeches from politicians and laws controlling their lives, until such time as society provides
May 24, 1990

an alternative that they may consider in their personal decision-making process.
A woman who wants an abortion, and we must believe there are people who want abortions for many different reasons, and who has the means to obtain one will find the way to have that abortion regardless of the law. That was proved prior to the passing of Canada's first abortion law in 1967.
The true test of our society and our law-makers is our tolerance of the different needs and acts of individuals who make up our society. Governments and individuals have a responsibility to promote positive decision-making, to create a society which stimulates and encourages the joy of childbirth and child rearing. The protection of the child and the protection of the family is as important to the future of our society as is the protection of the rights of those who are yet to be bom.
There is a certain amount of the current debate which refuses to acknowledge the existence of factors beyond the individual control and therefore allows little room for tolerance of any kind. On an issue of this importance, society must accept that there is no specific or definitive answer to the question of what is right and what is wrong.
The answer lies, rather, in a series of programs aimed at improving the conditions of the poor, the unfortunate, and the confused. The aim is to prevent abortions from taking place. We will not stop abortions by creating new criminals. We will, however, stop abortions by creating a society which not only wants children but also offers those children through their families and our communities a future full of hope, optimism, and joy.
Canada, you may know, Mr. Speaker, has no children's policy. No government action has ever been taken on the recommendations of the health and welfare committee of this House in 1981. The committee's recommendations were based on the United Nations Commission during the International Year of the Child and called for the establishment of a children's ministry, a children's bureau. That committee, supported by the New Democratic Party's social issues critic, called for the develop-
Govemment Orders
ment and implementation of a comprehensive national family policy. It has never been done.
The purpose of the ministry and the policy would be to ensure that all Canada's children in whatever region they live have equal opportunities to develop as healthy, self-reliant, caring human beings.
The family as a basic human, working unit, has undergone major changes in the past decade. The extended family off the Indian reserves in this country is almost non-existent. Divorces are common. Children are being raised by single parents and teenage pregnancies are on the rise.
Almost every decision of government during this past decade has encouraged the trend toward a smaller and less caring family. It is encouraged by a society driven by the market-oriented economy. A government which cares only for those able to help themselves is a government which encourages abortion, crime, and death.
Inflation, unemployment, rising personal taxes, the increased cost of goods, have all taken their toll on people across this country. There is little hope among young people, a situation which is directly related to a less-motivated work force and a higher incidence of poverty and crime. Unemployment and job insecurity for parents have contributed to increased incidents of child abuse and wife battering.
There is a denial of certain human rights, rights which should be considered inherent in citizenship, a denial which helps to maintain the poor situation, the right to a decent standard of living, the right to free, efficient, and accessible health care, the right to a good education and a right to opportunities which will develop fully one's potential and aspirations. These are rights which only New Democrats have said in this House are a responsibility and priority of a government at the will of the people.
How does this way of thinking jibe with what has been happening in Canada during the past few years? Essentially, it flies in the face of government practice which has been to erode the place of the family and erode family benefits or basic rights of families from coast to coast.
Take, for example, the partial de-indexing of the family allowance and the change in the threshold rate, the rate at which benefits begin to be taxed back, from $26,800 to $23,500, a position taken in 1986. This effec-

May 24, 1990
Government Orders
tively meant that many families below the official poverty line had their benefits cut. The net loss to the family benefit program by 1991 because of these two cuts will be $1.5 billion per year. These are cuts to programs that essentially aided children.
The NDP sees the family allowance as the most effective way to deliver benefits to families, particularly those at the poverty line. The party is strongly advocating a significant increase in the family allowance and restoration of full indexation with a raised threshold level.
In addition, the party continues to call for a 20 per cent increase in the refundable child tax credit, also to be fully indexed.
New Democrats recognize the right of men and women to continue being an effective parent or worker with equal opportunity and employment. A decline in the support to young families and a desire and need by women with children to pursue work outside the home has steadily increased the need for quality child care. A system of universally accessible, affordable, high-quality, licensed child care and parent support policies are prerequisites. If mothers are unable to find affordable, quality child care, most will be forced to accept only temporary, part-time, poorly-paid work or stay at home or, worst of all, accept inadequate child care.
The tax reform package outlined by the government is another example of current government policies being grossly unfair to families, particularly those in the low and middle-income brackets.
Under the new rules we find that profitable corporations will continue to pay no income tax. Wealthy individuals will continue to see their taxes go down from what they were paying in 1984 when the Conservatives were elected.
Taxes for the average family are increasing faster than their incomes. Since 1984, sales tax hikes have generated almost 60 per cent of all new government revenues. That means an additional $600 per year from the average family.
What is most depressing about that is that a Statistics Canada report indicates that 56 per cent of all low-income Canadians are women, women who are either
elderly or are single parents struggling to raise a child on their own.
Families with small children and the elderly are most susceptible to illness. This government at the federal level succeeded in passing legislation providing for lengthy patent protection to American drug companies, the end result being that the cost of prescription drugs in this country has almost tripled.
In the province of Saskatchewan the Conservative government made it more difficult to obtain those drugs because of a ridiculous refund scheme for prescription drug costs. Neither federal nor provincial government has considered the implications of their actions on a young family or the elderly.
We are often told that children are this nation's most precious resource. We often talk in this Chamber about protection afforded to other resources such as forestry, mining and fish stocks. Yet when it comes to that precious resource of children what do we say and what do we do?
Mr. Speaker, let me just give you some statistics for the province of Saskatchewan. One out of every six Saskatchewan families is poor. Newfoundland is the only province in Canada with a higher rate.
In 1986, 42,600 Saskatchewan families were officially living in poverty, up from 36,900 in 1981. That is a 15.3 per cent increase. Add to this nearly 9,000 on-reserve Indian families who are not counted in the official surveys. Indian families in Saskatchewan, and I know across the country, are among the poorest of the poor.
One in every four Saskatchewan families with children under 16 earned less than $20,000 per year in 1986. In Saskatchewan, 64,560 children, or one child in every four, lives in poverty. In all of Canada one child in every six is growing up poor.
Between 1980 and 1986 the number of poor children in Saskatchewan increased by 12.8 per cent, even though the total number of children in the province declined by almost 4 per cent.
Nearly 70 per cent of Saskatchewan poor families live in single parent families headed by women.
Children make up 40 per cent of people receiving social assistance. The number of Saskatchewan children under 16 in families on welfare jumped by more than 50 per cent from 1981 to 1986. Since 1986 the social services
May 24, 1990

department in Saskatchewan no longer publishes this data. Children receiving benefits from the Indian affairs department are not included.
Public begging and private charity have been the major response of the Saskatchewan government to child hunger and family poverty in the province. Food bank use in Regina, Saskatoon and Prince Albert has jumped by 50 per cent in two years.
However, the number of people receiving government social assistance in those three cities has fallen by almost 10 per cent in that same period of time. Many people are simply being cut off welfare or denied eligibility and forced into the streets.
Obviously, for too many families in our province, their home situation is characterized by poverty, hunger and profound stress. The numbers indicate that Saskatchewan, as I mentioned, has the second highest level of family poverty in Canada, second only to Newfoundland. Across Canada the poverty rate for children has reached an astonishing 17 per cent-an intolerable situation.
I suspect the situation will only get worse. Current government programs and proposals are taking more away from the poor and middle-income Canadians, in turn creating more poverty, more malnourished and less cared for children.
Of course the whole process is doubly difficult on those living in northern and remote areas where this government has just eliminated or is proposing to eliminate existing tax benefits that will increase tax payable from Canadians in northern Canada by almost 100 per cent.
You are motioning that I am almost out of time, Mr. Speaker.
Our goal is to reduce or eliminate the need for abortion, to stop the wanton destruction of life yet to be, but legislative force will not stop abortion.
As a colleague of mine said recently: "You cannot legislate against fear and desperation. Only sanity and common sense will produce the desired results".
When we create a society which protects families, whether it is the extended families that so many of our ancestors preferred, two parent families which many of
Government Orders
us enjoy, or the single parent family which is becoming more prevalent throughout our country, then we protect the family from poverty, violence and hunger, then we protect the future of the countless yet unborn children.
Here in Canada we need a government willing to take its leadership role seriously. We need a government which is prepared to take a stand toward creating that caring society that is built on a platform of co-operation and hope. We do not need a government like we have witnessed that has brought in this bill today.
I am voting against this bill as I did at second reading because our responsibility is to the future. It is to the common good of all. If we are to prevent abortions, we have to care for the society we are developing for our children to grow up in.
The bill before us is an easy way out. I am not looking for the easy way out. I have seen what the easy way out does. The pictures that we have seen on our television screens of children in Romania who have been born into families that did not want them and ushered away into institutions and homes where they have been forced to live naked and alone is something that I do not believe we can allow to happen in Canada. Those images on the television screen haunt me daily.
Voting against this bill is step number one. The next step is the difficult step. The next step is the one that we have to take using a government that has the courage to create a society of which we can all be proud.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague who, incidentally, I want to note has been doing a tremendous job here in the House on a bill of rights for children. It is tremendous work that I greatly support. I believe that if the government were listening we would have a real start to correct some of the problems that are affecting our children across Canada and, as she mentions, in Saskatchewan.
The Saskatchewan situation is a doubly horrendous one, not just because there is lack of child care in the urban centres where a lot of families-and I use the word families here to mean two-parent families-are looking for child care where both parents need to work but, more important, in the large rural parts of the province where farm families are being forced to secure second incomes in order to stay on the farm. Second incomes have resulted in a number of different situations, situations where one spouse works the farm and also works off the farm. There are other situations in which both spouses are forced to work off the farm, creating a situation which is dangerous for children.
One of the things that I find absolutely incredible when I read the newspapers concerning some of these things concerns children who are killed on the farm by machinery. When one looks at these things one has a tendency to think that there is carelessness on the farm. But when one examines more closely what is happening, it is that parents are attempting to care for their child because they do not have any child care but get the job done on the farm.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, many people who work on the farm use both spouses, one to drive the combine and one to drive the truck. The children are left close by to watch carefully what has been going on. The next thing you know when the business at hand gets moving, a child is under the wheel of a combine, a tractor or a truck in the field.
It is a horrendous situation that could be corrected if there was full-time accessible child care in the rural areas of our country.
I want to mention in reaction to my colleague's question one other thing. Until recently the Saskatchewan Ombudsman was Dave Tickell, a person who worked constantly on the needs of Saskatchewan children in foster care homes. The Ombudsman who worked
for 10 years in the province of Saskatchewan warned constantly of the abuse and neglect of children who are in the care of the province.
I worked in the newspaper business before I became a member of Parliament and I talked to Saskatchewan Ombudsman, Mr. Tickell on many occasions. He consistently talked about the government's lack of desire to make any changes in the provincial foster care program. He said that the provincial government was ignoring the plight of children in foster homes who were complaining of emotional, physical and sexual abuse. He said that the policy of the provincial government offers foster children less protection from physical harm than that offered to children in day care centres, to young offenders in the care of the province, or even to the adult inmates of the provincial correctional centre.
Obviously, children in the province of Saskatchewan, in the eyes of the provincial government, are not and were not a priority for that government. Obviously, if we are going to take life seriously at at any level, we have to ensure that their care is ensured from day one. The provincial government of Saskatchewan had ignored that throughout its recent term of office.
I do not know if that completely answers my colleague's question, but I thank her for putting it. It allows me to expand a little further on what I had to say earlier. I very much appreciate the question she put.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: On questions or comments, the hon. member for Mission-Coquitlam.

I would like to thank my colleague for his answers to my questions. From the point of view of some of the comments that were made earlier today about the partisanship of this debate, I would like to ask him if he has thoughts in terms of how this debate has taken place in this House.

Again, I appreciate the question that was put by my hon. colleague. The debate today has been most interesting. Actually, the debate over the course of this entire time has been very interesting. I have found it most unusual in the sense of members rising to talk in a non-partisan way, yet at the same time through their actions being extremely partisan in the way in which all of this comes together.
May 24, 1990

The people in my constituency have often talked to me about New Democrats. They ask: "Why is it that New Democrats want to kill all these unborn babies?" In the same breath, they talk about the Conservatives and the Liberals wanting to save all the unborn in the country. It seems to me from the debate here that the members of both parties opposite have very clear, defined, distinct positions that are easily read. When we look at the Prime Minister's statements when he opened the debate some time ago, when we look at the statement of the Minister of Justice when she opened the debate earlier today, and when we look at the statements of the former leader of the Liberal party in the debate on second reading, we find very clear statements of opinion from the members of all parties.
I will be able to take the Hansard of this debate to my constituency and show throughout the constituency the official positions that have been taken by the members of the opposite parties.
I do not want to have to defend my party's position on every doorstep in my constituency when much of the debate has been along similar lines. I feel very strongly that when the next election rolls around, if this bill is in place, the debate will continue to be as strong and as difficult as it has been through this time.
The people who have been arguing strongly on both sides of this issue are obviously going to continue to speak as loudly and as strongly as they have in the course of this debate. That is something that I believe is not very healthy, not in the interests of Canada as a whole. If we are to get on and build the society that is necessary to achieve equitable goals, fairness for all, decisions that are based on all of the factors and not just a minute few, we have got to have a strong understanding statement from the government.
I do not believe that this bill offers it. I do not believe that this debate here today has provided us with that.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.
I look around me and it is with great dismay that I think it is important to say that it would appear that in this House there is not a quorum.

Point of order, Mr. Speaker.
